### Lab 02 discrepancies and import cautions

- **Server host:** PDF p. 6 gives `10.7.1.127`; PDF p. 11 gives `10.7.1.36/[DATABASE_NAME]`; both supplied Java files use `10.7.1.127/[DATABASE NAME]`. A 24 September 2026 reachability probe connected to `10.7.1.127:3306`, while `.36:3306` did not respond within three seconds; no university authentication or SQL was attempted.
- **Java filename:** PDF p. 11 names `JDBCIndex.java`, while the supplied official files are `JDBC.java` and `JDBCandIndex.java`.
- **SQL width:** `yeast_prosite.sql` declares `mmatch varchar(12)`, but static inspection finds 771 supplied non-`NULL` values longer than 12 characters, with a maximum of 89. The original is preserved; import errors/warnings depend on the actual server mode and must be inspected.
- **SQL bootstrap:** the dataset begins with unconditional `drop table Orf_Motif;`, which can report a missing-table error in a fresh schema.
- **Date mapping wording:** PDF p. 24 says `java.Date`; the mapping table on p. 25 specifies `java.sql.Date`. The lab note preserves the discrepancy and uses the fully qualified JDBC type shown in the table.
- **Performance:** the two official Task 1 Java files do not time the query or inspect a plan. The separate Task 2 solution times only `executeQuery`, compares logical results, and verifies `key=numIndex`; its one local timing pair is not a universal speedup, I/O, or physical B+ tree claim.

The two official Java files compile together with JDK 17 without Connector/J on the compile classpath. A separate [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Labs/Lab 02 - JDBC and Index/Solution/Lab2Solution.java|reference solution]] was compiled with JDK 17.0.18 and Connector/J 9.4.0 and executed against isolated local MySQL instances. Tasks 1.1 and 1.2 returned the same 607 final rows, and the indexed plan named `numIndex`. The released Task 2 run then measured 8.723 ms without the index and 2.083 ms with it, again returned the same 607 logical rows, and confirmed `EXPLAIN key=numIndex`. This did not authenticate to or execute SQL on the university server. The SQL contains one table definition with columns `orf`, `acc_num`, `num`, `pos`, `len`, and `mmatch`; 285 inserts use `NULL` for both `pos` and `mmatch`. Static parsing finds 614 `INSERT` statements with `num=7`, while later deletions produced 607 final matches in that controlled local import.

## Conventions and clarifications for Units 02–04

- **B+ tree order:** maximum internal child pointers; leaf capacity is one fewer key. Lecture 2b p. 4's leaf-root “children” wording is clarified as key entries. The root has its own minimum-occupancy exception.
- **B+ tree deletion:** follow the source's merge-first rule. Retained internal separators may be absent from leaves while still defining valid ranges (Lecture 2b pp. 9, 27, 32–33). The source does not prescribe a universal sibling preference when both are valid.
- **Height calculation:** the million-key, order-100 example has at most four visited index nodes under the course occupancy model. The displayed logarithm on Lecture 2b p. 11 is rounded; the chapter derives the bound and separates edges, node visits, cache effects and data-page reads.
- **Hash bit direction:** Lecture 3a reads high-order bits from the left; preserve leading zeros in fixed-width hashes. Directory size is $2^i$ pointers and physical buckets number **at most** $2^i$ (p. 13 uses a strict inequality that excludes the equality case).
- **Failed hash splits:** retain the course's rollback-before-overflow convention. The city case permits exactly two unsuccessful splits (pp. 32–40). Its initial Taiyuan is a real existing record; the new Taiyuan is another record with the same city name.
- **Hash-source ambiguities:** p. 5 repeats G in the J position and gives X as 25; punctuation/spacing encoding is unspecified. Page 11 shows index ID 33456 but a Gold row labelled 33465. Preserve source-local IDs; do not silently equate them. The department overflow example supplies no numeric hash or exact trial limit, so only its supported duplicate-key overflow result is claimed.
- **Vendor correction:** Lecture 3a p. 42's PostgreSQL statement is contradicted by [PostgreSQL 18's official on-disk hash-index documentation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/hash-index.html). The correction is supplementary; it does not identify the course DBMS. Other vendor mentions remain lecture context, not a verified current support matrix.
- **LSM deletion:** the slide's matching deletion/record removal is a simplified merge model. The new chapter explains why older unmerged versions must not be resurrected by prematurely discarding a tombstone.
- **Bloom estimates:** Lecture 3b p. 12's 10% and 1% are rounded estimates; the chapter derives approximately 9.52% and 0.819% under its stated model. The tiny lab deliberately uses different, correlated functions and reports its actual finite-domain result.
- **Time endpoints:** the slides do not fully specify interval inclusion. Unit 04 declares half-open intervals `[start,end)` for its worked queries; this remains an instructor-convention uncertainty rather than an asserted source rule.

Lecture 3b p. 6 names BigTable, Cassandra, MongoDB, SQLite4, LevelDB and MyRocks in its discussion of LSM-related systems. Those names are preserved here as source examples only; the supplied material does not establish a specific installed engine, version, or configuration. The new material teaches the depicted abstract mechanism rather than inferring identical current behaviour across those products.

The new Python 3.14.6 lab executed 98 bitmap predicate comparisons and 4356 spatial rectangle comparisons against direct predicates. Its observed output and limits are recorded with the unchanged script hash in staging. It makes no DBMS, disk-I/O or latency claim.

## How to use it

# Unit 01 — Physical storage, files and introductory indexes

[[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Tutor Mode/00 Start Here|Tutor Start]] · [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Tutor Mode/Unit 01 - Physical Storage/02 Recall and Exam Practice|Recall and practice]] · [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 01 - Physical Storage/01 Notes|Reference notes]] · [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 01 - Physical Storage/03 Lab|Reference lab]]

## In 60 Seconds

This unit explains how logical rows become physical records, how whole records fit into fixed-size blocks, and how file order and index density change the route to a record. The central ideas are:

1. a query ultimately needs pages, not isolated bytes;
2. unspanned capacity uses `floor(block size / item size)` before counting blocks;
3. clustered groups must be packed as groups when the question says they stay together;
4. a primary index follows physical file order, while dense/sparse describes coverage;
5. an index is useful only if its entries can lead to every required match.

After study, you should be able to calculate record and index blocks, trace a disk-read model, and justify an access path without inventing overhead or performance results.

## Concept Preview

> [!note] Page and buffer
> **Plain-language meaning:** the DBMS transfers a page/block and then reads records from the in-memory copy. A buffer hit avoids that data-page fetch.
>
> **Why it matters:** row count alone does not determine physical I/O.
>
> **Connects to:** record packing, file organisation and indexes.
>
> **Source:** `Lecture1b - Data Storage Structures.pdf`, PDF pp. 3–10.

> [!note] Blocking factor
> **Plain-language meaning:** the maximum number of whole, unspanned records that fit in one block.
>
> **Why it matters:** rounding in the wrong order changes every later result.
>
> **Connects to:** dense and sparse index sizing.
>
> **Source:** `Lecture1b - Data Storage Structures.pdf`, PDF pp. 16–18; Tutorial Q3–Q6.

> [!note] File organisation
> **Plain-language meaning:** the physical rule used to place records—heap, sequential, hashed or clustered.
>
> **Why it matters:** the same logical table can support very different access and maintenance costs.
>
> **Connects to:** primary indexes and range access.
>
> **Source:** `Lecture1b - Data Storage Structures.pdf`, PDF pp. 24–29.

> [!note] Dense and sparse indexes
> **Plain-language meaning:** dense coverage normally has an entry for every search-key occurrence/record; sparse coverage samples ordered data blocks.
>
> **Why it matters:** a sparse entry is safe only when the file order lets the search continue to every match.
>
> **Connects to:** primary versus secondary access paths.
>
> **Source:** `Lecture2a - Indexing Techniques (1).pdf`, PDF pp. 5–18.

## Exam Evidence Snapshot

| Topic | Observed papers | Known marks | Observed demand | Priority |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| Record/block packing and introductory index sizing/selection | 4/4 | 20 | calculate, discuss, justify | **HIGH EXAM RELEVANCE** |
| HDD timing, variable records and slotted pages | 0/4 | 0 observed | not observed | NOT OBSERVED IN AVAILABLE PAST-PAPER SAMPLE |

Evidence: [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Tutor Mode/_System/past-paper-intelligence#Source-supported aggregates|past-paper intelligence]]. Historical occurrence is not a prediction.

## Before You Start

You need integer division, ceilings and the distinction between a logical tuple and a physical record.

> [!question] Prerequisite check
> A 4096-byte block stores unspanned 350-byte records. Which operation determines records per block: floor or ceiling?

> [!success]- Check your answer
> Floor: $\lfloor4096/350\rfloor=11$. A twelfth record would cross the block boundary.
>
> Source: Tutorial Q3, `Lab1-Tutorial (1).pdf`, PDF p. 4.

## A motivating question

**Synthetic case using Tutorial Q3's physical model.** A registry has 25,000 fixed 350-byte records in 4096-byte blocks. Records are ordered by a 10-byte `student_ID`. A sparse primary-index entry is the 10-byte key plus a 10-byte pointer.

1. How many data blocks are required?
2. How many sparse entries and index blocks are required?
3. Why is the index sparse only because the file is ordered on the same search key?

**Success criteria:** keep records and entries unspanned, show both floor and ceiling steps, and explain the access invariant rather than reporting numbers alone.

| Question | Knowledge needed |
|---|---|
| Data blocks | blocking factor, ceiling of record demand |
| Index blocks | one sparse entry per data block, entry capacity |
| Correctness | physical order and candidate-block selection |

## Learn the mechanism

### From tuple to page fetch

A tuple is a logical row. Its encoded record lives inside a page/block. The buffer holds page copies in memory. On a buffer miss, the page is fetched; on a hit, the record can be read from the resident page. Index pages and data pages are separate costs unless a problem explicitly combines them.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Q["Row predicate"] --> A["Choose access path"]
    A --> I["Read index page(s), if used"]
    I --> D["Locate data block"]
    A --> D
    D --> B{"Data block buffered?"}
    B -->|no| F["Fetch block"]
    B -->|yes| R["Read record"]
    F --> R
```

**Figure 1 — A logical lookup becomes page work**

**Read it:** follow either the index route or direct file route; both converge on a data block.

**Key takeaway:** a short index does not prove a query is cheap when qualifying records occupy many scattered data pages.

**Provenance:** teaching construction from `Lecture1b`, PDF pp. 3–10, and `Lecture2a`, PDF pp. 5–18.

### Whole-record capacity

For block size $B$, record size $R$, and $N$ records:

$$bfr=\left\lfloor\frac{B}{R}\right\rfloor, \qquad b=\left\lceil\frac{N}{bfr}\right\rceil.$$

`bfr` is the blocking factor. Floor first because only whole records fit; ceiling second because a partially filled final block still occupies a block.

> [!warning] Pedagogical trap — dividing total bytes directly
> $\lceil NR/B\rceil$ permits unused bytes from one block to combine with another. That contradicts the unspanned-record condition whenever the remainder cannot hold another complete record.

### Groups that must stay together

Tutorial Q4 requires one 300-byte student and five 200-byte module records in the same block. The indivisible group is

$$G=300+5(200)=1300\text{ bytes}.$$

Then $\lfloor4096/1300\rfloor=3$ groups fit per block and $\lceil1000/3\rceil=334$ blocks are needed. Pooling all student and module bytes would violate the clustering constraint.

### Dense, sparse, primary and secondary are different axes

| Term | Decisive question |
|---|---|
| Primary index | Is the data file physically ordered by this search key? |
| Secondary index | Is the index on a different order from the data file? |
| Dense index | Is every search-key value represented, with a route to all records having that value? |
| Sparse index | Can representative entries select a block/range because the file order completes the search? |

A logical primary key need not be the primary **index** key. In Tutorial Q6 the file is ordered by the non-key `name`; an index following that physical order is primary in the lecture terminology.

### Index capacity

For key length $K$, pointer length $P$, and $E$ entries:

$$e=K+P,\qquad bfr_I=\left\lfloor\frac{B}{e}\right\rfloor,\qquad b_I=\left\lceil\frac{E}{bfr_I}\right\rceil.$$

For a sparse primary index in this course, $E$ is normally the number of data blocks. For a dense index, read the question: Tutorial Q4 explicitly requires one entry per student tuple.

### HDD read phases

The source model separates seek, rotational waiting and transfer:

$$T_{read}=T_{seek}+T_{rotation}+T_{transfer}.$$

Minimum, maximum and average cases choose different seek/rotation assumptions. Tutorial Q2 averages seek as half the stated maximum and rotation as half a revolution, while retaining the full transfer time. This is the course approximation, not a universal disk benchmark.

> [!question] Explain it yourself
> Why can a sparse index on unordered IDs miss a matching record even if every index entry is correct?

> [!success]- Check your explanation
> Sampling blocks works only when file order makes the selected block/range contain every possible match. Unordered IDs can occur outside that range.
>
> Source: `Lecture2a - Indexing Techniques (1).pdf`, PDF pp. 8–18; Tutorial Q6.

## Worked example — solve the motivating question

**Step 1 — Data records per block**

$$bfr=\lfloor4096/350\rfloor=11.$$

**Step 2 — Data blocks**

$$b=\lceil25000/11\rceil=\lceil2272.727\ldots\rceil=2273.$$

**Step 3 — Sparse entries**

One entry per data block gives $E=2273$ entries. Each entry is $10+10=20$ bytes.

**Step 4 — Index entries per block and index blocks**

$$bfr_I=\lfloor4096/20\rfloor=204,$$

$$b_I=\lceil2273/204\rceil=\lceil11.142\ldots\rceil=12.$$

**Interpretation:** the sparse index occupies 12 blocks and selects among 2273 ordered data blocks. A lookup still needs its index traversal and at least the candidate data block; cache state is unspecified.

**Source:** Tutorial Q3, `Lab1-Tutorial (1).pdf`, PDF p. 4; supplied answer, `Lab1-Tutorial_Answers.pdf`, PDF p. 8.

## Return to the motivating question

The answers are **2273 data blocks**, **2273 sparse entries**, and **12 index blocks**. The sparse design is correct because data blocks are sequentially ordered by `student_ID`; an entry representing a block identifies the candidate range, and the search continues within that block. Remove the order assumption and the same sampling no longer guarantees complete lookup.

## Definitions and distinctions

| Term A | Term B | Decisive distinction | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tuple | Record | logical row versus encoded physical representation | Lecture1b, pp. 3–4 |
| Page/block | Record | transfer/container unit versus one stored item | Lecture1b, pp. 7–10 |
| Primary key | Search key | logical uniqueness constraint versus lookup attribute(s) that may repeat | Lecture2a, pp. 5–7 |
| Dense index | Sparse index | direct complete coverage versus representative coverage relying on order | Lecture2a, pp. 8–18 |
| Primary index | Secondary index | follows physical file order versus indexes another order | Lecture2a, pp. 8–18 |

## Common confusions

- **Ceiling too early:** records per block uses floor; required blocks uses ceiling.
- **Invented overhead:** add page headers or slots only when supplied.
- **Logical key = physical order:** not necessarily.
- **Fewer index blocks = faster:** retrieval may still touch many data blocks.
- **Sparse = one entry per arbitrary block:** only safe with an ordering/routing invariant.

## Review

### Full Understanding

Return to [[#Learn the mechanism]] and [[#Worked example — solve the motivating question]].

## 5-Minute Review

1. Identify the indivisible item: record, clustered group or index entry.
2. Compute whole items per block with floor.
3. Compute blocks with ceiling.
4. Decide entry count from dense/sparse coverage.
5. Verify that physical order makes the access path complete.
6. Keep index-node, data-page and buffer assumptions separate.

## 60-Second Recall

- tuple → record → page → file
- buffer hit versus miss
- `floor(B/R)` then `ceil(N/bfr)`
- clustered group as indivisible item
- primary versus secondary
- dense versus sparse
- key bytes + pointer bytes
- seek + rotation + transfer

## Sources

- `Lecture1b - Data Storage Structures.pdf`, PDF pp. 2–29.
- `Lecture2a - Indexing Techniques (1).pdf`, PDF pp. 5–18. `(2)` is a byte-identical duplicate.
- `Lab1-Tutorial (1).pdf`, PDF pp. 2–8, and `Lab1-Tutorial_Answers.pdf`, cited answer pages.
- `SOE201-EXAMS.pdf`, inspected P23F/P23R/P24F/P24R question pages; see [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Tutor Mode/_System/past-paper-intelligence|intelligence]].

# Unit 01 — Recall and exam practice

[[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Tutor Mode/Unit 01 - Physical Storage/01 Tutor Notes|Tutor notes]] · [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 01 - Physical Storage/02 Exercises|Reference exercises]] · [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Tutor Mode/_System/past-paper-intelligence|Exam evidence]]

Attempt each item with references closed. Open the hint only if needed, then compare every reasoning step with the complete solution.

## Atomic recall

### Card 01 — What is the blocking factor for unspanned fixed records?

> [!success]- Answer
> $\lfloor\text{block size}/\text{record size}\rfloor$: the number of complete records that fit in one block.
>
> Source: Lecture1b, PDF pp. 16–18.

### Card 02 — Why is the final block count rounded upward?

> [!success]- Answer
> Any remaining record needs a real block even when that block is not full.
>
> Source: Lecture1b, PDF pp. 16–18.

### Card 03 — What makes an index primary in this course?

> [!success]- Answer
> Its search-key order matches the physical sequential order of the data file.
>
> Source: Lecture2a, PDF pp. 8–12.

### Card 04 — What does a dense index represent, and how are duplicate search-key values handled?

> [!success]- Answer
> Every search-key value in the data file has an index entry. Duplicate values must lead to all their matching records, for example via a run or pointer list. One entry per record is a particular layout, not the only dense layout.
>
> Source: Lecture2a, PDF pp. 8–18.

### Card 05 — What invariant makes a sparse primary index usable?

> [!success]- Answer
> Ordered data lets a representative entry select the block/range containing the target.
>
> Source: Lecture2a, PDF pp. 8–18.

### Card 06 — What is an index entry's basic size here?

> [!success]- Answer
> Search-key bytes plus pointer bytes, unless the source explicitly supplies additional overhead.
>
> Source: Tutorial Q3–Q6.

### Card 07 — What are the HDD read-time phases?

> [!success]- Answer
> Seek time, rotational waiting and transfer time.
>
> Source: Tutorial Q1–Q2; Lecture1b, PDF pp. 11–15.

### Card 08 — Why can one page fetch serve several rows?

> [!success]- Answer
> Several rows may share the fetched page, which remains available while buffered.
>
> Source: Lecture1b, PDF pp. 7–10.

### Card 09 — One 300-byte student and its five 200-byte module records must stay together. What group size must the block-capacity calculation use, and why?

> [!success]- Answer
> One 300-byte student record together with its five 200-byte module records: a 1300-byte group.
>
> Source: Tutorial Q4, PDF pp. 5–6.

### Card 10 — Why does a small index not prove a cheap query?

> [!success]- Answer
> Qualifying records may still occupy many scattered data pages; cache and clustering are unspecified.
>
> Source: Lecture2a, PDF pp. 5–18.

## Guided → independent → transfer practice

> [!danger] HIGH EXAM RELEVANCE
> Record/block packing and introductory index sizing/selection appear in 4/4 inspected papers, with 20 known observed marks. This is a study priority, not a prediction.

### Practice 1 — Complete the packing method

**SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE.** A file has 12,000 unspanned 180-byte records and 4096-byte blocks. Calculate record capacity and required blocks.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Compute whole records per block before dividing the record count.

> [!success]- Solution
> **Capacity:** $\lfloor4096/180\rfloor=22$ records because $22(180)=3960$ and $23(180)=4140>4096$.
>
> **Blocks:** $\lceil12000/22\rceil=\lceil545.45\ldots\rceil=546$.
>
> **Interpretation:** the last block is partially filled. Directly dividing total bytes by 4096 would incorrectly combine unusable fragments across blocks.
>
> Source principles: Lecture1b, PDF pp. 16–18.

### Practice 2 — Size a sparse index

**SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE.** The file in Practice 1 is ordered by an 8-byte search key. One sparse entry per data block uses that key and an 8-byte pointer. Calculate entries per index block and index blocks.

> [!tip]- Hint
> There are as many sparse entries as data blocks from Practice 1.

> [!success]- Solution
> Entry size is $8+8=16$ bytes. Capacity is $\lfloor4096/16\rfloor=256$ entries per index block.
>
> There are 546 entries, so $\lceil546/256\rceil=3$ index blocks.
>
> The result depends on the file being ordered by this search key. Without that order, one representative per block would not create a complete search route.
>
> Source principles: Lecture2a, PDF pp. 8–18.

> [!danger] HIGH EXAM RELEVANCE
> The following preserves the source data of Tutorial Q3, a pattern closely matching repeated historical questions.

### Practice 3 — ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE: Tutorial Q3

For 25,000 unspanned 350-byte student records in 4096-byte blocks, calculate data blocks. Then size a sparse primary index on a 10-byte `student_ID` with a 10-byte pointer.

**Source:** `Lab1-Tutorial (1).pdf`, PDF p. 4, Q3.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Use four stages: data capacity → data blocks → index-entry capacity → index blocks.

> [!success]- Solution
> Data capacity: $\lfloor4096/350\rfloor=11$ records/block.
>
> Data blocks: $\lceil25000/11\rceil=2273$.
>
> Sparse entries: one per data block, so 2273.
>
> Entry size: $10+10=20$ bytes; index capacity $\lfloor4096/20\rfloor=204$.
>
> Index blocks: $\lceil2273/204\rceil=12$.
>
> The file is ordered by `student_ID`, so a representative entry can select the candidate data block.
>
> Answer source: `Lab1-Tutorial_Answers.pdf`, PDF p. 8.

### Practice 4 — Diagnose a tempting shortcut

**SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE.** A student claims Tutorial Q4 needs $\lceil(1000\cdot300+5000\cdot200)/4096\rceil=318$ blocks. Diagnose the error and calculate the source-compliant answer.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Identify the indivisible physical group before using the block size.

> [!success]- Solution
> The shortcut pools byte fragments across unrelated blocks and breaks the rule that each student and exactly five module records reside in the same block.
>
> One group is $300+5(200)=1300$ bytes. A block holds $\lfloor4096/1300\rfloor=3$ groups. Therefore $\lceil1000/3\rceil=334$ blocks.
>
> Source: Tutorial Q4, `Lab1-Tutorial (1).pdf`, PDF pp. 5–6; answer PDF p. 11.

### Practice 5 — Independent access-path decision

**SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE.** A file is physically ordered by `surname`, which repeats. Queries ask for every row with one surname and for exact `student_ID` values. Explain which of these claims is defensible: (a) a sparse surname index can select the first candidate block and scan the run; (b) a sparse `student_ID` index is automatically complete; (c) a dense `student_ID` secondary index can cover every ID.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Separate physical order from logical uniqueness, then test complete coverage.

> [!success]- Solution
> (a) is defensible if duplicate surname runs are kept in physical order and the index can reach the run's beginning.
>
> (b) is not defensible: IDs are unordered in the file, so block sampling can miss matches.
>
> (c) is defensible when the dense secondary index has an entry/pointer for every required record or unique ID.
>
> Source principles: Lecture2a, PDF pp. 8–18; Tutorial Q6.

### Practice 6 — Transfer to a storage-group constraint

**SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE.** An order and its four 240-byte line items must remain in one 4096-byte block. The order record is 320 bytes. There are 2500 orders. Calculate blocks and explain why a byte-stream calculation is invalid.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Treat each order plus its four lines as one unspanned item.

> [!success]- Solution
> Group size is $320+4(240)=1280$ bytes. Capacity is $\lfloor4096/1280\rfloor=3$ groups per block.
>
> Blocks are $\lceil2500/3\rceil=834$.
>
> A byte-stream calculation would move line items into spare space belonging to another block and violate the co-location constraint.
>
> Source principle: Tutorial Q4's clustered-group model, PDF pp. 5–6. Values are synthetic.

The approved ordinary edition contains complete worked solutions for all supplied Tutorial 1 questions:

No official marking scheme is supplied. Check whether an answer: identifies the indivisible item, uses floor then ceiling, preserves stated constraints, sizes entries explicitly, and explains why the access path is complete.

# Physical Storage & File Organisation

**SOE201 · Unit 01**  
From logical rows to physical pages—and the cost of finding them.

[[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/SOE201 - Advanced Database Development|Course home]] · [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 01 - Physical Storage/02 Exercises|Practise]] · [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 01 - Physical Storage/03 Lab|Try the lab]]

## Unit Roadmap

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Pages and buffers"] --> B["Storage and I/O"]
    B --> C["Record layouts"]
    C --> D["Page updates"]
    D --> E["File organisation"]
    E --> F["Index access"]
    classDef default fill:#E6F3F1,stroke:#117D83,color:#172B42,stroke-width:1.5px;
```

> [!abstract] What You Will Be Able to Do
> - Explain when a logical lookup causes a physical page fetch.
> - Separate seek, rotational wait, and transfer costs.
> - Calculate space for whole records, related groups, and index entries.
> - Trace deletion, insertion, and compaction while preserving valid references.
> - Justify file organisation and index coverage for a stated workload.
> - Interpret the SQLite lab's results without inferring unmeasured performance.

## Topic overview

A database stores **records in pages**, arranges those pages into files, and uses access structures to find the right data. This unit connects the layout of bytes with space, reads, insertions, and deletions.

| Learn to… | Start here |
|---|---|
| Explain where a lookup's cost comes from | [[#From rows to pages and the buffer]] · [[#HDD geometry and read phases]] |
| Calculate storage without losing whole-record constraints | [[#Fixed-length records and blocking factor]] |
| Trace records as they grow, move, or disappear | [[#Variable-length records]] · [[#Slotted pages and stable references]] |
| Choose an organisation for a workload | [[#File organisations]] |
| Size an index and explain how it finds a record | [[#Introductory indexes]] |
| Revise the tutorial calculations | [[#Worked examples]] · [[#Exam-style summary]] |

**Scope:** Lecture1b, PDF pp. 2–29; introductory indexing from Lecture2a, PDF pp. 5–18; Tutorial 1, Q1–Q6. B+ tree balancing and hashing algorithms are outside this unit. You need rows, attributes, keys, basic SQL, and integer division.

> [!info] Key Idea — Keep the model explicit
> Tutorial records and index entries are ==unspanned==, with maximum packing and no invented overhead. Count overhead when a question explicitly supplies it. The HDD question transfers ==16 384 bytes== per block; the file-sizing questions use ==4096-byte blocks==. These are separate cases.
>
> The course DBMS and dialect are unconfirmed. The optional SQLite lab demonstrates logical behaviour; it does not reproduce the tutorial's physical layout.

## Why this matters

Imagine a university registry during registration week. Staff need quick student lookups, address updates, ordered reports, and student-plus-module information. Each task favours different properties:

| Task | Storage question |
|---|---|
| Find one student | How many pages must be located and fetched? |
| Store new registrations | Where can new records fit, and what must be maintained? |
| Change a long address | Can the record grow without invalidating references? |
| Read a student and five modules | Would keeping related records together save data-page fetches? |
| Produce an ordered report | Does logical order also provide physical locality? |

A good design explains **space, access, and maintenance together**. Fewer index pages alone do not prove faster queries.

## Key concepts

Follow the storage path from a logical row to its page, then examine how records and access structures change.

### From rows to pages and the buffer

A query asks for rows; storage retrieves the pages that contain them.

A **schema** defines attributes and constraints; a **tuple** is a logical row. A physical **record** contains the encoded fields, and a ==page/block== holds records. A file groups pages. Databases also need metadata, statistics, indexes, and logs, which are outside a tutorial count of data blocks.[^logical][^architecture]

| Aspect | Logical view | Physical view |
|---|---|---|
| Unit of data | Tuple and attribute | Record and encoded field |
| Grouping | Relation | File and pages |
| Lookup | A requested row | An access path plus buffer state |

A ==primary key== is a logical unique, non-null identifier; a **search key** is an attribute set used for lookup and may repeat. A foreign key connects a child value to a referenced key. DDL declares structures; DML reads or changes their contents.

> [!note] Definition
> A ==buffer== holds page copies in memory. A **hit** uses a resident page; a **miss** requires fetching it. A **dirty page** has changes not yet reflected in its persistent copy.[^buffer]

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Locate required page"] --> B{"In buffer?"}
    B -->|"Hit"| C["Read record in memory"]
    B -->|"Miss"| D["Fetch page into a frame"]
    D --> C
    C --> E{"Changed?"}
    E -->|"Yes"| F["Mark dirty; later writeback"]
    E -->|"No"| G["Read complete"]
    classDef default fill:#E6F3F1,stroke:#117D83,color:#172B42,stroke-width:1.5px;
```

**Figure 1 — A logical request meets the buffer**

**Read it:** choose the hit or miss branch before reading the record.

### Storage hierarchy and units

Before comparing costs, identify both the storage layer and the unit being transferred.

| Layer in the course model | Examples | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Primary | Cache, main memory | Fast working copies; volatile in this model |
| Secondary | Flash, magnetic disk | Persistent database storage |
| Tertiary | Optical storage, tape | Archival storage |

The course hierarchy describes roles, not current hardware prices or a rule covering every memory technology.[^media] **1 byte = 8 bits; 1 KiB = 1024 bytes.** Thus 4096 bytes = 4 KiB, while four 4096-byte sectors = 16 KiB. A disk transfer block, a DBMS page, a NAND page, and a NAND erase block are different objects.[^blocks]

Larger pages may reduce transfer counts but also bring unwanted data into memory or waste space. Keep the ==unit and storage layer== explicit.

### HDD geometry and read phases

Reaching the right track and reaching the right sector are separate operations.

A **platter** is a disk with recording surfaces. Each surface has circular **tracks**, divided into **sectors**. A ==cylinder== groups tracks of equal radius across surfaces.[^hdd]

![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 01 - Physical Storage/Attachments/figure-02-hdd-geometry.svg]]

**Figure 2 — Platter, track, sector, cylinder**

**Read it:** follow the highlighted ring; the highlighted arcs across the stack share its radius.  
**Key takeaway:** moving to a track is radial positioning; reaching a sector also depends on angular position. The geometry is schematic.

| Phase | What happens | Symbol |
|---|---|---|
| ==Seek time== | Move the head to the required track | $T_s$ |
| ==Rotational wait== (latency) | Wait for the starting sector | $T_w$ |
| ==Transfer time== | Read all requested sectors | $T_t$ |

#### Formula — Read time

For $r$ revolutions/minute, $S$ sectors/track, and $q$ contiguous sectors/block:

$$
T_r=\frac{60\,000}{r}\text{ ms},\qquad T_t=\frac{q}{S}T_r,\qquad
T_{\text{read}}=T_s+T_w+T_t.
$$

| Symbol | Meaning | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| $T_r$ | Time for one revolution | ms |
| $T_s$, $T_w$, $T_t$ | Seek, rotational wait, transfer | ms |

> [!info] Interpretation
> Transfer occupies the fraction $q/S$ of one revolution. Faster rotation reduces the rotation and transfer terms in this model; seek remains a separate input.

![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 01 - Physical Storage/Attachments/figure-03-read-phases.svg]]

**Figure 3 — Position first, then transfer the complete block**

**Read it:** compare the worst-case and course-average bars; transfer has the same duration.  
**Key takeaway:** averaging the positioning costs does not halve the number of sectors read. Segment widths are schematic; the labels give the times.

We use **total read time**, including transfer. The textbook's “access time” ends when transfer begins; the lecture also allows a definition including transfer.[^timing] Uniform angular arrival gives half a revolution on average. The tutorial additionally approximates average seek as ==half the maximum==; that is a course convention, not a universal probability law.[^q2-answers]

> [!info]- Optional depth — why an average needs a model
> For independent continuous uniform positions $X,Y$ across a span of $L$ tracks,
> $$\mathbb{E}|X-Y|=\frac{2}{L^2}\int_0^L\int_0^x(x-y)\,dy\,dx=\frac{L}{3}.$$
> A positive-distance seek model $1+d/1000$ ms would then give approximately $1+L/3000$ ms. This alternative is **not substituted** for the tutorial's half-maximum convention.

**Elevator scheduling.** The lecture's policy serves pending requests in one direction, then reverses when none remain in that direction.[^elevator] Starting at 40, moving upwards:

| Current head | Next request | Movement | Pending after service |
|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 40 | 45 | 5 tracks | 10, 20, 70 |
| 45 | 70 | 25 tracks | 10, 20 |
| 70 | 20 | 50 tracks | 10 |
| 20 | 10 | 10 tracks | None |

The path is **40 → 45 → 70 → 20 → 10**, totalling **90 tracks**. Under $1+d/1000$ ms per positive seek, its seek component is $4+90/1000=4.09$ ms. Rotation and transfer are additional. Some scheduling variants travel to the physical disk end before reversing; they require a different trace. Sequential reads can exploit proximity, but this is not a measured timing guarantee.[^sequential-book]

### SSDs, mirroring, and striping

Different mechanisms change access costs, placement, and protection against failure.

NAND flash has no mechanical seek or rotation. It still has read, program, transfer, controller, and reclamation costs. Programming and erasing operate at different granularities: pages are programmed, while groups of pages form ==erase blocks==. A translation layer may remap logical addresses.[^ssd][^flash-book]

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Logical page L maps to X"] --> B["Program new content into erased Y"]
    B --> C["Remap L to Y; X becomes obsolete"]
    C --> D["Later: move live pages, erase old block"]
    classDef default fill:#E6F3F1,stroke:#117D83,color:#172B42,stroke-width:1.5px;
```

**Figure 4 — A logical overwrite can change physical location**

**Read it:** L keeps its logical identity while X and Y are physical locations.  
**Key takeaway:** deleting a row need not immediately erase a NAND page. This diagram does not prescribe crash-safe ordering.

![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 01 - Physical Storage/Attachments/figure-05-mirroring-striping.svg]]

**Figure 5 — Copies versus distribution**

**Read it:** identical page labels denote copies; different labels denote different data.  
**Key takeaway:** a mirror can retain data after one device fails under the shown assumptions; striping alone cannot.[^raid]

| Mechanism | What it provides | Limit to remember |
|---|---|---|
| Striping | Independent devices may work concurrently | No exact speedup is guaranteed |
| Mirroring | Redundancy against some failures | A mistaken deletion can propagate to every mirror; no exact speedup is guaranteed |

**Key distinction:** ==redundancy== is not historical recovery or backup.

> [!question] Before continuing
> Can two row requests cause just one data-page fetch? Would replacing the HDD with an SSD make every remaining access cost disappear?

> [!success]- Check
> Yes, if both rows share a page that remains buffered. An SSD removes mechanical seek and rotation, but electronic access, controller work, transfer, and possible reclamation remain.

### Fixed-length records and blocking factor

The first question is how many complete records fit in one page.

In ==fixed-length== storage, every record in the model occupies $R$ bytes. **Unspanned** means each record stays within one page; **spanned** storage permits a record to continue across pages and needs an appropriate continuation representation.[^records]

| Aspect | ==Unspanned== | ==Spanned== |
|---|---|---|
| Page boundary | A record stays within one page | A record may continue across pages |
| Leftover tail | Cannot complete a record on another page | May hold a fragment under the chosen representation |
| Model used here | Tutorial capacity calculations | Contrast only; continuation overhead is unspecified |

![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 01 - Physical Storage/Attachments/figure-06-blocking-and-spanning.svg]]

**Figure 6 — Why leftover bytes do not combine across unspanned pages**

**Read it:** the twelfth record needs 350 bytes but the tail has only 246.  
**Key takeaway:** calculate whole records per page before counting pages. The spanned alternative illustrates a different model; its continuation overhead is not specified.

#### Formula — Whole-record capacity

Let $N$ be records, $B$ bytes/page, $H$ fixed overhead/page, and $U=B-H$ usable bytes:

$$
\boxed{f=\left\lfloor\frac{U}{R}\right\rfloor}
\qquad
\boxed{b=\left\lceil\frac{N}{f}\right\rceil}
\qquad
w=U-fR.
$$

> [!info] Interpretation
> Capacity changes in whole-record steps. More usable space helps only when another complete record fits; any remaining records still need another page.

- $f$: ==blocking factor== — whole records/page, because $fR\leq U$.
- $b$: required data pages, because $bf\geq N$.
- $w$: residual bytes in a maximally packed page.

**Check the model before calculating:**

- Use $H=0$ for the tutorial unless overhead is supplied. Do not count a record header twice if already included in $R$.
- The formula assumes $N\geq0$ and $0<R\leq U$.
- If $R>U$, the unspanned representation cannot store even one record; do not divide by $f=0$.
- Zero records imply zero data pages in this model, not a zero-byte database.

> [!tip] Exam Tip — Round according to the constraint
> ==Floor== capacity; ==ceiling== demand. First find how many complete objects fit. Then allocate enough complete pages for all objects. The object might be a record, a whole related group, or an index entry.

### Deletion and free lists

Deleting a record is useful only if its space can be found and reused.

A ==free list== links reusable fixed-size record positions from a header pointer. Each free position stores the next link.[^free-list] In this teaching example, deletion adds a slot at the front.

![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 01 - Physical Storage/Attachments/figure-07-free-list.svg]]

**Figure 7 — Delete slot 3, then reuse it**

**Read it:** follow the header through free slots; occupied slots are outside the chain.  
**Key takeaway:** ==save a free slot's successor== before overwriting its bytes. Other occupied records need not move.

A deleted flag marks a hole but does not efficiently locate it. A free list helps discover space; it does not preserve a sequential file's key order or guarantee that a variable-length record fits. Affected indexes still need maintenance. The sequence shown is a logical trace, not a concurrent or crash-recovery protocol.

### Variable-length records

When a field grows, the record must still describe where its fields begin and end.

> [!note] Definition
> If field lengths vary, a fixed prefix can store ==(offset, length)== pairs. A field offset is relative to the **record start**. A ==null bitmap== distinguishes a missing value from a present empty string.[^variable][^variable-book]

| Aspect | Fixed-length records | ==Variable-length records== |
|---|---|---|
| Size in the model | Every record occupies $R$ bytes | Field values can change the record length |
| Finding fields | Predetermined boundaries | Offset/length descriptors in the illustrated layout |
| Growth | Must fit the chosen representation | May require new space and updated offsets |

| Question | Metadata to consult |
|---|---|
| Where are the field's bytes, and how long are they? | The field's `(offset, length)` descriptor |
| Is the value missing rather than a present empty string? | The null bitmap |

![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 01 - Physical Storage/Attachments/figure-08-record-layouts.svg]]

**Figure 8 — Fixed fields and variable-field descriptors**

**Read it:** follow each descriptor to its bytes.  
**Key takeaway:** an unchanged offset can still need a new length; growth must also fit in the containing page. Widths are schematic; the variable example assumes a 16-byte prefix and one byte per character.

In the example, `Ana` occupies bytes 16–18. Changing `Hall` to `Hall-B` changes the address pair from `(19,4)` to `(19,6)` and the total record length from 23 to 25 bytes. If the *name* instead grows by two bytes, the following address begins at 21. Character count is not generally byte count.

The lecture's `instructor` example uses three 4-byte pairs at bytes 0–11: `ID` `(21,5)`, `name` `(26,10)`, and `department` `(36,10)`. `salary` uses bytes 12–19, and the null bitmap is at 20. The last field ends at byte 45, so the total is **46 bytes**. These are that figure's encoding assumptions, not a universal format.[^variable][^variable-book]

### Slotted pages and stable references

A small directory lets record bytes move without rewriting every surviving reference.

> [!note] Definition
> A ==slotted page== has a header, a directory of record locations and lengths, free space, and record bytes. Referencing a record through **(page, slot)** lets its bytes move *within the page* while its slot stays stable.[^slotted][^slotted-book]

#### Formula — Page free space

For $n$ allocated slots of $s$ bytes each—including ==retained deleted slots==—the free space after compaction is:

$$
F=B-H-ns-\sum_{i\in\mathrm{live}}R_i.
$$

> [!info] Interpretation
> Both live records and allocated slots consume page space. Deleting a record releases its payload bytes; retaining its slot keeps the directory cost.

| Insertion situation | Free bytes required |
|---|---:|
| Allocate a new slot | $R_{\mathrm{new}}+s$ |
| Reuse a retained slot | $R_{\mathrm{new}}$ |

![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 01 - Physical Storage/Attachments/figure-09-slotted-page.svg]]

**Figure 9 — Delete, compact, reuse**

**Read it:** left-to-right bars show byte order; track record C and slot 2 through compaction.  
**Key takeaway:** contiguous free space grows when C moves, while updating slot 2 keeps surviving references valid. Intervals are half-open: `[start,end)` has length `end − start`; directory widths are enlarged for readability.

> [!warning] Common Mistake — Counting only record bytes
> **Wrong:** If the page has enough free bytes for the record, insertion must fit.
>
> **Why it fails:** Total free bytes may be fragmented; contiguous free bytes may be smaller. A new slot also consumes space, and a retained deleted slot still occupies directory bytes.
>
> **Correct idea:** Check a ==usable extent== and include any directory growth.

**Reference limits:**

- Compaction does not preserve the identity of a **deleted record** when its slot is reused.
- Moving a record to **another page** needs additional reference handling.
- A **raw byte pointer** becomes stale when its record moves.

Immediate compaction is the course's explanatory model, not every DBMS's deletion policy.

> [!question] Before continuing
> When C moves during compaction, what must change so that `(page, slot 2)` still finds it? Why does a deleted-but-retained slot still count toward page occupancy?

> [!success]- Check
> Update slot 2 to C's new offset. The directory entry remains allocated even when its record is deleted, so its bytes remain part of the page's occupied space.

### File organisations

Choose what should stay together: free space, nearby keys, or related records.

| Organisation | Layout and access | Update cost or trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| ==Heap== | No record ordering; use free space where available | Easy placement; searches need a scan or suitable complete index |
| ==Sequential / ordered== | Records follow a search-key order | Good ordered locality; insertion may need movement or overflow |
| ==Multitable clustering== | Related records from different relations share pages | Helps grouped access; single-relation scans fetch other relation bytes |
| B+ tree / hashing | Named alternatives in the lecture taxonomy | Their algorithms are deferred beyond this unit |

These are the course's layout concepts.[^file-organisations] Choose using query frequency, ranges, joins, insertions, memory, and maintenance—not a universal ranking.

#### Heap free-space map

A map advertises approximate available space per page; a higher level can summarise groups with their maximum.[^heap] With illustrative buckets `[1,4,0,2]`, a group maximum of 4 directs a request needing 3/8 of a page toward the page with bucket 4. The actual page must still be checked.

For the teaching rule $v=\min(7,\lfloor8F/B\rfloor)$, a 4096-byte page with 2100 free bytes has bucket 4. Inserting 1536 bytes, including any slot cost, leaves 564 bytes and bucket 1; the group maximum becomes 2. Stale maps or fragmentation may require retrying or compaction. This rounding rule is illustrative, not a specified course implementation.

![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 01 - Physical Storage/Attachments/figure-10-file-organisations.svg]]

**Figure 10 — Three ways to organise records**

**Read it:** distinguish physical boxes from the logical chain in the ordered example.  
**Key takeaway:** order, free-space discovery, and locality solve different problems. The small page capacities are teaching assumptions.

#### Sequential insertion and reorganisation

Into full pages `[10,14,19]` and `[23,28,35]`, insert 16 by allocating an overflow record, setting its successor to 19, then redirecting 14 to 16. The logical sequence is now **10 → 14 → 16 → 19 → 23 → 28 → 35**. An ordered scan must include ==overflow==.[^sequential]

Reorganisation rewrites the sequence into `[10,14,16]`, `[19,23,28]`, `[35]`, with affected references and indexes repaired. It restores locality at the cost of reads and writes. On a **separate branch from the post-insertion state**, delete 19 by saving successor 23, redirecting `16.next` to 23, and reclaiming 19 under the free-space policy. Do not mix this branch with the seven-record reorganisation result.

#### Multitable clustering

Keep one `student(sID, ...)` record with its five related `module(sID, ...)` records. `module.sID` references the student's key; the module record's own key is unspecified. Tutorial Q4 requires all six records in the same block, so pack ==whole groups==.[^clustering][^q4]

#### Formula — Whole-group capacity

$G$ is bytes/group, $R_s$ and $R_m$ are bytes/student and bytes/module, $m$ is modules/student, and $N_s$ is the number of student groups.

$$
G=R_s+mR_m,\qquad f_G=\lfloor B/G\rfloor,\qquad b_G=\lceil N_s/f_G\rceil.
$$

> [!info] Interpretation
> More child records make each group larger. The packing unit is the entire related group, so leftover bytes cannot be pooled across pages to complete it.

With variable child counts, group lengths vary even if each record type has fixed length. A student with 25 modules would need $300+25(200)=5300$ bytes, violating a 4096-byte one-page requirement. Per-relation pointer chains can skip module records logically during a student-only scan, but fetched pages still contain their bytes.

### Introductory indexes

An index must provide a complete route from the requested value to every matching record.

An ==index entry== stores a search-key value and a pointer. Ordered indexes sort search values; hash indexes map them to buckets without preserving key order.[^index-key][^ordered-hash]

| File-order category | Meaning in this course | Distinction |
|---|---|---|
| ==Primary index== | Index on the file's ordering key | Different from the relational primary-key constraint |
| Secondary index | Index on a different key | Sorting its directory does not make unordered data suitable for simple sparse lookup |

| Aspect | ==Dense index== | ==Sparse index== |
|---|---|---|
| Coverage | Every search-key value; all matching records must be reachable | Selected representatives; default here is one per data block |
| Entry count | Depends on the duplicate representation | Depends on the representative rule |
| Absence reasoning | No matching entry can establish absence when coverage is complete | No matching representative does not establish absence from the data |

The slides also use clustering/clustered and non-clustering/non-clustered as aliases for primary and secondary. Product terminology can differ. Multitable clustering is a related-record layout, not the same definition.[^index-types]

![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 01 - Physical Storage/Attachments/figure-11-index-coverage.svg]]

**Figure 11 — When sparse lookup works, and when sampling fails**

**Read it:** for target 28 choose the largest block minimum ≤ 28; compare the missing route to ID 20 below.  
**Key takeaway:** sparse lookup needs a valid continuation rule in the underlying file, not merely sorted sampled index entries.[^sparse]

For ==unique keys== and **block-minimum representatives**, choose the largest representative **≤ K** and inspect that block. With representatives 10, 23, 40:

| Target | Candidate and result |
|---:|---|
| 23 | Choose D1 directly; equality matters |
| 9 | Below the first minimum: absent |
| 39 | Search D1; absent before next minimum 40 |
| 99 | Search D2 to its end; absent |

The slide uses `< K` followed by a forward scan. That can work with proper first-key handling; it is not universally wrong. Our `≤ K` rule directly chooses the target block under the stated assumptions. Duplicate runs spanning pages need adaptation.

#### Duplicate values and complete coverage

Name-ordered `[Ana,id7] [Ana,id2] [Bo,id9]` can use one value entry for `Ana` pointing to its first occurrence, then scan its contiguous run. On an ID-ordered file, a secondary name index can instead use `Ana → {id2 location, id7 location}`. Count any pointer-bucket storage separately.[^dense] Q4 explicitly requires one dense entry ==per student tuple==; that local rule controls its calculation.

A complete dense index can establish absence when no entry matches. A sparse directory cannot: 28 is absent from the directory but present in D1.

#### Formula — Index capacity

For $K_b$ key bytes, $P_b$ pointer bytes, and $n_I$ entries, with no extra overhead:

$$
E=K_b+P_b,\qquad f_I=\lfloor B/E\rfloor,\qquad b_I=\lceil n_I/f_I\rceil.
$$

> [!info] Interpretation
> Decide what one entry represents before counting entries. A sparse directory may use fewer entries, but that space saving is useful only if the access path remains complete.

#### Index maintenance

- **Changed indexed value:** remove its old entry/pointer and add its new one consistently with the data change.
- **Insertion or deletion:** index entries and page allocation can change.
- **Deleted block minimum:** its sparse representative can change; deleting a non-minimum may leave it unchanged.
- **Empty page:** remove or redirect its entry.
- **Unindexed field update without record movement:** an index may remain unchanged.[^index-metrics]

#### Multilevel directories

A small outer index can describe the pages of an inner ordered index.[^multilevel]

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Outer index: 1 page, 12 entries"] -->|"Choose one inner page"| B["Inner sparse index: 12 pages"]
    B -->|"Choose one data page"| C["Registry: 2273 data pages"]
    classDef default fill:#E6F3F1,stroke:#117D83,color:#172B42,stroke-width:1.5px;
```

**Figure 12 — A directory over a directory**

**Read it:** follow one selected page at each level.  
**Key takeaway:** a cold lookup on this path uses three fetches; with the outer page resident it needs two more. This extension has **13 index pages**, while Q3's requested single-level index has **12**.

A secondary-index scan may jump among scattered data pages while a primary-index scan follows nearby ones. This locality argument depends on the access pattern and buffer; neither index size nor correct results alone establishes a speedup. ### Example 2 — HDD timing · Q1–Q2

> [!example] Worked Example — HDD timing · Q1–Q2
> **Given**
>
> - **16 384 tracks/surface**; **128 sectors/track**; **4096 bytes/sector**.
> - **7200 rpm**; four contiguous sectors per transfer block; **no gaps**.
> - For positive distance $d$, seek time is $1+d/1000$ ms; **no movement costs zero seek time** in the best case.[^q1][^q2]
>
> **Find** · Calculate the seek cases and the best, approximate worst, and course-average read times.
>
> **Method** · Keep seek, rotational wait, and full-block transfer separate; state the distance convention.
>
> **Calculation and answer**
>
> **One-track seek:** $1+1/1000=1.001$ ms. The answer sheet uses 16 384 as the end-to-end distance, yielding **17.384 ms**. Literally, 16 384 track centres have 16 383 gaps, yielding **17.383 ms**. State which convention you use.[^q1-answer]
>
> $$
> T_r=60\,000/7200=8.333333\ldots\text{ ms},\qquad
> T_t=(4/128)T_r=0.2604167\text{ ms}.
> $$
>
> | Read case | Seek + wait + full transfer | Total |
> |---|---|---:|
> | Best | $0+0+0.2604167$ | **0.2604 ms** |
> | Approximate worst | $17.384+8.3333333+0.2604167$ | **25.9778 ms** |
> | Course average | $17.384/2+8.3333333/2+0.2604167$ | ==13.1191 ms== |
>
> A near-full revolution is the worst rotational bound. The published answer rounds intermediate values to 17.38, 8.33, and 0.2603, producing about **25.9703** and **13.1153 ms**. Retaining precision until the end explains the difference; it does not change the model.[^q2-answers]

### Example 3 — Page insertion and compaction

> [!example] Worked Example — Page insertion and compaction
> **Given — teaching assumptions**
>
> - **4096-byte page**; **64-byte header**; **three 8-byte slots**.
> - Records: **A = 600 bytes**, **B = 800**, **C = 1000**.
> - Records are packed **from the end downwards**.
>
> **Find** · Decide what fits, then track deletion, compaction, and slot reuse.
>
> **Method** · Account for the header, all allocated slots, live records, and free bytes on each independent branch.
>
> **Calculation and answer**
>
> $$F=4096-64-3(8)-(600+800+1000)=1608\text{ bytes}.$$
>
> A new **1600-byte** record plus an **8-byte** slot fits exactly; **1601 bytes** plus its slot does not. These are ==independent tests== from the original page.
>
> Now **restart** from that original page, delete B, compact, and insert D = 1600 using B's retained slot:
>
> | State | Slot 0 → A | Slot 1 | Slot 2 → C | Free space |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | Initial | `(3496,600)` | B `(2696,800)` | `(1696,1000)` | 1608 contiguous bytes |
> | Delete B | Unchanged | Retained, marked free | Unchanged | 2408 total, split into two gaps |
> | Compact | Unchanged | Still free | `(2496,1000)` | 2408 contiguous bytes |
> | Insert D | Unchanged | D `(896,1600)` | `(2496,1000)` | ==808 contiguous bytes== |
>
> The final check is $64+24+600+1600+1000+808=4096$. Slot count remains three; surviving C is still reachable through slot 2 after its offset changes. Use Figure 9 to connect the arithmetic with the byte movement.

### Example 4 — Student and module groups · Q4

> [!example] Worked Example — Student and module groups · Q4
> **Given**
>
> - **1000 `student` records**, **300 bytes** each; **5000 `module` records**, **200 bytes** each.
> - Exactly **five modules per student**; each whole group must share a **4096-byte block**.
> - Groups are ordered by **20-byte `sID`**.
> - A **10-byte pointer** contains an **8-byte block ID** and a **2-byte offset**.[^q4]
>
> **Find** · Calculate combined data blocks and the two alternative index sizes.
>
> **Method** · Pack a whole student-plus-five-module group before counting data blocks; count each index alternative separately.
>
> **Calculation and answer**
>
> $$G=300+5(200)=1300,\qquad f_G=\lfloor4096/1300\rfloor=3,\qquad
> b_G=\lceil1000/3\rceil=\mathbf{334}.$$
>
> Three groups leave **196 bytes** per full block. The last block holds one group. Entries are $20+10=30$ bytes, so each index block holds $\lfloor4096/30\rfloor=136$ entries.
>
> | Index alternative | What one entry represents | Required index blocks |
> |---|---|---:|
> | Dense, as Q4 defines it | One student tuple: 1000 entries | **8** |
> | Sparse primary | One combined data block: 334 entries | **3** |
>
> These are alternatives, not two indexes to add together by default.[^q4-answer] After locating a group, one data block contains all six records; locating it may still require index reads.
>
> Separate files would use $\lceil1000/13\rceil=77$ student blocks and $\lceil5000/20\rceil=250$ module blocks: **327 total**. Clustering spends ==7 extra blocks== for guaranteed group locality. A student-only scan must fetch pages containing module bytes.

### Example 5 — Product file · Q5

> [!example] Worked Example — Product file · Q5
> **Given**
>
> - **10 000 `product` records**, **50 bytes** each.
> - Ordered by unique **2-byte `productID`**.
> - **4096-byte blocks**; **10-byte pointers**; **sparse primary index**.[^q5]
>
> **Find** · Calculate data blocks and a single-level sparse primary index.
>
> **Method** · Find whole-record capacity, then count one sparse entry per data block.
>
> **Calculation and answer**
>
> $$
> f=\lfloor4096/50\rfloor=81,\quad b=\lceil10\,000/81\rceil=124,
> \quad E=2+10=12,\quad f_I=341,\quad b_I=\lceil124/341\rceil=1.
> $$
>
> **Answer:** ==124 data blocks + 1 index block==. The last data block contains $10\,000-123(81)=37$ products. There are 124 sparse entries, not 10 000.[^q5-answer]

### Example 6 — A file ordered by a non-key name · Q6

> [!example] Worked Example — A file ordered by a non-key name · Q6
> **Given**
>
> - **30 000 `students` records**, **30 bytes** each; ordered by **non-key `name` (4 bytes)**.
> - `studentID` is the **2-byte primary key**.
> - Blocks are **4096 bytes**; index pointers are **6 bytes**.[^q6]
>
> **Find** · Identify the primary-index key, calculate its maximum compact dense size, and assess ID sampling.
>
> **Method** · Use the file ordering to classify the index, then state how dense entries cover duplicates.
>
> **Calculation and answer**
>
> The primary-index key is **`name`**, because it determines file order.
>
> $$
> f=\lfloor4096/30\rfloor=136,\quad b=\lceil30\,000/136\rceil=221,
> \quad E=4+6=10,\quad f_I=409.
> $$
>
> The last data block holds **80 records**. If $D$ is the number of distinct names, a compact dense-by-value directory has $D\leq30\,000$ entries, giving a **maximum of $\lceil30\,000/409\rceil=74$ index blocks**. Non-key status permits duplicates; it does not require them in every dataset. Unspecified duplicate buckets, headers, and spare space are excluded. A one-entry-per-tuple format also yields 74, so that total alone does not establish the representation.
>
> A simple sparse secondary index on unordered `studentID` cannot locate all omitted IDs (Figure 11). A dense secondary ID index would provide complete coverage while preserving name order. The valid primary index supports ==name searches==; it does not automatically answer an ID predicate better.[^q6-answer]

## Common mistakes

Use the left column to spot a tempting shortcut and the right column to repair the model behind it.

| Tempting shortcut | Better reasoning |
|---|---|
| Divide total row bytes by block bytes once | Unspanned packing requires the per-block floor first |
| Add the registry's 50-byte address again | It is already inside the 350-byte record |
| Primary key = primary-index key | The course's primary index follows **file order** |
| Sorting sampled IDs makes a valid sparse secondary index | The underlying records still need a complete continuation path |
| Dense always means one entry per tuple | State how duplicates are reached; obey explicit local definitions |
| Average read = half worst read | All requested sectors still transfer |
| 90 tracks = 90 ms | Apply the seek model, then include wait and transfer |
| A 1600-byte gap always fits a 1600-byte record | A new slot can require additional bytes |
| `(page, slot)` is permanent object identity | It protects surviving within-page moves under this model |
| Free bytes are always one usable gap | Distinguish total space from contiguous space |
| A smaller index is always faster | Account for coverage, cache, selectivity, locality, and maintenance |
| SSD writes are cost-free overwrites | Programming, remapping, and erasure still cost work |
| Mirroring is a backup | Logical mistakes can propagate to every current copy |
| Expected output is observed output | Only an actual run establishes an observation |

## Exam-style summary

Use these relationships to build a justified answer to the tutorial problem types.

> [!summary] Takeaway — Six relationships to remember
> **Packing:** $f=\lfloor(B-H)/R\rfloor$, then $b=\lceil N/f\rceil$.
>
> **Indexing:** count what an entry represents; then $E=K_b+P_b$, $f_I=\lfloor B/E\rfloor$, $b_I=\lceil n_I/f_I\rceil$.
>
> **Timing:** total read = seek + rotational wait + full transfer.
>
> **Page updates:** header + allocated directory + live records + free space = page size.
>
> **Sparse access:** representatives need compatible file order and boundary handling.
>
> **Design:** space savings, locality, update cost, and reliability answer different questions.

## 60-Second Review

> [!summary] Takeaway

An index helps only if its coverage and continuation rules can find all required records, and every update must preserve that property.

## A. Quick Retrieval

Explain each distinction in a few sentences before revealing help.

### Exercise A1 — Explain an access path

Draw fields → record → page → file, and show where memory enters a lookup.

Why can two row requests cause ==one data-page fetch==?

> [!tip]- Hint
>
> - Separate **row requests** from **page fetches**.
> - Check whether the same page remains in the buffer for the second request.

> [!success]- Solution
> **Step 1 — Follow the storage hierarchy**
>
> Fields form records, records occupy pages, and pages form a file. A requested page is fetched into a buffer on a miss.
>
> **Step 2 — Apply buffer state**
>
> If it remains resident and contains both rows, the second request hits that same buffer page. Index and metadata access require separate accounting.
>
> **Key idea:** A ==buffer hit== can satisfy a second row request without another data-page fetch.

### Exercise A2 — Derive rather than memorise

Why does records-per-block use ==floor== while required block count uses ==ceiling==?

What happens if one record is larger than the usable block?

> [!tip]- Hint
>
> - Ask how many **complete records** can fit inside one block.
> - Then ask how many complete blocks are needed for all records.
> - Check whether even one record fits before dividing.

> [!success]- Solution
> **Step 1 — Enforce whole-record capacity**
>
> Only whole unspanned records fit, so fractional capacity is discarded.
>
> **Step 2 — Allocate enough blocks**
>
> Any remaining records still need a whole additional block.
>
> **Step 3 — Check the domain**
>
> If a record exceeds usable capacity, the assumed unspanned layout is impossible; a zero blocking factor cannot be used as a divisor.
>
> **Key idea:** ==Whole objects== determine both rounding decisions.

### Exercise A3 — Predict a boundary lookup

> [!info] Key Data
>
> - The file is ==ordered by a unique key==.
> - Pages: D0 `[10,14,19]`; D1 `[23,28,35]`; D2 `[40,47]`.
> - Index representatives are the ==block minima==: 10, 23, and 40.

For a lookup of **key 23**:

- Which block should be chosen?
- What extra rule is needed if the implementation uses a **strict predecessor**?

> [!tip]- Hint
>
> - Test **equality with a block minimum**.
> - For a strict predecessor, identify what must happen after reading the preceding block.
> - Consider the first representative as a boundary case.

> [!success]- Solution
> **Step 1 — Choose the direct candidate**
>
> Choose D1 through representative 23.
>
> **Step 2 — Handle a strict predecessor**
>
> A strict-predecessor rule chooses the preceding representative and must explicitly continue forward and handle the first-key boundary. It cannot simply inspect only the predecessor block and stop.
>
> **Key idea:** The ==equality boundary== and continuation rule determine whether lookup is complete.

### Exercise A4 — Interpret a diagram

During ==compaction==, C moves from offset **1696** to **2496**.

- Which pointer remains useful?
- What must be changed?

> [!tip]- Hint
>
> - Compare a **raw byte offset** with a reference through a **slot**.
> - Identify which directory value must follow the moved record.

> [!success]- Solution
> **Step 1 — Maintain indirection**
>
> `(page, slot 2)` remains useful if slot 2's directory offset is changed to ==2496==.
>
> **Step 2 — State the limit**
>
> A raw pointer to offset 1696 does not follow C. Slot identity is not a guarantee for deleted records or movement between pages.
>
> **Key idea:** Stable slots protect surviving ==within-page references== under the stated model.

### Exercise A5 — Compare mechanisms

> [!info] Key Data
>
> - The `students` file is ==ordered by `name`==; its logical primary key is `studentID`.
> - A **separate advising layout** groups students with module records.

Distinguish **primary key**, **primary index**, and **multitable clustering** using these two cases.

> [!tip]- Hint
>
> - Identify the logical row identifier.
> - Identify the actual file-ordering attribute.
> - For advising, ask which related records occupy the same page.

> [!success]- Solution
> **Step 1 — Identify the logical key**
>
> `studentID` is a logical unique identifier in the legacy relation.
>
> **Step 2 — Identify file order**
>
> Its primary index follows the actual ordering attribute `name`.
>
> **Step 3 — Identify co-location**
>
> Advising multitable clustering instead co-locates a student's record with five records from another relation. These answer different questions.
>
> **Key idea:** Logical identity, file order, and co-location are ==different properties==.

### Exercise A6 — Explain a timing model

Which HDD terms disappear as ==mechanical mechanisms== on an SSD?

Does that leave exactly the old transfer time?

> [!tip]- Hint
>
> - First identify the delays that require **moving parts**.
> - Then list the work still needed to deliver the data.

> [!success]- Solution
>
> - ==Arm seek and rotational waiting== disappear.
> - Electronic access, controller processing, data transfer, and possible reclamation remain; the HDD transfer formula does not specify those costs.
>
> **Key idea:** Removing moving parts does not remove every access cost.

### Exercise A7 — Reason about SQL and NULL

A table has ==250 missing addresses==.

Why do `address = NULL` and `address IS NULL` produce different counts?

> [!tip]- Hint
>
> - Determine the truth value of equality with NULL.
> - Recall which truth value `WHERE` retains.
> - Compare that with an explicit missing-value test.

> [!success]- Solution
>
> - Equality with NULL is unknown, which `WHERE` does not retain; `IS NULL` directly tests missingness.
> - The counts are ==0 and 250== respectively.
> - This is not evidence of an index losing the missing-address rows.
>
> **Key idea:** ==Missingness== is not tested by ordinary equality.

### Exercise A8 — Compare reliability claims

Why does ==mirroring== not provide the same protection as restoring an ==older backup== after an accidental deletion?

> [!tip]- Hint
>
> - Follow the same logical deletion on both live copies.
> - Ask whether either copy still retains the earlier state.

> [!success]- Solution
>
> - A mirror can preserve service after some device failures while also applying the same logical deletion to every current copy.
> - Recovering a former state requires suitable historical recovery or backup facilities.
>
> **Key idea:** Device redundancy does not by itself preserve an earlier logical state.

### Exercise A9 — Interpret dense duplicates

> [!info] Key Data
>
> - `name` has ==5000 distinct values==.
> - The file contains **30 000 rows**.

Must every **dense index** have exactly 30 000 search-value entries?

> [!tip]- Hint
>
> - Count **distinct values** separately from **rows**.
> - Explain how a lookup reaches the second and later matches.

> [!success]- Solution
> **Step 1 — Count value entries**
>
> No. A dense-by-value representation can have ==5000 value entries== plus a way to reach all matching records, such as contiguous runs or pointer buckets.
>
> **Step 2 — Compare the tuple representation**
>
> One-entry-per-tuple representations have ==30 000 entries==. State the representation and include additional storage before counting physical blocks.
>
> **Key idea:** State the ==duplicate representation== before counting blocks.

What additional evidence is needed to replace the registry's academic block count with a ==real DBMS file-size estimate==?

## B. Guided Problems

Use the supplied structure; justify the rounding and the timing model.

### Exercise B1 — Complete the missing steps

**Difficulty:** ★★☆

> [!info] Key Data
>
> - **Records:** 12 000 records; ==180 bytes== per record.
> - **Block size:** ==4096 bytes==; **no extra header**.
> - **Organisation:** ==ordered by a unique key==; records are **unspanned**.
> - **Index fields:** key **8 bytes**; pointer **8 bytes**.

Complete the missing steps and **justify each rounding decision**.

> [!question] What You Need to Find
>
> - Records/block: $f=\lfloor4096/180\rfloor=\square$.
> - Data blocks: $b=\lceil12\,000/f\rceil=\square$. The last block holds $\square$ records.
> - A full block leaves $4096-f(180)=\square$ bytes.
> - Index entry length is $8+8=16$ bytes; capacity is $\square$ entries/block.
> - ==Sparse== entries = $\square$, hence sparse index blocks = $\square$.
> - ==Dense== entries = $\square$, hence dense index blocks = $\square$.
> - Which quantity changes between the indexes, and what property makes the sparse index valid?

> [!tip]- Hint
>
> - Find whole-record capacity with ==floor==, then required blocks with ==ceiling==.
> - Do not size the index until you know **what one entry represents**.
> - For the last data block, subtract the records in all preceding full blocks.

> [!success]- Solution
> **Step 1 — Pack the data file**
>
> $f=22$; $b=546$. The first 545 blocks hold $545(22)=11\,990$ records, leaving ==10==. A full block leaves $4096-22(180)=136$ bytes.
>
> **Step 2 — Size one index block**
>
> Entries occupy 16 bytes, so $f_I=256$.
>
> **Step 3 — Count the two alternatives**
>
> Sparse: 546 entries and $\lceil546/256\rceil=3$ blocks. Dense: 12 000 entries and $\lceil12\,000/256\rceil=47$ blocks.
>
> **Step 4 — Explain the rounding and coverage**
>
> The entry count changes, not entry length. Sparse representatives work because the data are ==ordered by the represented unique key==. Floor prevents partial records/entries; ceiling reserves space for remainders.
>
> **Answer:** ==546 data blocks==; **3 sparse** or **47 dense index blocks**.
>
> **Key idea:** The ==entry count== changes; the ==entry length== does not.

### Exercise B2 — Transfer the timing model

**Difficulty:** ★★☆

> [!info] Key Data
>
> - **Rotation:** ==6000 rpm==.
> - **Track:** 200 sectors.
> - **Transfer block:** ==five contiguous sectors==.
> - **Maximum seek time:** **12 ms**.

> [!question] What You Need to Find
>
> - Revolution time and transfer time.
> - Best, approximate worst, and ==course-average read time==.
> - Why the average is **not half the worst total**.

> [!tip]- Hint
>
> - Convert minutes to milliseconds once.
> - Use the fraction of a revolution occupied by the block.
> - Apply the course's half-maximum approximation to **seek and rotational wait** only.

> [!success]- Solution
> **Step 1 — Separate revolution and transfer**
>
> Revolution: $60\,000/6000=10$ ms. Transfer: $(5/200)(10)=0.25$ ms.
>
> **Step 2 — Combine the three costs**
>
> Best: ==0.25 ms==. Approximate worst: $12+10+0.25=\mathbf{22.25}$ ms. Course average: $12/2+10/2+0.25=\mathbf{11.25}$ ms.
>
> **Step 3 — Interpret the average**
>
> Half of the worst total, 11.125 ms, incorrectly halves the transfer. All calculations assume no queue or controller overhead and contiguous sectors without gaps.
>
> **Answer:** best **0.25 ms**; worst **22.25 ms**; course average ==11.25 ms==.
>
> **Key idea:** The average still includes the ==full transfer==.
