> - **Pointer:** **10 bytes**.

> [!question] What You Need to Find
>
> - Data blocks and ==sparse-index blocks==.
> - The number of records in the last data block.

> [!tip]- Hint
>
> - Determine the object stored in one data page.
> - Determine what one **sparse entry** represents.
> - Use the last-block remainder as a separate check.

> [!success]- Solution
> **Step 1 — Pack and check the data file**
>
> $f=27$, $b=667$; 666 blocks hold 17 982 records, leaving 18.
>
> **Step 2 — Count the sparse index**
>
> Index entries are 16 bytes, capacity 256; one entry per data block gives 667 entries and ==3 index blocks==.
>
> **Answer:** ==667 data blocks== and **3 sparse index blocks**; last data block **18 records**.
>
> **Key idea:** A ==sparse entry== represents a data block in this model.

### Exercise C2 — Transfer to a changed workload

**Difficulty:** ★★☆

Compare advising clustering under two workloads:

- Why might it help a ==join== but hurt a ==student-only scan==?
- What happens if a group grows **beyond one page**?

> [!tip]- Hint
>
> - Compare the bytes needed by a **grouped lookup** with those needed by a **student-only scan**.
> - Test whether one whole group still fits in a page.

> [!success]- Solution
> **Step 1 — Compare the workloads**
>
> Related records share one page for the group lookup, but a student-only scan reads pages full of module bytes.
>
> **Step 2 — Check the group-size limit**
>
> If a group exceeds usable page capacity, the one-page requirement becomes impossible; change the layout or the constraint rather than applying the same floor formula blindly.
>
> **Key idea:** A one-page group is a constraint, not an automatic guarantee.

## D. Error Diagnosis

Identify the first faulty assumption, then repair the reasoning.

### Exercise D1 — Diagnose a wrong solution

**Difficulty:** ★★☆

The file is ==ordered by `surname`==; `personID` is its **primary key**. A classmate writes:

> “The primary key is `personID`, so a primary index must use `personID`. Store only the first ID in each block, sort those IDs in the index, and use the greatest stored ID no greater than the query. Every record will then be found.”

> [!question] What You Need to Find
>
> - Identify the **first incorrect assumption** and the later error.
> - Give a **concrete failure**.
> - Propose a correction that ==preserves the current file order==.

> [!tip]- Hint
>
> - Try surname-ordered pages containing IDs **90, 20** and then **70, 10**.
> - Identify the sampled IDs.
> - Ask how the proposed access path would find an omitted ID.

> [!success]- Solution
> **Step 1 — Find the two assumptions**
>
> The first error equates the relational primary key with the course's file-order primary index. Here the primary index follows `surname`. The second error assumes sorting sampled `personID` values creates ordering in the underlying records.
>
> **Step 2 — Construct a failure**
>
> Counterexample: surname-ordered block A contains `(Adams,90),(Brown,20)` and block B contains `(Clark,70),(Davis,10)`. Sampling 90 and 70 gives no complete path for ID 20. Sorting the two entries still cannot reveal the omitted identifier's location.
>
> **Step 3 — Repair the proposal**
>
> Retain surname order and use a ==dense secondary index== with a reference for every `personID`. Reordering the entire file by `personID` could enable a sparse primary alternative, but would change the stated condition.
>
> **Key idea:** Sorting sampled values does not sort the underlying file.

### Exercise D2 — Debug a free-list update

**Difficulty:** ★☆☆

An insertion overwrites the head slot ==before reading== its `next` field.

What information can be lost?

> [!tip]- Hint
>
> - Locate the free slot's **successor pointer**.
> - Identify which write destroys that value.

> [!success]- Solution
>
> - The pointer to the remainder of the free list.
> - Save that pointer first, update the header, and only then overwrite the slot's bytes, within the assumed single-operation model.
>
> **Key idea:** ==Save the successor== before overwriting the free slot.

### Exercise D3 — Predict an overflow scan

**Difficulty:** ★☆☆

> [!info] Key Data
>
> - The ==ordered file== has full pages D0 `[10,14,19]` and D1 `[23,28,35]`.
> - Record **16** is inserted into an ==overflow page== linked between 14 and 19.
> - The later scan reads **only D0 and D1**.

What is wrong with the scan's result?

> [!tip]- Hint
>
> - List the physical pages the scan visits.
> - Compare them with the full live logical sequence.

> [!success]- Solution
>
> - It omits the overflow record 16.
> - Until reorganisation or another complete access method incorporates it, traversal must follow the structure containing the overflow record.
>
> **Key idea:** A complete scan must include ==overflow==.

### Exercise D4 — Diagnose an unjustified measurement claim

**Difficulty:** ★★☆

A report says “2273 blocks means 2273 physical reads at 13 ms each.”

Give ==at least three missing assumptions==.

> [!tip]- Hint
>
> - Separate **file capacity** from the pages visited by this query.
> - Check **buffer state**, access pattern, and the device model.

> [!success]- Solution
> **Step 1 — Identify missing access assumptions**
>
> The query may not scan all blocks; some may be buffered; reads may be sequential or prefetched; index pages may add work; the actual device and transfer block size may differ; contention may matter.
>
> **Step 2 — Interpret the timing claim**
>
> The 13 ms figure is an approximate tutorial model, not a measured latency for this file.
>
> **Key idea:** ==Stored blocks== and ==physical reads== are different quantities.

### Exercise D5 — Debug an index experiment

**Difficulty:** ★★☆

The row sequence changed after `CREATE INDEX`, but the query had ==no `ORDER BY`==.

> [!question] What You Need to Find
>
> - What should you compare?
> - Which claim remains unsupported?

> [!tip]- Hint
>
> - Separate row membership from **requested output order**.
> - Ask what evidence establishes correctness, index use, or speed.

> [!success]- Solution
> **Step 1 — Make the results comparable**
>
> Compare the same multiset of rows, or add a deterministic ordering before comparing sequences.
>
> **Step 2 — State what the evidence proves**
>
> Equivalent results establish correctness for those tests. Unforced comparisons do not establish that the optimiser used the new index or that execution became faster. The lab’s separately required index probes verify a named access path, not its unforced selection or speed.
>
> **Key idea:** ==Correctness==, index selection, and speed require different evidence.

## E. Exam-Style Problems

Combine calculation, interpretation, and limitations in one defensible answer.

### Exercise E1 — Choose and justify a file organisation

**Difficulty:** ★★★

> [!info] Key Data
>
> - **Workload:** many new registrations; frequent ==unique-identifier lookups==; occasional name-ordered reports.
> - **Records:** **18 000**, each **150 bytes**; blocks contain **4096 bytes**.
> - **Index fields:** identifier **6 bytes**; pointer **10 bytes**.
> - **Storage contract:** ==unspanned records and entries==; **ignore other overhead**.
> - You may **choose the file organisation**.

> [!question] What You Need to Find
>
> - Propose a layout and access structure; justify them against the workload.
> - Calculate ==data and index blocks== under your chosen model.
> - State what evidence could reverse your decision.
> - Compare a file **ordered by the identifier**, using **one representative per block**.

> [!tip]- Hint
>
> - Start with the **frequent operations**.
> - Explain how the chosen access structure finds **every identifier**.
> - Compare the cost of maintaining order with the saving in index entries; fewer entries alone do not settle the choice.

> [!success]- Solution
> **Step 1 — Choose a complete access structure**
>
> A defensible provisional choice is a ==heap with a dense secondary index== on the unique identifier. It avoids maintaining a name-ordered sequential layout for frequent arrivals and gives complete identifier coverage; name reports can sort explicitly.
>
> **Step 2 — Size the data file**
>
> With maximal packing, $f=\lfloor4096/150\rfloor=27$, $b=\lceil18\,000/27\rceil=667$. The first 666 blocks hold 17 982 records, leaving 18.
>
> **Step 3 — Size the dense index**
>
> Entry length is $6+10=16$ bytes, so 256 entries/block. Dense entries = 18 000, requiring $\lceil18\,000/256\rceil=71$ blocks. This includes no spare capacity or extra index levels.
>
> **Step 4 — Compare an ordered alternative**
>
> If identifier order were maintained, a sparse primary index would have 667 entries and need $\lceil667/256\rceil=3$ blocks.
>
> **Step 5 — Revisit the workload**
>
> That saving must be weighed against maintaining order and the actual search path. High report/range frequency, expensive sorting, or different insertion patterns could change the decision. Frequencies, memory, actual implementation, and measurements are needed for a performance conclusion; a justified alternative can be correct.
>
> **Answer under the stated models:** **667 data blocks**; ==71 dense index blocks== for the heap choice, or **3 sparse index blocks** if identifier order is maintained.
>
> **Key idea:** Choose ==complete coverage== first, then compare space and maintenance costs.

### Exercise E2 — Track page capacity through two branches

**Difficulty:** ★★★

> [!info] Key Data
>
> - **Page size:** ==4096 bytes==.
> - **Overhead:** **96-byte header** plus **three 8-byte slots**.
> - **Existing records:** **500, 900, and 700 bytes**.
> - Initially, the free region is ==contiguous== and **no slot is reusable**.

> [!question] What You Need to Find
>
> - **Branch A:** find the ==largest new record== that fits.
> - **Branch B:** restart from the initial state; delete the **900-byte record**, compact, **retain and reuse its slot**, and find the largest replacement.
> - State the **reference guarantee**.

> [!tip]- Hint
>
> - Treat the two branches **independently**.
> - Branch A needs a **new directory slot**.
> - Branch B reuses a **retained slot**; deleting payload bytes does not delete the slot entry.

> [!success]- Solution
> **Step 1 — Account for initial occupancy**
>
> Initial occupancy is $96+3(8)+500+900+700=2220$ bytes, leaving 1876.
>
> **Step 2 — Branch A: allocate a new slot**
>
> A new slot costs 8, so the maximum new record is ==1868 bytes==.
>
> **Step 3 — Branch B: restart and reuse**
>
> On the restarted deletion branch, free bytes become $1876+900=2776$. After compaction and slot reuse, a ==2776-byte replacement== fits because no new slot is needed.
>
> **Step 4 — State the reference guarantee**
>
> Both branches exactly fill 4096 bytes. Surviving records can retain `(page, slot)` references if their directory offsets are updated; the deleted record's identity is not preserved, and movement between pages needs additional mechanisms.
>
> **Key idea:** A ==new slot== costs bytes; a ==reused slot== is already counted.

# What changes when we add an index?

[[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 01 - Physical Storage/01 Notes|Notes]] · [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 01 - Physical Storage/02 Exercises|Exercises]]

## Purpose

See how an additional index preserves logical query results and remains consistent when records change. The lab connects the unit's index-maintenance ideas to an executable example using ==synthetic student data==.

> [!info] General database concept
> Adding a non-unique index changes an access structure. It should preserve the tested answers, including duplicate addresses and NULL values. Updates and deletions must remain visible through that index.

> [!warning] SQLite-specific behaviour
> This is a supplementary SQLite experiment. It does not reproduce 350-byte physical records, measure query speed, or identify the course DBMS.

## Environment used

The existing recorded run used **SQLite 3.53.1**, through Python's standard-library `sqlite3` module, on **20 September 2026 at 12:42:10 UTC**. It used one connection and an isolated temporary on-disk database, configured with `PRAGMA page_size = 4096` before table creation. No server or additional Python packages are needed.

Your Python installation may bundle a different SQLite version. The runner prints its actual version and flags a difference from the recorded environment. The previous observed results are summarised below; this presentation refactor did not rerun the experiment.[^sqlite-release][^sqlite-pragma]

## Files and how to run

All six executable source files are in this unit's **Attachments** folder, with their original filenames and contents.

| File | What to inspect |
|---|---|
| [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 01 - Physical Storage/Attachments/schema.sql|schema.sql]] | Table, explicit `NOT NULL`, primary key, length constraint |
| [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 01 - Physical Storage/Attachments/seed.sql|seed.sql]] | Deterministic generation of 25 000 rows |
| [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 01 - Physical Storage/Attachments/queries.sql|queries.sql]] | Fourteen named queries, including duplicates, NULLs, ranges, and ordered results |
| [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 01 - Physical Storage/Attachments/indexes.sql|indexes.sql]] | Non-unique `idx_student_address` |
| [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 01 - Physical Storage/Attachments/experiment.sql|experiment.sql]] | Address update and record deletion |
| [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 01 - Physical Storage/Attachments/run_lab.py|run_lab.py]] | Controlled sequence, comparisons, and reversible edge cases |

Open a terminal in the **SOE201 course folder** and run:

```sh
python3 "Unit 01 - Physical Storage/Attachments/run_lab.py"
```

The runner creates a temporary database beside the scripts, closes and removes it afterwards, and prints a concise result. It needs no report option for studying. A failed assertion stops the run instead of reporting success. The scripts use their own folder to locate one another, so relocating them together preserves how they work.

## Follow the experiment

Track the baseline, the changed state, and the restored state as separate observations.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Create schema and synthetic rows"] --> B["Record baseline answers"]
    B --> C["Add idx_student_address; compare answers"]
    C --> D["Savepoint: update ID 1, delete ID 2"]
    D --> E["Check counts and required-index ID sets"]
    E --> F["Roll back; baseline returns"]
    F --> G["Reversible branches: constraints, empty table, BLOB ID"]
    G --> H["Drop added index; compare again; clean up"]
    classDef default fill:#E6F3F1,stroke:#117D83,color:#172B42,stroke-width:1.5px;
```

**Figure 13 — Change one part, compare with a known state**

**Read it:** each reversible branch returns to the baseline before continuing.  
**Key takeaway:** these comparisons test correctness and index consistency; they do not measure an unforced optimiser plan or latency.

1. **Understand the schema.** `student_ID TEXT NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY` supplies explicit uniqueness and non-nullness. `name` is non-null; `address` permits NULL. `CHECK(length(student_ID) = 10)` tests reported length, not a complete ==ten-digit text domain==.[^sqlite-table]
2. **Read the seed.** `WITH RECURSIVE numbers(n)` generates 1–25 000; `UNION ALL` keeps those generated rows. `printf('%010d', n)` makes padded IDs. `n % 100` produces 100 names; multiples of 100 get NULL addresses, while other rows get hall values.[^sqlite-with][^sqlite-functions]
3. **Predict the baseline.** Multiples of 100 give 250 missing addresses. `Hall-01` and `Hall-02` each contain 2500 rows. The padded text-ID range 100–110 contains 11 rows because `BETWEEN` includes both ends.[^sqlite-expr][^sqlite-aggregate]
4. **Add the address index.** The table already has SQLite's primary-key support. “Before the index” means before the ==additional address index==, not before all indexes. Duplicate addresses remain allowed.[^sqlite-index]
5. **Change data under a savepoint.** ID `0000000001` moves from `Hall-01` to `Hall-02`; ID `0000000002` is then deleted. `ROLLBACK TO` restores the saved state; `RELEASE` closes the savepoint. The runner checks complete expected ID sets using separate `INDEXED BY` diagnostics.[^sqlite-savepoint][^sqlite-indexedby]
6. **Inspect edge cases.** Duplicate, NULL, and wrong-length IDs are rejected. Separate branches empty the table and probe a ten-byte BLOB ID; each is rolled back. Finally, drop only `idx_student_address` and compare the original queries again.

## Observed results summary

> [!summary] Takeaway
> These values come from the **existing recorded execution**, which passed **45 of 45 checks**. Adding the address index preserved all 14 tested query results; the update and deletion changed the expected memberships, and rollback restored the ==baseline==.

| Stage | Observed result | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline | 25 000 rows; 250 NULL addresses; 100 distinct names | Seed matches its construction |
| Duplicate name | `N001` matches 250 rows | A search value need not be unique |
| Address queries | `Hall-01` 2500; `Hall-02` 2500; `Hall-00` 2250 | The NULL rule removes 250 would-be `Hall-00` values |
| NULL comparison | `IS NULL` → 250; `= NULL` → 0 | Equality with NULL is unknown, so `WHERE` does not retain it |
| Point / range / missing key | ID 1 returns its row; range 100–110 returns 11; absent ID returns none | Lookup boundaries agree with expectations |
| Add index | All 14 query results unchanged | The additional index preserves tested answers |
| Update ID 1 | `Hall-01` 2499; `Hall-02` 2501; total 25 000 | Both the record and indexed memberships reflect the change |
| Delete ID 2 | `Hall-02` 2500; total 24 999 | Deleted membership disappears |
| Rollback | Baseline restored | The reversible branch returns to its starting state |
| Invalid values | Duplicate / NULL / short IDs, NULL name, and short-ID update rejected | Explicit constraints take effect for these cases |
| Empty-table branch | Count 0; no point or indexed results | Empty-state behaviour is consistent |
| Ten-byte BLOB ID | Accepted; reported storage class `blob`, length 10 | The ordinary non-STRICT table does not enforce a text-only ID domain |
| Drop index / integrity | Baseline answers unchanged; integrity check `ok` | Removing the added structure preserves tested data |

## General ideas and SQLite-specific details

Use the distinction below when transferring the lesson to another database engine.

| General idea illustrated | SQLite detail used here |
|---|---|
| Indexes must preserve logical answers | `CREATE INDEX idx_student_address ON student(address)` |
| Results need a requested order for sequence comparison | `ORDER BY student_ID` in full-result queries |
| Missing values differ from ordinary values | `IS NULL` versus `= NULL` |
| Changes must maintain access structures | Diagnostic `INDEXED BY idx_student_address` requires that named index |
| A reversible experiment needs a known earlier state | `SAVEPOINT`, `ROLLBACK TO`, `RELEASE` |
| Declared types and constraints need precise interpretation | Explicit text-key `NOT NULL`; ordinary SQLite affinity can still accept BLOBs |
| Storage configuration belongs to an implementation | `PRAGMA page_size`, `sqlite_master`, `sqlite_source_id()`, and integrity checks |

Explicit `ORDER BY` defines output order; a changed sequence without it is not by itself an incorrect result.[^sqlite-select]

For seeded text without embedded NUL characters, SQLite's `length` counts Unicode code points; for BLOB values, it counts bytes. Ten ASCII digits happen to be ten UTF-8 bytes, but that does not make the full stored record ten bytes or reproduce the tutorial's fixed-size layout. `printf`, recursive seed syntax, transaction interfaces, and typing behaviour should not be assumed portable to an unidentified course engine.

> [!warning] SQLite-specific behaviour — Required-index probes
> ==Equal results== do not prove that an unforced query used the new index or became faster. The separate `INDEXED BY` probes require the named index for those probes; they are not an optimiser hint or a benchmark. No full plans, timings, concurrency conflicts, or crash-recovery behaviour were measured.

The detailed execution tables, source identity, fingerprints, and earlier review evidence remain in the unchanged `_AI Staging` archive. They are not required for this study workflow.

[^sqlite-release]: External official documentation: [SQLite 3.53.1 release log, release identity and hashes](https://www.sqlite.org/releaselog/3_53_1.html), consulted 20 September 2026. The installed `sqlite_source_id()` matches the published identifier; the course engine remains unconfirmed.
[^sqlite-pragma]: External official documentation: [SQLite PRAGMA page_size](https://www.sqlite.org/pragma.html#pragma_page_size), consulted 20 September 2026; actual configured value queried and verified in the SQLite 3.53.1 lab.
[^sqlite-table]: External official documentation: [SQLite CREATE TABLE, §3.1 typing and §§3.5–3.8 constraints](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_createtable.html), consulted 20 September 2026; the relevant behaviour was tested on SQLite 3.53.1.
[^sqlite-with]: External official documentation: [SQLite WITH Clause, §3 Recursive Common Table Expressions](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_with.html), consulted 20 September 2026; deterministic seed executed on SQLite 3.53.1.
[^sqlite-functions]: External official documentation: [SQLite Built-In Scalar SQL Functions, length and printf](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_corefunc.html), consulted 20 September 2026; used by the SQLite 3.53.1 schema and seed.
[^sqlite-expr]: External official documentation: [SQLite SQL Language Expressions, §2 operators and §6 BETWEEN](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_expr.html), consulted 20 September 2026; NULL and range cases tested on SQLite 3.53.1.
[^sqlite-aggregate]: External official documentation: [SQLite Built-In Aggregate Functions, DISTINCT and count](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_aggfunc.html), consulted 20 September 2026. Supports row counts and distinct-value aggregation in the supplementary SQLite lab.
[^sqlite-index]: External official documentation: [SQLite CREATE INDEX, introductory semantics and §1.1](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_createindex.html), consulted 20 September 2026; the lab's non-unique index was tested on SQLite 3.53.1.
[^sqlite-savepoint]: External official documentation: [SQLite Savepoints, §2](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_savepoint.html), consulted 20 September 2026; update/deletion rollback tested on SQLite 3.53.1.
[^sqlite-indexedby]: External official documentation: [SQLite INDEXED BY, §1](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_indexedby.html), consulted 20 September 2026. This SQLite-only clause requires the specified index; its diagnostic use here is not a recommendation to tune queries by forcing indexes.
[^sqlite-select]: External official documentation: [SQLite SELECT, §2.3 WHERE filtering and §4 ORDER BY](https://www.sqlite.org/lang_select.html), consulted 20 September 2026; applied to the SQLite 3.53.1 lab.

# Unit 02 — B+ tree indexing

[[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Tutor Mode/00 Start Here|Tutor Start]] · [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Tutor Mode/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/02 Recall and Exam Practice|Recall and practice]] · [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/01 Notes|Reference notes]]

## In 60 Seconds

A B+ tree is a balanced ordered index. Internal nodes route by separator ranges; leaves hold the searchable key entries and are linked for range scans. In this course, order $n$ means at most $n$ child pointers in an internal node and therefore at most $n-1$ leaf keys. Lookup follows boundaries to a leaf. Insertion splits overflowing nodes. Deletion repairs underflow using the lecture's **merge-first, otherwise redistribute** rule. The root has special occupancy rules.

After study, you should be able to trace lookup/range access, apply insertion and deletion one state at a time, and validate occupancy, order, routing, leaf links and equal depth.

## Concept Preview

> [!note] Separator boundary
> **Plain-language meaning:** an internal key divides child ranges; it is not itself proof that a record exists.
>
> **Why it matters:** membership is confirmed only at a leaf.
>
> **Connects to:** lookup and separator maintenance.
>
> **Source:** `Lecture2b - B+Tree Indexing (1).pdf`, PDF pp. 4–9.

> [!note] Occupancy
> **Plain-language meaning:** non-root nodes have minimum and maximum capacities; the root is allowed to be smaller.
>
> **Why it matters:** overflow triggers splitting and underflow triggers repair.
>
> **Connects to:** insertion, deletion and height.
>
> **Source:** Lecture2b, PDF pp. 4–6, 12–27.

> [!note] Copy versus promote
> **Plain-language meaning:** a leaf split copies a boundary upward while retaining data keys in leaves; an internal split promotes a separator.
>
> **Why it matters:** treating both splits identically loses a searchable leaf key or duplicates routing incorrectly.
>
> **Connects to:** cascading splits.
>
> **Source:** Lecture2b, PDF pp. 12–18.

> [!note] Merge-first deletion
> **Plain-language meaning:** when a node underflows, the supplied algorithm first merges with an eligible sibling if the combined content fits; otherwise it redistributes.
>
> **Why it matters:** it determines the exact intermediate tree expected by the source examples.
>
> **Connects to:** parent deletion and root contraction.
>
> **Source:** Lecture2b, PDF pp. 19–27.

## Exam Evidence Snapshot

| Topic | Observed papers | Known marks | Observed demand | Priority |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| Deletion and repair | 3/4 | 6 | explain, describe, draw | **HIGH EXAM RELEVANCE** |
| Lookup trace | 1/4 | 2 | describe | MEDIUM |
| Insertion, capacity and range scan | 0/4 | 0 observed | not observed | NOT OBSERVED IN AVAILABLE PAST-PAPER SAMPLE |

Evidence: [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Tutor Mode/_System/past-paper-intelligence#Source-supported aggregates|past-paper intelligence]].

## Before You Start

Recall ordered keys, pointers and the distinction between an index block and a data block.

> [!question] Prerequisite check
> If an internal node has separators `[10, 20]`, how many child ranges does it have?

> [!success]- Check your answer
> Three: values below 10, values from 10 to below 20, and values at least 20.
>
> Source principle: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 4–9.

## A motivating question

Use the exact order-4 initial tree from Lecture2b, PDF p. 34:

```text
                 [7 | 13 | 19]
             /       |       |       \
          [4,5]    [7,9]  [13,17]  [19,25,31]
```

Apply **insert 33, insert 11, delete 25** in that order. How can the tree remain balanced while only local nodes change? What evidence proves the final tree is valid?

| Question | Knowledge needed |
|---|---|
| Insert 33 and 11 | leaf overflow, split, copied separator, parent capacity |
| Delete 25 | underflow test, merge-first repair, parent/root repair |
| Validate | sorted leaves, range boundaries, occupancy, equal depth |

## Learn the mechanism

### Course order and occupancy

For order $n$:

| Node | Minimum | Maximum |
|---|---:|---:|
| non-root internal | $\lceil n/2\rceil$ child pointers | $n$ pointers |
| non-root leaf | $\lceil(n-1)/2\rceil$ keys | $n-1$ keys |
| internal root | 2 child pointers | $n$ pointers |
| root that is a leaf | 0 keys | $n-1$ keys |

For order 4, non-root leaves hold 2–3 keys and non-root internal nodes have 2–4 children. Count child pointers, not separator labels, when checking an internal node.

### Lookup is interval routing

At separator equality, route right into the range beginning at that boundary. Continue until a leaf, then compare actual leaf keys. An internal separator may remain as a valid boundary after the equal leaf key has been deleted; it need not be duplicated in a leaf under the lecture's retained-boundary examples.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    R["root: 13"] -->|"x < 13"| L["left subtree"]
    R -->|"x ≥ 13"| G["right subtree"]
    G --> C{"leaf contains x?"}
    C -->|yes| P["follow record pointer"]
    C -->|no| N["not present"]
```

**Figure 1 — A separator chooses a range, not membership**

**Read it:** equality takes the right branch; only the leaf decides presence.

**Key takeaway:** routing correctness is about ranges, not whether every separator is currently stored as a leaf key.

**Provenance:** teaching construction from Lecture2b, PDF pp. 4–9.

### Range scans use linked leaves

Descend once to the first leaf that can contain the lower bound, then scan right through leaf links until the upper bound is exceeded. The index preserves order; a hash index does not provide this route.

### Insertion: copy at leaves, promote internally

1. Route to the target leaf.
2. Insert in sorted order if capacity remains.
3. On leaf overflow, split the ordered entries. Keep all data keys in leaves and **copy** the first key of the new right leaf into the parent.
4. If the parent overflows, split the internal node and **promote** its middle separator; that separator leaves the split internal children.
5. If the root splits, create a new root. All leaves remain at the same depth.

> [!warning] Common confusion
> A leaf split and an internal split are not interchangeable. Leaf entries represent searchable keys, so the boundary is copied. Internal separators route only, so the middle separator is promoted.

### Deletion: remove, test, repair upward

1. Route to the leaf and remove the key if present.
2. If occupancy remains valid, update a separator only when its routing range requires it.
3. If the node underflows, apply the lecture's rule: merge with an eligible sibling when combined content fits; otherwise redistribute and adjust the parent boundary.
4. A merge deletes one parent child pointer and its separator. This may make the parent underflow, so repair can propagate upward.
5. If the root has one remaining child, replace the root with that child; height decreases by one.

Sibling choice is not universally fixed when both sides satisfy the rule. State and use a consistent supported choice rather than claiming the source prescribes one.

> [!question] Explain it yourself
> Why can deleting one leaf key cause a root contraction even though most of the tree is unchanged?

> [!success]- Check your explanation
> Leaf underflow can cause a merge; deleting the corresponding parent pointer can propagate underflow upward until the root has only one child.
>
> Source: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 19–27.

### Height and access cost

If $h$ counts edges from root to leaf, an uncached equality lookup visits $h+1$ index nodes. Fetching the data record can require another data-page read. Cache residency can reduce physical reads, so height is a structural bound under a stated cache model, not a measured latency.

## Worked example — the opening update sequence

Initial leaves: `[4,5]`, `[7,9]`, `[13,17]`, `[19,25,31]`; root `[7,13,19]`.

**Insert 33**

The rightmost leaf becomes `[19,25,31,33]` and overflows. Split it into `[19,25]` and `[31,33]`; copy boundary 31 upward. The root would have five children, so it also overflows. Promote 19 into a new root, producing two internal children whose leaf ranges remain ordered.

**Insert 11**

Route through the left internal subtree to leaf `[7,9]`. Insert to obtain `[7,9,11]`; this is within leaf capacity, so no split occurs.

**Delete 25**

Route to `[19,25]`; deletion leaves `[19]`, below the minimum of two. Under the lecture's merge-first rule, merge it with eligible sibling `[31,33]` to form `[19,31,33]`, then delete the redundant parent pointer/boundary. The right internal node now has only one child, below the minimum of two. Merge it with the left internal sibling: their 3 + 1 children fit order 4. Move the old root separator 19 down between the merged ranges. The old root then has one child, so contract it. The new root is `[7,13,19]` with four leaf children.

The final leaves are `[4,5] → [7,9,11] → [13,17] → [19,31,33]`.

**Validation:** every surviving key appears once; leaf order and links are correct; all leaves share a depth; each non-root leaf has 2–3 keys; internal ranges contain their leaf keys; the final root has four children, every leaf is one edge below it, and the temporary extra level has disappeared.

**Source:** Lecture2b, PDF pp. 34–37; full illustrated sequence in [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/01 Notes#Solve the opening case|reference notes]].

## Return to the motivating question

The tree stays balanced because each overflow or underflow is repaired locally and the repair propagates only when its parent violates capacity. The proof is invariant-based: sorted keys, correct ranges, valid occupancy, linked leaves and equal depth—not resemblance to one drawing.

## Definitions and distinctions

| Term A | Term B | Decisive distinction | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| separator | leaf key | routing boundary versus searchable key entry | Lecture2b, pp. 4–9 |
| leaf split | internal split | copy right-leaf minimum versus promote middle separator | Lecture2b, pp. 12–18 |
| merge | redistribution | combine nodes and remove a parent pointer versus move entries while keeping both nodes | Lecture2b, pp. 19–27 |
| height edge count | node visits | a path of $h$ edges visits $h+1$ index nodes | Lecture2b, pp. 10–11 |

## Review

### Full Understanding

Return to [[#Learn the mechanism]] and [[#Worked example — the opening update sequence]].

## 5-Minute Review

- route by ranges and confirm at a leaf;
- leaves are ordered and linked;
- order controls maximum pointers/keys;
- leaf split copies; internal split promotes;
- deletion uses merge-first, otherwise redistribute;
- repair may propagate and contract the root;
- validate invariants after every operation.

## 60-Second Recall

- order = max internal pointers
- leaf max = order − 1
- root exception
- equality routes right
- membership at leaf
- copy vs promote
- merge vs redistribute
- root contraction
- linked-leaf range scan

## Sources

- `Lecture2b - B+Tree Indexing (1).pdf`, PDF pp. 2–37; p. 38 is reading context.
- `SOE201-EXAMS.pdf`: P23F A4, P23R A3 and P24R A3–A4; exact inventory in past-paper intelligence.

[[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Tutor Mode/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/01 Tutor Notes|Tutor notes]] · [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/02 Exercises|Reference exercises]]

## Atomic recall

### Card 01 — What does B+ tree order mean in this course?
> [!success]- Answer
> The maximum number of child pointers in an internal node.
>
> Source: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 4–6.

### Card 02 — How many keys can an order-$n$ leaf hold at most?
> [!success]- Answer
> $n-1$ search-key entries.
>
> Source: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 4–6.

### Card 03 — In a B+ tree lookup, where is key membership confirmed?
> [!success]- Answer
> At the reached leaf, not at an internal separator.
>
> Source: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 7–9.

### Card 04 — In this course’s B+ tree convention, which child range is chosen when the search key equals a separator?
> [!success]- Answer
> Route to the right-hand range beginning at that separator.
>
> Source: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 7–9.

### Card 05 — After splitting a B+ tree leaf, which key is copied into the parent?
> [!success]- Answer
> The first key of the new right leaf is copied into the parent.
>
> Source: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 12–18.

### Card 06 — After splitting a B+ tree internal node, which separator is promoted?
> [!success]- Answer
> The middle separator moves to the parent and is removed from the split children.
>
> Source: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 12–18.

### Card 07 — What repair preference does the lecture use after underflow?
> [!success]- Answer
> Merge first when an eligible sibling combination fits; otherwise redistribute.
>
> Source: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 19–27.

### Card 08 — When does deletion reduce the height of a B+ tree?
> [!success]- Answer
> When an internal root is left with one child and that child replaces it.
>
> Source: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 19–27.

### Card 09 — Why are leaves linked?
> [!success]- Answer
> To continue ordered range scans without returning to the root for each next key.
>
> Source: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 4–9.

### Card 10 — What must every root-to-leaf path share?
> [!success]- Answer
> The same depth; this is the tree's height-balance invariant.
>
> Source: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 4–6.

## Practice

### Practice 1 — Guided lookup

**ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE — relevant routing data transcribed.** Root `[33]` has left internal `[11,22]` and right internal `[44]`. The left internal child for keys at least 22 is leaf `[29]`; the right internal child for keys below 44 is leaf `[37,41]`. Trace searches for 29, 31 and 33. State each route and decide membership only at the leaf.

Source: Lecture2b, PDF pp.8–9; the other children are not visited by these searches.

> [!tip]- Hint
> At each separator choose an interval; do not report success until the leaf comparison.

> [!success]- Solution
> All three start at root `[33]`. Values 29 and 31 route left to internal `[11,22]`, then to leaf `[29]`; 29 is present and 31 absent. Value 33 routes right at equality, then left at internal `[44]`, reaching leaf `[37,41]`; 33 is absent.
>
> The root separator 33 is a routing boundary, not proof of a leaf entry.
>
> Source: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 8–9.

### Practice 2 — Guided insertion

**SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE.** An order-4 leaf `[10,20,30]` receives 25. Show the leaf split and parent separator.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Sort four keys, split into two legal leaves and copy the right leaf's first key.

> [!success]- Solution
> Sorted overflow is `[10,20,25,30]`. A legal even split is `[10,20]` and `[25,30]`. Copy 25 into the parent as the boundary for the new right leaf. All data keys remain in leaves.
>
> Source principle: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 12–18. Values are synthetic.

> [!danger] HIGH EXAM RELEVANCE
> B+ deletion/repair is directly observed in 3/4 papers (6 known marks), including diagram updates. This is descriptive evidence, not a prediction.

### Practice 3 — ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE: delete 5, then 11

**ORIGINAL COURSE EXERCISE.** Use this order-3 starting tree. Delete 5, then delete 11 from the resulting tree. Choose a legal sibling consistently, use merge-first repair and show both intermediate states.

![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/delete-initial.svg]]

Text equivalent: root `[11]`; left internal `[5,7]` with leaves `[2,3]`, `[5]`, `[7]`; right internal `[13]` with leaves `[11]`, `[13,17]`. Source: Lecture2b, PDF pp.31–32.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Treat this as one sequence. After the first deletion, the second begins from the changed tree.

> [!success]- Solution
> After deleting 5, merge the empty leaf with its left sibling `[2,3]`. Remove boundary 5: root `[11]` now has left internal `[7]` over `[2,3]`, `[7]`, and unchanged right internal `[13]` over `[11]`, `[13,17]`.
>
> Then delete 11 and merge its empty leaf with `[13,17]`. The right internal node has one child, so merge it with the left internal node: 2 + 1 children fit order 3. Bring down separator 11 and contract the old root. Final root `[7,11]` has leaves `[2,3]`, `[7]`, `[13,17]`. Separator 11 remains a valid range boundary although 11 is no longer a leaf key.
>
> ![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/delete5.svg]]
> ![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/delete5-11.svg]]
>
> The decisive checks after each step are: every remaining key present once, leaf order/linkage, legal occupancy and equal depth. The complete source-specific drawings are preserved at [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/02 Exercises#C2 — Two deletion paths from the same initial tree|C2 complete solution]].
>
> Source: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 31–33. The linked ordinary solution is used because the source diagram state is essential and already fully audited.

> [!danger] HIGH EXAM RELEVANCE
> This supplementary item practises the repeated historical deletion pattern without copying a paper question.

### Practice 4 — Independent deletion decision

**SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE.** In an order-4 tree, leaf A contains `[4,7]`, leaf B contains `[10,13,16]`, and their parent separates B at 10. Delete 7. State whether to merge or redistribute under the course rule, then show the result.

> [!tip]- Hint
> After deletion, A underflows. Test whether A and B together fit in one leaf before redistributing.

> [!success]- Solution
> A becomes `[4]`, below the minimum of two. Combined with B there would be four keys, exceeding the leaf maximum of three, so merge is impossible. Redistribute the smallest key 10 from B to A.
>
> New leaves are A `[4,10]` and B `[13,16]`; update the parent boundary from 10 to 13. Both leaves now satisfy occupancy.
>
> Source principle: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 19–27. Values are synthetic.

### Practice 5 — Diagnose three claims

**SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE.** Diagnose: (a) every internal separator must occur in a leaf; (b) a range search repeats root lookup for every answer; (c) height 3 means three index-node visits.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Use retained boundaries, leaf links, and the difference between edges and nodes.

> [!success]- Solution
> (a) False under the lecture's retained-boundary convention; a separator can remain a valid range boundary after that leaf key is gone.
>
> (b) False; descend once, then follow linked leaves.
>
> (c) False when height counts edges: three edges visit four index nodes. State the convention explicitly.
>
> Source: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 7–11 and 19–27.

### Practice 6 — Transfer: choose B+ tree or hashing

**SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE.** A workload performs exact ID lookups, ordered pagination and frequent range queries. Explain why a B+ tree remains a coherent single-index choice even if a hash index may shorten some equality routes.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Compare maintained order and linked leaves with computed bucket addresses.

> [!success]- Solution
> The B+ tree supports equality by logarithmic-height routing and range/pagination by ordered linked leaves. A hash index is organised by bucket address and provides no adjacent-key traversal. The answer is a workload trade-off, not a universal speed claim; cache, clustering and implementation remain unspecified.
>
> Source: Lecture2b, PDF pp. 2–11; Lecture3a, PDF pp. 41–43.

# B+ tree indexing

## Opening case — keep a changing registry searchable

**Synthetic teaching case using the exact tree and update sequence of Lecture 2b, PDF p. 34.** A registry stores unique numerical search keys. Its index has ==order 4==: at most four child pointers in an internal node and three key entries in a leaf. Each index node occupies one block; data records are stored separately. The initial tree appears below. Treat this as a logical block model, with no DBMS selected.

![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/case-initial.svg]]

**Figure 1 — The opening registry index**

**Read it:** Start at the root; each downward arrow selects an interval. Horizontal arrows link leaves.

**Key takeaway:** The root has four children; each leaf holds actual search keys.



**Given:** the four leaves are `[4,5]`, `[7,9]`, `[13,17]`, `[19,25,31]`. Internal separators are `7,13,19`. All leaves have the same depth and are linked in that order.

**Questions**

1. How do equality lookup for 17 and the inclusive range 9–25 reach their records?
2. What happens after inserting 33, then 11, then deleting 25, in that exact order?
3. What invariants prove the final tree is valid? How many index blocks does one uncached equality lookup read before and after the complete sequence?

**Constraints and success criteria:** retain all undeleted keys exactly once in leaves; use the lecturer's leaf and internal split rules; ==merge before redistribution== when an eligible sibling pair fits; keep all leaves at one depth. Explain every separator change and distinguish index reads from data-record reads.

| Question | Concepts needed |
|---|---|
| Find 17 and 9–25 | Separators, equality routing, leaf links |
| Apply the update sequence | Occupancy, split propagation, merge and root contraction |
| Defend the result | Invariants, height and block-I/O model |

Prerequisite: Unit 1's records, blocks, pointers, sparse and dense indexes. This chapter covers Lecture 2b, PDF pp. 2–37. All page locators below are **PDF pages**, which also match the displayed slide numbers in this lecture.

## Why an index must reorganise locally

A static multilevel index can locate a block quickly, but growth can accumulate overflow blocks and require expensive reorganisation. A B+ tree changes a small number of nodes around the affected search path. Its extra space and update work buy bounded depth and continued ordered access.[^motivation]

Intuitively, an internal node is a directory of key intervals; a leaf is the searchable catalogue entry. A large block can hold many directory pointers, so each step narrows the search by a large factor. This is why the tree is “short and fat”. Logical neighbours need not occupy physically adjacent disk blocks: pointers encode the relationships.[^structure]

> [!note] Definition and order convention
> A ==B+ tree== is an ordered, height-balanced index: every path from the root to a leaf has the same length. In this course, order $n$ is the **maximum number of child pointers per internal node**, so an internal node has at most $n-1$ separator keys. Leaf entries contain a search-key value and a record pointer or pointer to a duplicate-record bucket; a leaf also has a next-leaf pointer.[^structure]

### Occupancy and the root exception

| Node | Minimum | Maximum |
|---|---:|---:|
| Non-root internal node | $\lceil n/2\rceil$ child pointers | $n$ child pointers |
| Non-root leaf | $\lceil(n-1)/2\rceil$ key entries | $n-1$ key entries |
| Root with internal children or leaf children | 2 child pointers | $n$ child pointers |
| Root that is itself a leaf | 0 key entries | $n-1$ key entries |

Ceilings mean rounding upward to the next integer. For $n=4$, internal nodes need at least two children; non-root leaves need at least two keys. For $n=3$, the respective minima are two children and one key. For $n=6$, they are three children and three keys; leaves hold at most five keys, as in the source's name index on p. 6.

**Source wording clarification:** p. 4 calls the contents of a leaf-root “children”; a leaf has no child subtrees. Here the 0 to $n-1$ bound is stated correctly in **key entries**. The root exception also takes precedence over the slide's blanket minimum for non-leaf nodes. These are terminology clarifications, not a change to the supplied exercises.

### A separator is a routing boundary

For ordered separators $K_1<\cdots<K_m$ and child pointers $P_1,\ldots,P_{m+1}$:

- $P_1$ covers values below $K_1$.
- $P_j$ covers $K_{j-1}\le V<K_j$ for middle children.
- $P_{m+1}$ covers values at least $K_m$.

A separator may be copied from the smallest key in its right subtree when created. After deletion it may remain a valid boundary even when that key no longer exists. The invariant is that every left-side key is smaller than the separator and every right-side key is at least the separator. **Membership is established at a leaf.** The source deliberately illustrates absent separators 33 and 11.[^lookup][^delete-examples]

![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/lookup.svg]]

**Figure 2 — The lecture lookup tree**

**Read it:** Compare target 33 with the root, then 44; inspect the reached leaf.

**Key takeaway:** Routing boundaries can be absent from the data; source PDF pp. 5, 8–9.



**Worked counterexample:** in Figure 2, 33 routes right at the root and left at separator 44, reaching `[37,41]`; it is absent. Seeing 33 at the root is insufficient. This also explains why “every internal key must currently occur in a leaf” is too strong for the lecturer's retained-boundary convention.

> [!question] Check your understanding
> In an order-4 non-root internal node, do two separator keys mean the node is underfull? Explain using **three child pointers**.

## Lookup and ordered range access

### Equality lookup

1. Start at the root. At each internal node, choose the interval containing the target $V$; ==equality goes right== of the matching separator.
2. Follow that child pointer. Repeat until reaching a leaf.
3. Search the leaf for $V$. If present, follow its record or bucket pointer. Otherwise report absence.
4. If multiple records share $V$, retrieve every record referenced by its bucket. Search keys remain distinct in the course node model; duplicate records do not require repeated separator values.[^lookup][^insert]

For the source tree in Figure 2, search 29 visits root `[33]`, internal `[11,22]`, then leaf `[29]`. It takes **three index-node reads** with an empty cache. Retrieving the actual record is additional work, not a fourth tree level.

### Range lookup

**Pedagogical extension of the ordered leaves shown in the source:** descend once to the first leaf that can contain the lower bound, scan entries from that bound, then follow next-leaf pointers until exceeding the upper bound. A leaf skipped by equality routing may still be needed for the next range value. The linked leaves avoid restarting at the root for each result.

For the opening tree and range $9\le V\le25$, read root `[7,13,19]`, reach leaf `[7,9]`, emit 9, follow to `[13,17]`, emit both, and follow to `[19,25,31]`, emit 19 and 25, then stop before 31. There are four index-node reads in this example: one root and three leaves. Five qualifying records do not imply five data-block reads; their physical placement is unspecified.

**Limitation:** an unclustered index may point to scattered data pages. Fast index traversal does not guarantee cheap retrieval of a large fraction of a table.

## Why height controls search cost

Let $h$ count **edges** from root to leaf, $K$ count distinct leaf search keys, $m=\lceil n/2\rceil$ be minimum internal fan-out, and $\ell=\lceil(n-1)/2\rceil$ be minimum keys per non-root leaf. These counts are dimensionless. For $h\ge1$:

$$K\ge 2m^{h-1}\ell.$$

**Derivation:** the root has at least two children. Each of the next $h-1$ internal branching stages multiplies the minimum leaf count by $m$. Each resulting leaf has at least $\ell$ keys. A proposed height is impossible if the available $K$ cannot fill those leaves. The root-as-leaf case $h=0$ is handled separately.

For one million distinct keys and $n=100$, $m=50$ and $\ell=50$:

| Proposed edge height | Minimum keys |
|---|---:|
| $h=3$ | $2\times50^2\times50=250,000$ |
| $h=4$ | $2\times50^3\times50=12,500,000$ |

One million is too small for height 4. Therefore at most **three edges and four index nodes** are visited. This derives the slide's four-node result while stating root and leaf occupancy explicitly.[^height]

> [!warning] Logarithms, rounding, and measurements
> PDF p. 11 writes $\log_{50}(1{,}000{,}000)=4$. The logarithm is approximately **3.532**, whose ceiling is 4. Page 10's compact logarithmic bound leaves the height convention implicit; use the occupancy argument above when precision matters. A four-node bound is not a measured latency and excludes data pages. Cached nodes reduce physical reads, not logical tree depth.

The source's approximately 100 pointers per 4 KB node is an illustrative scale, not a universal node format. For a synthetic internal layout with a 4096-byte block, a 16-byte header, 8-byte pointers, and 32-byte separator keys, capacity obeys

$$16+8n+32(n-1)\le4096.$$

Combine terms: $40n-16\le4096$, so $n\le102.8$. Since pointers come in whole units, choose $n=102$. Check: 4064 bytes fit; $n=103$ would need 4104 bytes. Actual DBMS overhead and leaf layouts can differ.

## Insertion — copy at a leaf, promote internally

Why split? An overflowing node cannot remain inside the block capacity, while relocating the whole tree would defeat local maintenance. Splitting creates two valid nodes and one new routing boundary.[^insert]

1. Descend to the target leaf. If the key exists, add the new record pointer to its bucket where appropriate.
2. Otherwise insert the key-pointer entry in order. If the leaf still has at most $n-1$ entries, stop.
3. On leaf overflow there are $n$ entries in a temporary memory area. Keep the first $\lceil n/2\rceil$ entries in the original leaf and put the remainder in a new right leaf.
4. Repair the leaf chain: old leaf → new leaf → old successor. **Copy** the new right leaf's minimum key into the parent together with the new pointer. The key remains in the leaf.
5. If the parent overflows, it contains $n$ separators and $n+1$ children. Set $c=\lceil(n+1)/2\rceil$. Keep pointers $P_1\ldots P_c$ and keys $K_1\ldots K_{c-1}$ on the left; move $K_c$ to the parent; put pointers $P_{c+1}\ldots P_{n+1}$ and keys $K_{c+1}\ldots K_n$ on the right.
6. Continue upward. Splitting a root creates a new root with two children and increases every root-to-leaf path by one edge.

![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/split-rules.svg]]

**Figure 3 — Two different split rules**

**Read it:** Read each column downward; compare where the promoted or copied key remains.

**Key takeaway:** Leaf entries survive in leaves; an internal promoted separator leaves both children. Synthetic leaf example, source internal mechanism pp. 13–16.



**Worked internal split:** with $n=4$, an overflowing internal node has separators `[7,13,19,31]` and five children. $c=\lceil5/2\rceil=3$. Promote the third separator, 19. The left node has `[7,13]` and three children; the right has `[31]` and two children. Neither internal child retains 19.

**Limitation:** a leaf split need not increase height. It does so only if propagation reaches an overflowing root. Different valid splitting policies exist; source exercises use the precise distribution above.

## Deletion — repair occupancy without losing ranges

Deleting one record is different from deleting an entire search-key entry. If a duplicate bucket still contains records, keep its leaf entry. Remove the key entry only when its bucket is empty, or when the indexed key itself is to be deleted.[^delete]

For an underfull node, consider an adjacent sibling **with the same parent**. The course checks merging first: merge if the pair fits in one node; otherwise redistribute. It does not prescribe a universal left-versus-right preference when both choices are valid. State the sibling chosen.

| Repair | What moves | Parent action |
|---|---|---|
| Merge leaves | Combine leaf entries; reconnect leaf chain | Remove separating key and redundant child pointer |
| Redistribute leaves | Move enough boundary entries to satisfy both minima | Replace separator by the new right-leaf lower boundary |
| Merge internal nodes | Combine children **and pull down the parent separator** | Remove that separator and redundant pointer |
| Redistribute internal nodes | Move boundary child pointer; rotate keys through parent | Old parent separator moves down; donor boundary key moves up |

**Leaf worked example, order 4:** after a deletion, `[10,20,30]` and `[40]` contain four keys together. Maximum leaf capacity is three, so merging is impossible. Move 30 from the left leaf to the right: `[10,20]`, `[30,40]`; replace parent separator 40 by 30. Both leaves now contain the required two keys.

![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/internal-redistribute.svg]]

**Figure 4 — Internal redistribution**

**Read it:** A–D denote ordered child subtrees. Follow C from left to right and the boundary keys through the parent.

**Key takeaway:** Pointers and routing boundaries move together. Synthetic example of PDF p. 24.



**Internal worked example, order 3:** the left internal node in Figure 4 has three children; the underfull right node has one. Four children exceed the three-child capacity of a merged internal node. Move left's last child C to the right. Separator 50 descends to separate C from D, while 35 rises to separate the two internal nodes. Both finish with two children. Moving only a key without its child pointer would disconnect an entire subtree.

After a merge, the parent can itself become underfull; repeat at that level. If the root is left with a single child, make that child the new root and decrease the height by one. A final empty leaf-root is valid. This is local reorganisation along a search path, not a full rebuild.[^delete]

## Solve the opening case

### 1 — Lookup and range

For 17, choose the root interval $13\le17<19$ and find 17 in `[13,17]`: **two index blocks**, followed by the record pointer. For range 9–25, the earlier leaf-chain trace returns **9,13,17,19,25**, reading the root and three leaves. Both answer the original predicates completely.

### 2 — Insert 33, then 11, then delete 25

**Insert 33.** The leaf `[19,25,31]` is full. Its temporary entries are `[19,25,31,33]`. Keep the first $\lceil4/2\rceil=2$ entries and create `[31,33]`. Copy 31 upward. The old root becomes `[7,13,19,31]` with five child pointers, so promote 19 as derived above. The tree now has three node levels.

![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/case-insert33.svg]]

**Figure 5 — After inserting 33**

**Read it:** 19 becomes the new root; the leaves remain linked and at equal depth.

**Key takeaway:** The root split adds one level; source PDF p. 35.



**Insert 11.** At root 19 go left; at `[7,13]` choose the middle child. `[7,9]` becomes `[7,9,11]`. Three entries fit; no separator or height change is needed.

![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/case-insert11.svg]]

**Figure 6 — After inserting 11**

**Read it:** Find 11 in the second leaf; compare the upper nodes with Figure 5.

**Key takeaway:** Insertion can be entirely local; source PDF p. 36.



**Delete 25.** Route right at 19 and left at 31. `[19,25]` becomes `[19]`, below the two-key leaf minimum. Its sibling `[31,33]` allows a three-key merge, yielding `[19,31,33]`. Remove separator 31 and one pointer from their parent. That internal node now has only one child. Merge it with the left internal sibling: their $3+1=4$ children fit order 4, and parent separator 19 moves down between them. The former root now has one child, so contract it.

![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/case-delete25.svg]]

**Figure 7 — After deleting 25**

**Read it:** The rightmost leaf now contains 19,31,33; its parent became the root.

**Key takeaway:** Merge propagation can undo the earlier height increase; source PDF p. 37.



### 3 — Validate and interpret

The final root has three separators and four children. Its leaves contain 2, 3, 2, and 3 keys, each within 2–3. Every leaf is one edge below the root. The leaf sequence is `[4,5,7,9,11,13,17,19,31,33]`: both inserted keys survive and only 25 is removed. Intervals remain correct at 7, 13, and 19. Equality lookup again reads **two index nodes** with no cache; it temporarily required three after the root split. This completes all opening success criteria.

## Exam-style answer and reusable method

> [!summary] A defensible short answer
> Order 4 permits at most three leaf entries. Inserting 33 splits the rightmost leaf and then the full root; promote 19. Inserting 11 fits its leaf. Deleting 25 causes a leaf merge, an internal merge, and root contraction. The final root is `[7,13,19]` with leaves `[4,5]`, `[7,9,11]`, `[13,17]`, `[19,31,33]`. Occupancy, routing, key preservation, and equal leaf depth all hold.

For an unfamiliar problem: write the order and minima first; preserve the supplied starting tree; trace the target; make the local change; test overflow/underflow; propagate only when necessary; finally check all leaves and every child range. Count **child pointers** for internal occupancy and **keys** for leaf occupancy. This method assumes the course model and its merge-first policy, not a confirmed commercial implementation.

## Misconceptions and quick review

| Tempting claim | Correct reasoning |
|---|---|
| A separator proves a record exists | Only a matching leaf entry establishes membership |
| Order 4 means four keys per leaf | It means up to four internal child pointers; three leaf keys |
| A leaf merge pulls down the parent key | Only an internal merge needs that separator as an internal boundary |
| Any two neighbouring leaves are eligible siblings | Local repair uses siblings with the same parent |
| Every insert changes the root | Most fit locally; only root overflow increases height |
| One matching key means one record | A duplicate bucket can reference multiple records |

Before looking at a solution, be able to draw a leaf split, rotate an internal child through its parent, explain an absent separator, and derive the four-node million-key example. Then attempt the original lecture tasks in Exercises. **Study status remains untested.**

# B+ tree exercises

Attempt each task before opening its hint. Every original lecture task and worked update appears below; A–E headings indicate retrieval, guided, independent, diagnosis, and exam practice. Original tasks retain their data. Brackets denote keys within one node, never an unordered bag of whole-tree keys. All original page references are to `Lecture2b - B+Tree Indexing (1).pdf`.

## A1 — Read the order correctly

**Supplementary practice · Difficulty: ★☆☆**

For orders 3, 4, and 6, give minimum and maximum non-root internal child counts and leaf key counts. Explain the root exception.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Keep pointers and keys separate.

> [!success]- Solution
> Internal child ranges are **2–3**, **2–4**, and **3–6**. Leaf key ranges are **1–2**, **2–3**, and **3–5**. These follow from ceilings of $n/2$ and $(n-1)/2$, respectively. An internal root requires only two children; a leaf-root may contain zero through $n-1$ keys. Two children imply one separator, not two.

## B1 — Find 29, 31, and 33

**Original course worked lookup and questions · PDF pp. 8–9 · Difficulty: ★☆☆**

Using the source tree below, trace lookup for **29**, **31**, and **33**. State whether each exists and where the decision is made.

![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/lookup.svg]]

**Figure E1 — Original lookup starting tree**

**Read it:** Use the key intervals at each internal node.

**Key takeaway:** An internal match is a routing instruction, not a final answer.


> [!tip]- Hint
> At separator equality choose the right child. Always finish in a leaf.

> [!success]- Solution
> **Step 1 — Route 29.** At 33 go left, then at `[11,22]` take the rightmost pointer. Leaf `[29]` contains 29. Follow its record pointer.
>
> **Step 2 — Route 31.** Take the same path as 29. Leaf `[29]` contains no 31, so the search is unsuccessful.
>
> **Step 3 — Route 33.** Equality at root 33 selects the right child. In `[44]`, 33 is smaller than 44, so visit `[37,41]`. No 33 exists there.
>
> Each search examines three index nodes in the empty-cache model. ==33 is absent== despite appearing as an internal separator. These paths match the algorithm on PDF p. 7.

## B2 — Insert Adams, then follow the name deletions

**Original course worked updates · PDF pp. 17–18 and 25–27 · Difficulty: ★★★**

The source tree has ==order 4==, visible from its node capacities. Use the tree below; names are search keys ordered lexicographically. Apply these operations **sequentially**, drawing each state:

1. Insert `Adams`.
2. Delete `Srinivasan`.
3. Delete `Singh`, then `Wu`, showing both intermediate results.
4. Delete `Gold`.

![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/names-0.svg]]

**Figure E2 — Initial name index**

**Read it:** The root separates names at Mozart; each lower internal node points to its own leaves.

**Key takeaway:** Only same-parent adjacent nodes are eligible for the immediate local repair.


> [!tip]- Hint
> Leaves hold 2–3 keys; non-root internal nodes need 2–4 children. Try merging first. Internal merging must count child pointers.

> [!success]- Solution
> **Step 1 — Insert Adams.** `[Brandt,Califieri,Crick]` overflows into `[Adams,Brandt,Califieri,Crick]`. Split 2+2 and copy `Califieri` into the left internal parent. That parent now has four children and fits.
>
> ![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/names-1.svg]]
>
> **Figure E3 — After Adams**
>
> **Read it:** The new boundary is Califieri.
>
> **Key takeaway:** The root remains Mozart.
>
> **Step 2 — Delete Srinivasan.** The rightmost leaf becomes `[Wu]`, under the two-key minimum. Merge it with `[Mozart,Singh]` into `[Mozart,Singh,Wu]`. The right internal node is left with one child. Merging the internal siblings would require $4+1=5$ child pointers, exceeding order 4, so redistribute instead: move leaf `[Gold,Katz,Kim]` from the left internal node to the right. The root separator changes from `Mozart` to `Gold`; old root boundary `Mozart` moves down into the right internal node.
>
> ![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/names-2.svg]]
>
> **Figure E4 — After Srinivasan**
>
> **Read it:** Gold rises; Mozart moves down.
>
> **Key takeaway:** A leaf merge can trigger internal redistribution.
>
> **Step 3a — Delete Singh.** `[Mozart,Singh,Wu]` becomes `[Mozart,Wu]`; two entries remain, so stop.
>
> ![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/names-3.svg]]
>
> **Figure E5 — After Singh**
>
> **Read it:** Only one leaf changes.
>
> **Key takeaway:** Minimum occupancy is still satisfied.
>
> **Step 3b — Delete Wu.** The leaf becomes `[Mozart]`. With sibling `[Gold,Katz,Kim]`, the total is four keys, so a three-key leaf merge cannot fit. Move `Kim` right and update their parent boundary from `Mozart` to `Kim`. The leaves become `[Gold,Katz]` and `[Kim,Mozart]`.
>
> ![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/names-4.svg]]
>
> **Figure E6 — After Wu**
>
> **Read it:** Kim becomes the new right-leaf minimum.
>
> **Key takeaway:** Redistribution preserves two leaves.
>
> **Step 4 — Delete Gold.** `[Gold,Katz]` becomes `[Katz]`; merge with `[Kim,Mozart]` into `[Katz,Kim,Mozart]`. The right internal node has one child. Its sibling has three children, so an internal merge fits four pointers. Pull down the root separator `Gold`, then remove the redundant root level.
>
> ![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/names-5.svg]]
>
> **Figure E7 — After Gold**
>
> **Read it:** The new root is Califieri, Einstein, Gold.
>
> **Key takeaway:** Gold remains a valid boundary even though its data entry was deleted.
>
> **Interpretation:** the final leaves contain exactly the original names plus Adams, minus Srinivasan, Singh, Wu, and Gold. `Gold` in the root separates `El Said` on the left from `Katz` on the right; it need not be a current leaf key. This matches the source's retained-boundary convention.

## C1 — Construct the order-3 tree

**Original course exercise · PDF p. 28; source stages pp. 29–30 · Difficulty: ★★☆**

Start with an **empty** B+ tree of ==order 3==. Insert `(2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17)` in that **exact order**. Draw the tree after each insertion.

> [!tip]- Hint
> A leaf copies its new right minimum upward; an internal split removes the promoted key from its children.

> [!success]- Solution
> Leaves hold at most two keys. On overflow, keep $\lceil3/2\rceil=2$ keys in the left leaf and put one in the right. An overflowing internal node has three separators and four children; promote separator $\lceil(3+1)/2\rceil=2$.
>
> **Step 1.** Insert 2 into the leaf-root.
>
> ![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/construct-1.svg]]
>
> **Figure E8 — Construction stage 1**
>
> **Read it:** Read the tree from root to leaves.
>
> **Key takeaway:** The leaf sequence preserves all keys inserted so far.
>
> **Step 2.** Insert 3 into the same leaf; it now reaches capacity.
>
> ![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/construct-2.svg]]
>
> **Figure E9 — Construction stage 2**
>
> **Read it:** Read the tree from root to leaves.
>

> **Step 3.** Insert 5: split [2,3,5] into [2,3] and [5]; copy 5 to a new root.

>
> **Read it:** Read the tree from root to leaves.
>

> ![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/construct-4.svg]]
>
> **Figure E11 — Construction stage 4**
>
> **Read it:** Read the tree from root to leaves.
>
> **Key takeaway:** The leaf sequence preserves all keys inserted so far.

> **Step 5.** Insert 11: split [5,7,11] into [5,7] and [11]; root becomes [5,11].
>
> ![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/construct-5.svg]]
>
> **Figure E12 — Construction stage 5**
>
> **Read it:** Read the tree from root to leaves.
>
> **Key takeaway:** The leaf sequence preserves all keys inserted so far.
>
> **Step 6.** Insert 13: the final leaf becomes [11,13].
>
> ![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/construct-6.svg]]
>
> **Figure E13 — Construction stage 6**
>
> **Read it:** Read the tree from root to leaves.
>

> **Step 7.** Insert 17: split the final leaf into [11,13] and [17]. The root temporarily has [5,11,17] and four children; promote 11 to a new root, leaving internal children [5] and [17].

## C2 — Two deletion paths from the same initial tree

**Original course exercise · PDF p. 31, parts (1)–(2); solutions pp. 32–33 · Difficulty: ★★★**

Use the ==order-3== tree below. It is **not** the final tree of C1.

1. Delete 5, then delete 11. Draw both states.
2. Restart from the original tree below and delete 11 only. Draw the result.

![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/delete-initial.svg]]

**Figure E15 — Original deletion starting tree**

**Read it:** The left internal node has three children; the right has two.

**Key takeaway:** The reset in part 2 is essential.


> [!tip]- Hint
> For part 1, state which sibling you choose for the empty [5] leaf. After any leaf merge, inspect the parent child count.

> [!success]- Solution
> **Part 1, delete 5.** Its leaf becomes empty. Choose the left sibling `[2,3]`; combining two keys fits the maximum of two. Remove the old separator 5 and redundant pointer. The left internal node becomes `[7]` with two children. Choosing the right sibling is also a permitted source alternative, but this solution follows the displayed result on p. 32.
>
> ![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/delete5.svg]]
>
> **Figure E16 — After deleting 5**
>
> **Read it:** Left internal separator is 7.
>
> **Key takeaway:** No height change is needed yet.
>
> **Part 1, then delete 11.** Its leaf becomes empty. Merge with `[13,17]`. The right internal node is left with one child. Merge it with the left internal sibling, which has two children: $2+1=3$ fits order 3. Bring down root separator 11 and contract the old root. The new root is `[7,11]`, with leaves `[2,3]`, `[7]`, `[13,17]`.

> **Figure E17 — Then delete 11**
>
> **Read it:** The tree is one level shorter.
>
> **Key takeaway:** Separator 11 still partitions 7 from 13 correctly.
>
> **Part 2, restart and delete 11.** The same leaf merge leaves the right internal node with one child. This time its left internal sibling still has three children. $3+1=4$ exceeds order 3, so merge-first now fails at the internal level. Redistribute the rightmost left child `[7]` to the right internal node. Root separator 11 moves down; left boundary 7 moves up. Final root `[7]`; left internal `[5]` over `[2,3]`, `[5]`; right internal `[11]` over `[7]`, `[13,17]`.

> ![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/delete11.svg]]
>
> **Figure E18 — Restart, then delete 11 only**

> **Read it:** Compare the still-present leaf [5] with part 1.

## D1 — Diagnose three incorrect explanations

**Supplementary practice · Difficulty: ★★☆**

A student says: (a) “The root contains 33, so record 33 exists”; (b) “An internal merge joins the two key lists but ignores the parent separator”; (c) “Deleting one record always removes its search key.” Correct each claim with a counterexample.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Use B1, the internal merge rule, and a bucket containing two record pointers.

> [!success]- Solution
> (a) B1 reaches leaf `[37,41]` and proves 33 absent; the root value is only a boundary. (b) If the left subtree covers values below 11 and the right begins above it, pulling 11 down preserves the boundary between their child-pointer groups; omitting it leaves one fewer separator than required for the combined children. (c) A leaf entry `Physics → [r1,r2]` remains after deleting r1 because r2 is still indexed. Remove the entry only after its bucket becomes empty.

## E1 — The sequential order-4 update exercise

**Original course exercise · PDF p. 34, operations (1)–(3); answers pp. 35–37 · Difficulty: ★★★**

Draw the trees after **(1) insert 33, (2) insert 11, (3) delete 25**. Each operation uses the preceding result. The source starting tree is reproduced here so that you can attempt this without returning to Notes.

![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/case-initial.svg]]

**Figure E19 — Original order-4 starting tree**

**Read it:** Use all four leaves and the supplied separators.

**Key takeaway:** Do not rebuild a different valid tree from the same data.


> [!tip]- Hint
> For insertion 33, test both the leaf and the root. After deletion 25, count the parent pointers again.

> [!success]- Solution
> **1 — Insert 33.** The rightmost leaf overflows to `[19,25,31,33]`; split 2+2, copy 31 upward. The root overflows to `[7,13,19,31]` with five children. Promote 19, leaving internal `[7,13]` and `[31]`.

> ![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/case-insert33.svg]]
>
> **Figure E20 — After operation 1**
>
> **Read it:** All leaves move one level farther from the new root.
>
> **Key takeaway:** A split cascade reaches the root.
>
> **2 — Insert 11.** Descend left of 19, then between 7 and 13. Leaf `[7,9]` becomes `[7,9,11]`, which fits.
>
> ![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/case-insert11.svg]]
>
> **Figure E21 — After operation 2**
>
> **Read it:** Only the second leaf changes.
>
> **Key takeaway:** No split is needed.
>
> **3 — Delete 25.** Leaf `[19,25]` becomes `[19]`; merge with `[31,33]` to get `[19,31,33]`. Remove parent separator 31. Its parent now has one child, so merge with the three-child left sibling, bringing separator 19 down. Contract the root. Final root `[7,13,19]` over `[4,5]`, `[7,9,11]`, `[13,17]`, `[19,31,33]`.
>
> ![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/Attachments/case-delete25.svg]]
>
> **Figure E22 — After operation 3**
>
> **Read it:** The final root again points directly to leaves.
>
> **Key takeaway:** Every non-root leaf has two or three entries, and all survivors appear once.

## E2 — Capacity and a search bound

**Supplementary transfer problem · Difficulty: ★★☆**

An internal-node block has 4096 bytes, a 16-byte header, 8-byte child pointers, and 32-byte separator keys. Find its maximum order. Separately, for order 100 and one million distinct leaf keys, prove a bound on uncached index-node reads. Do not assume that the computed byte-layout order and the stipulated order 100 are identical.

> [!tip]- Hint
> With n pointers there are n−1 keys. For height, count minimum leaves and keys at a proposed depth.

> [!success]- Solution
> **Step 1 — Capacity.** $16+8n+32(n-1)\le4096$ gives $40n\le4112$ and $n\le102.8$. Floor to ==102 pointers==. At 102, bytes used are $16+816+3232=4064$; 103 would use 4104 and fail.
>
> **Step 2 — Order-100 occupancy.** Minimum internal fan-out and leaf occupancy are both 50. A tree with four root-to-leaf edges would require at least $2\times50^3\times50=12,500,000$ keys. One million cannot fill it; at most three edges and ==four index-node reads== are possible. Data-record retrieval and caching are separate. The argument is about an academic structural model, not measured performance.
