# Advanced-indexing exercises

`Lecture3b - Advanced Indexing.pdf` supplies mechanisms and worked examples rather than a numbered exercise sheet. B1 and B2 reproduce its original worked data; other questions are labelled supplementary practice. Each answer follows its question in a collapsed callout. Bit strings are always read left to right as ascending record numbers.

## A1 — Match the question to the structure

**Supplementary retrieval · Difficulty: ★☆☆**

Choose a suitable family for (a) batched scattered inserts, (b) several low-cardinality category predicates, (c) rejection of irrelevant LSM trees, (d) rectangle intersection, and (e) point-in-time versions. Give one limitation for each.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Match the kind of work: writes, exact sets, approximate membership, geometry, time.

> [!success]- Solution
> (a) LSM or buffer tree: merging or buffered propagation still costs work. (b) Bitmap index: requires aligned record positions and maintained bits. (c) Bloom filter: positive answers can be false positives. (d) R-tree: overlapping bounding boxes can require multiple paths and exact geometry checks. (e) Temporal index combining current and historical records: both branches may need searching and endpoint semantics must be specified. The best choice also depends on updates and distribution; no single family dominates every workload.

## B1 — Reconstruct the lecture bitmaps and original AND query

**Original course worked example · PDF pp. 9–10 · Difficulty: ★☆☆**

| Record number | ID | gender | income_level |
|---:|---:|---|---|
| 0 | 76766 | m | L1 |
| 1 | 22222 | f | L2 |
| 2 | 12121 | f | L1 |
| 3 | 15151 | m | L4 |
| 4 | 58583 | f | L3 |

Reconstruct the supplied bitmaps for `m`, `f`, and L1–L5. Reproduce the original query **“males with income level L1”** and give its record number, ID, and count. The wording and source field values are retained.

> [!tip]- Hint
> For each value, mark the rows containing it. AND bits at the same positions.

> [!success]- Solution
> **Step 1 — Encode.** `m=10010`, `f=01101`; `L1=10100`, `L2=01000`, `L3=00001`, `L4=00010`, `L5=00000`. L5 is empty because none of the five records has that level.
>
> **Step 2 — Intersect.** `10010 AND 10100 = 10000`.
>
> **Step 3 — Interpret.** Only ==record 0== matches: **ID 76766**, and the count is **1**. Bits denote record numbers, not the numeric digits of the IDs.
>
> ![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 04 - Advanced Indexing/Attachments/bitmap-and.svg]]
>
> **Figure E1 — Original bitmap intersection**
>
> **Read it:** Match each source row to the bit directly above its position.
>
> **Key takeaway:** Counting the one set bit is enough for the count; returning the tuple uses record 0.

## B2 — Read the original temporal course table

**Source-derived practice using original worked data · PDF pp. 21–22 · Difficulty: ★★☆**

| course_id | title | dept_name | credits | start | end |
|---|---|---|---:|---|---|
| BIO-101 | Intro. to Biology | Biology | 4 | 1985-01-01 | 9999-12-31 |
| CS-201 | Intro. to C | Comp. Sci. | 4 | 1985-01-01 | 1990-01-01 |
| CS-201 | Intro. to Java | Comp. Sci. | 4 | 1990-01-01 | 2010-01-01 |
| CS-201 | Intro. to Python | Comp. Sci. | 4 | 2010-01-01 | 9999-12-31 |

Use the explicit teaching assumption ==[start,end)==. The source presents these records but does not specify these exact query dates or full endpoint semantics; the following questions are pedagogical applications:

1. Which CS-201 version is valid on 1989-06-01, 1990-01-01, and 2010-01-01?
2. Which records belong in the source's current-tuple index and which in its finite-interval historical index?
3. Why is searching only the current index insufficient for 1989-06-01?

> [!tip]- Hint
> The end is excluded. Current records have the large sentinel end date.

> [!success]- Solution
> **1 — Point-in-time results.** 1989-06-01 lies within [1985-01-01,1990-01-01), so return **Intro. to C**. At 1990-01-01, C has ended and **Intro. to Java** begins. At 2010-01-01, Java has ended and **Intro. to Python** begins. Each query includes the `course_id=CS-201` predicate, so BIO-101 is not returned.
>
> **2 — Index assignment.** Current index: BIO-101 Biology and CS-201 Python, both with sentinel `9999-12-31`. Historical index: CS-201 C and Java, whose end dates are finite historical boundaries. The current index can use `(course_id,start)`; historical rectangles represent the key dimension and time interval.
>
> **3 — Why both branches matter.** At 1989-06-01 the currently stored Python version has a later start, so it does not qualify; the matching C version is historical. A current-only lookup would incorrectly return no version. Endpoint inclusion remains a declared assumption; an instructor-specified convention takes precedence.

## C1 — LSM thresholds, merge work, and tombstones

**Supplementary guided calculation · Difficulty: ★★☆**

An LSM memory level has threshold 100 entries and each subsequent level threshold is four times the preceding one. Find L1, L2, and L3 thresholds. Merge sorted incoming `[1,7]` with old `[2,5,9]`. Finally, explain the error in discarding `delete A` from L0 while `A=old` survives in an unmerged L2.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Thresholds multiply; merging compares front entries; a tombstone protects against older versions.

> [!success]- Solution
> **Thresholds:** L1=$4\times100=400$ entries; L2=$4\times400=1600$; L3=$4\times1600=6400$. These are capacities, not simultaneous measured occupancies.
>
> **Merge:** choose 1 before 2, then 2 before 7, then 5 before 7, then 7 before 9; append 9. Output is **[1,2,5,7,9]**. Existing entries 2,5,9 are copied, so sequential I/O does not imply zero rewrite work.
>
> **Tombstone:** discarding `delete A` without accounting for the older L2 version can resurrect `A=old` on a later lookup. Retain deletion evidence until relevant older versions can safely be suppressed or removed. This counterexample explains the limitation of the lecture's simplified “drop matching pairs” merge description.

## C2 — A Bloom filter you can draw by hand

**Supplementary guided construction · Difficulty: ★★☆**

Start with 12 zero bits, $h_1(x)=x\bmod12$, and $h_2(x)=(5x+1)\bmod12$. Insert 2 and 5. Query 2,8,14. Then show why clearing the bits for 5 is an unsafe deletion procedure.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Different values can reuse a bit. Keep the exact set {2,5} separate from the filter answer.

> [!success]- Solution
> **Insert 2:** positions 2 and $(5\times2+1)\bmod12=11$. **Insert 5:** positions 5 and $26\bmod12=2$. Set bits are **{2,5,11}**.
>
> **Query 2:** positions {2,11}, both set; possibly present, and exact checking confirms membership. **Query 8:** positions {8,5}; bit 8 is zero, so definitely absent. **Query 14:** positions {2,11}; both set, but 14 is absent from {2,5}, so this is a **false positive**.
>
> To delete 5 by clearing its bits, the naive procedure clears both 5 and 2. But 2 still needs bit 2; its next query sees a zero and becomes a false negative. Ordinary Bloom-filter deletion cannot simply clear shared bits.
>
> ![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 04 - Advanced Indexing/Attachments/bloom-bits.svg]]
>
> **Figure E2 — Tiny Bloom state**
>
> **Read it:** Separate exact membership from the two queried bit positions.
>
> **Key takeaway:** The no-false-negative property depends on preserving bits needed by all inserted elements.

## C3 — Interpret the rounded false-positive estimates

**Supplementary mathematical clarification of PDF p. 12 · Difficulty: ★★☆**

Under the uniform independent-placement model, a Bloom filter has $m=10n$ bits. Estimate false-positive probability for $k=1$ and $k=7$ using $(1-e^{-kn/m})^k$. Interpret the expected number of positives among 1000 absent queries. Why is this not an execution result for C2's tiny filter?

> [!tip]- Hint
> Substitute n/m=0.1. The bit tests are approximated as independent.

> [!success]- Solution
> For $k=1$, $1-e^{-0.1}\approx0.0951626$, about **9.52%**. Among 1000 absent queries, the model's expected count is about **95.2**. For $k=7$, $(1-e^{-0.7})^7\approx0.00819372$, about **0.819%**, giving an expected count about **8.19**.
>
> The slide's 10% and 1% figures are rounded scale estimates. An expectation is not an exact observed count. C2 has a very small array and deliberately simple correlated hash functions, so the assumptions behind the estimate do not establish that filter's empirical false-positive rate. Actual finite-domain enumeration is a different measurement.

## D1 — Trace a spatial range and reject a false candidate

**Supplementary spatial diagnosis · Difficulty: ★★☆**

A=(1,1), B=(2,6), C=(4,3), D=(6,7), E=(7,2), F=(9,5). Find all points in x∈[3,8], y∈[1,6]. With a k-d root split x=5 and next-level splits y=4, explain which branches the query must visit. Separately, does query rectangle [3,4]×[3,4] intersect triangle T with vertices (0,0),(4,0),(0,4), or only its bounding rectangle?

> [!tip]- Hint
> Check both coordinates. A range can cross a split. For the triangle use x+y≤4.

> [!success]- Solution
> **Point result:** C and E meet both ranges. A,B fail the lower x bound, D exceeds y=6, and F exceeds x=8. The query crosses x=5 and y=4, so both relevant sides must be explored at each of those splits; reaching a leaf still requires exact coordinate comparisons.
>
> **Triangle result:** T's bounding rectangle is [0,4]×[0,4], so the query intersects it. But query points have x+y≥6, while triangle points satisfy x+y≤4. There is **no triangle intersection**. A bounding-box filter returns a candidate; exact geometry rejects it.

## E1 — Compare k-d and quadtree subdivision

**Supplementary independent construction · Difficulty: ★★☆**

Use D1's six points within [0,10]×[0,10]. A quadtree leaf holds at most one point. Assign split-boundary points to the right/top region. Draw the first root split and identify every quadrant that needs another split. Explain how this differs from choosing approximately balanced point-count splits in a k-d tree.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Root midpoints are (5,5). Count points in each quadrant, including F on y=5.

> [!success]- Solution
> Root quadrants: SW contains **A,C**, NW contains **B**, SE contains **E**, NE contains **D,F**. F=(9,5) belongs to NE under the stated boundary convention. Split SW at (2.5,2.5) and NE at (7.5,7.5); each occupied resulting leaf then contains one point, and empty leaves are allowed.
>
> A quadtree always divides a region into four equal geometric parts. A k-d tree splits into two, cycles dimensions, and may choose cut positions to balance point counts. Equal spatial area does not imply equal numbers of points.
>
> ![[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 04 - Advanced Indexing/Attachments/quadtree.svg]]
>
> **Figure E3 — Required quadtree refinement**
>
> **Read it:** SW and NE receive additional midpoint splits.
>
> **Key takeaway:** No split is needed for the one-point NW and SE quadrants.

## E2 — Defend the campus-service design

**Supplementary exam-style synthesis · Difficulty: ★★★**

For the opening case in Notes, give (a) a defensible write-oriented structure and its query cost, (b) exact matching record numbers for `sensor=101010 AND active=110011`, (c) the roles of Bloom filtering and exact checks, and (d) the versions of asset 42 at t=4 and t=5 when old=[1,5), new=[5,∞). State one assumption that would change the method.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Choose from predicate semantics. Explain every result, not only the index names.

> [!success]- Solution
> (a) LSM batching is reasonable for sustained scattered inserts because sorted batches can be merged sequentially; queries must search relevant levels and reconcile versions/tombstones. A buffer tree is an alternative with range-directed batches and pending-buffer checks.
>
> (b) Position-wise AND gives **100010**, selecting records **0 and 4**.
>
> (c) A Bloom zero safely rejects an absent value under correct filter maintenance; all-one tests produce candidates, so exact membership checking is still required. R-tree bounding regions similarly prune, but exact geometry may reject surviving candidates.
>
> (d) At t=4, 1≤4<5 selects **old**. At t=5, old fails its strict end test and 5≤5<∞ selects **new**. Search current and historical branches as needed.
>
> A change from half-open to closed intervals would make both versions include t=5 unless another rule resolved the overlap. A change to bitmap record numbering would require realigning the bitmaps before AND. A range-heavy workload could favour ordered structures over hashing.

# Lab — a candidate is not yet an answer

## Purpose and scope

Compare exact bitmap results with Bloom and spatial candidate filtering, then verify a temporal boundary. The five-row bitmap dataset is from `Lecture3b - Advanced Indexing.pdf`, PDF p. 9; the other datasets are labelled synthetic constructions from this unit. The mechanisms connect to source pp. 10–12 and 15–22.

This is a **supplementary Python model**, not a DBMS implementation or a measurement of an actual R-tree, LSM tree, or disk. Its benefit is that you can compare every filter result with an independent exhaustive predicate evaluation on a small inspectable dataset.

## Environment and files

- Python 3 with its standard library; no third-party packages, database server, network access, or installation is required by the lab script.
- [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 04 - Advanced Indexing/Attachments/filter_lab.py|filter_lab.py]] contains the source data, algorithms, and checks.
- The recorded execution used **Python 3.14.6**. This is a lab execution version, not a course-specified version.

Open a terminal in this unit's folder, then run:

```sh
python3 Attachments/filter_lab.py
```

The script prints JSON to standard output. It does not modify the vault or create files. It does not require an online service.

## Procedure

1. Read the source data and predict the bitmap AND result before execution. Notice that the displayed bit strings put record 0 on the left, while the program stores that record in integer bit 0.
2. Run the script and find `bitmap`. It builds masks from rows, then compares 98 AND/OR combinations with independent row predicates. A failed assertion stops the run.
3. Read `bloom`. It inserts {2,5}, probes all integers 0–59, compares candidate results with exact membership, and reports false positives. It also performs a deliberately incorrect bit-clearing deletion in a separate copy to demonstrate how a false negative is introduced.
4. Read `spatial`. The script groups points A,B,C and D,E,F under their bounding rectangles. It compares filtered answers with a full point scan for **4356** inclusive rectangles with integer endpoints from 0 through 10. This tests candidate completeness for this finite domain; it does not implement a complete R-tree.
5. Read `temporal_half_open` and inspect how strict end-time comparison changes the result at time 5.

## Results and interpretation

**OBSERVED — EXECUTED AND VERIFIED.** The unchanged script completed with Python 3.14.6 and printed:

| Check | Observed result | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Original bitmap query | `10000`; selected ID `[76766]` | One exact matching source record |
| Bitmap comparison | 98 predicate combinations passed | Mask results agree with row-wise AND/OR predicates |
| Bloom set bits | `[2,5,11]` | Bit positions encode membership evidence |
| Query 8 | Candidate false; exact member false | Zero bit correctly rejects it |
| Query 14 | Candidate true; exact member false | An actual false positive in this model |
| Finite-domain Bloom enumeration | 8 false positives among 58 absent queries; no false negatives for inserted {2,5} | This deliberately simple filter does not have the slide's approximate 1% behaviour |
| Naive deletion of 5 | Breaks membership evidence for 2 | Shared-bit clearing creates a false negative |
| Spatial query | Candidates A–F; exact matches C,E | Candidate pruning can still retain nonmatching points |
| Rectangle comparison | 4356 filtered results equal full scans | No false negatives for the checked finite rectangle set |
| Triangle query | Box candidate true; exact intersection false | Bounding-box intersection does not prove polygon intersection |
| Time 4 / time 5 | `old` / `new` | Half-open intervals avoid a duplicate boundary match |

The eight Bloom false positives are **14,17,26,29,38,41,50,53**. Their finite-domain fraction is $8/58\approx13.79\%$. This differs from the lecture's estimate because the toy filter's size, load and correlated functions are different; the lecture example assumes 10 bits per element with seven suitable hash functions.

The rectangle count can be recomputed: among 11 integer coordinates, inclusive intervals allowing equal endpoints number $11+10+\cdots+1=66$. Independent x/y choices give $66^2=4356$ rectangles. A degenerate interval representing a line or point remains a valid inclusive query in this model.

## Practice and reflection

### Lab task 1 — Explain the candidate set

Why can both spatial group boxes overlap the query while only C and E satisfy it?

> [!tip]- Hint
> A bounding rectangle encloses points but also empty space.

> [!success]- Solution
> The first group's bounding box spans x=1–4, y=1–6, and the second spans x=6–9, y=2–7. Both intersect query x=3–8,y=1–6, so neither group can be rejected. Testing the actual six points removes A,B,D,F. The group test is a conservative filter; exact comparisons finish the answer.

### Lab task 2 — Design a controlled change

Without changing record numbering, change the source query from `m AND L1` to `f AND L1`. Predict the result. Treat this variant as **EXPECTED — NOT EXECUTED** until you actually run your modified copy.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Use f=01101 and L1=10100.

> [!success]- Solution
> `01101 AND 10100 = 00100`, selecting record **2**, ID **12121**. The observed-run table above records the original query only. A modified run should report its own inputs and result rather than inherit the earlier evidence.

### Lab task 3 — Explain the limits of verification

Do 4356 passing rectangle checks prove correctness for every possible geometry, floating-point boundary, and DBMS implementation?

> [!tip]- Hint
> Describe exactly what was enumerated.

> [!success]- Solution
> No. The checks cover six fixed synthetic points, two fixed bounding groups, inclusive rectangular predicates, and integer endpoints 0–10. They do not cover arbitrary polygons, numerical robustness, disk layouts, concurrency, index update algorithms, or a specific DBMS. The finite check is strong evidence for this small model and no more.


## Reuse and cleanup

Keep the supplied script as a reproducible baseline. For experimentation, make a separate copy outside the vault or save an explicitly named variant so that the baseline evidence remains meaningful. The baseline script creates no files, so no generated database or cache needs deletion.

# Relational Algebra

Web tutor edition from `Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf`, PDF pp.1–40. The supplied slides are the authority. Examples marked supplementary are teaching variations, not official exam questions.

## In 60 Seconds

A query becomes easier to reason about when you treat each intermediate result as a relation. Selection keeps qualifying rows; projection keeps named columns; set operations combine compatible relations; product pairs tuples; rename resolves names. Joins and division express common combinations. These operators explain the meaning of a query before you choose how a DBMS executes it.

**Goal:** trace a query from its input relations to its result, explain duplicate removal, and translate “both” or “all” into the right operation. Source: Lecture4a, PDF pp.2,6–9,26–39.

## Before You Start

You need to distinguish a row from a column and read simple comparisons. The earlier storage and indexing units explain access paths; this unit explains which tuples the access path must eventually return. Relational algebra uses set semantics: duplicate tuples disappear and tuple order is irrelevant. SQL can use bag semantics, so do not silently assume every SQL query has this duplicate behaviour. Source: Lecture4a, PDF pp.6–7.

## A motivating question

The bank asks: “Which customers hold an account at **every** Brooklyn branch?” Why is finding customers at one Brooklyn branch insufficient? Keep this question in mind while learning the operators. This is the source query on Lecture4a, PDF p.39.

## 1. Describe the relation before changing it

A **schema** names the attributes; an **instance** is the current set of tuples over that schema. An attribute has a domain of allowed values. The slides introduce atomic values and `null` as an unknown value; they do not establish the full SQL three-valued logic rules, so the set examples below use ordinary, known values.

A superkey uniquely identifies tuples in every valid instance. A candidate key is a **minimal** superkey: removing any attribute destroys that guarantee. Choose one candidate key as the primary key. A foreign-key constraint links values to a referenced relation. `{ID, name}` may be a superkey without being a candidate key when `{ID}` already suffices. Source: Lecture4a, PDF pp.3–5.

## 2. Selection keeps rows; projection keeps columns

Selection is $\sigma_p(r)=\{t\in r\mid p(t)\}$. Its predicate can compare attributes or constants and combine terms with AND, OR and NOT. It retains the input attributes.

The source example contains `(a,a,1,7)`, `(a,b,5,7)`, `(b,b,12,3)`, `(b,b,23,10)` over `(A,B,C,D)`. Applying $\sigma_{A=B\land D>5}$ keeps the first and fourth tuples: the third has equal `A,B` but fails the second condition. Source: Lecture4a, PDF pp.10–11.

Projection $\pi_{A_1,\ldots,A_k}(r)$ keeps only the named attributes, then removes duplicate resulting tuples. The source projection from `(A,B,C)` to `(A,C)` turns four rows into `{(a,1),(b,1),(b,2)}` because two input rows map to `(a,1)`. Source: Lecture4a, PDF pp.12–13.

> [!question]- Try before continuing
> Can projection increase the number of tuples in set relational algebra?

> [!success]- Check
> No. Each input tuple produces one projected tuple, and duplicates can collapse. This is a definition-based consequence of Lecture4a, PDF pp.12–13.

## 3. Combine compatible sets

Union $r\cup s$ keeps tuples present in either input. Difference $r-s$ keeps tuples present in `r` and absent from `s`. Intersection $r\cap s$ keeps tuples in both and can be expressed as $r-(r-s)$.

These operations require the same arity and compatible attribute domains; align the corresponding attributes. They combine **whole tuples**, not independently selected cells. Difference is directional: $r-s$ usually differs from $s-r$.

For the source `r={(a,1),(a,2),(b,1)}` and `s={(a,2),(b,3)}`, union adds `(b,3)` once; difference is `{(a,1),(b,1)}`; intersection is `{(a,2)}`. Source: Lecture4a, PDF pp.14–17,27–28.

## 4. Product pairs tuples; rename makes the pairing unambiguous

Cartesian product $r\times s$ pairs every tuple of `r` with every tuple of `s`, concatenating their attributes. With disjoint attribute names, two input tuples paired with four give eight output tuples. If names overlap, rename or qualify attributes before referring to them. The source then selects matching `A=C` pairs from the product. Source: Lecture4a, PDF pp.18–20.

Rename $\rho_x(E)$ gives an expression a relation name; its extended form also names the attributes. It is particularly useful when a relation must be compared with another copy of itself. Rename changes identifiers, not the stored values. Source: Lecture4a, PDF p.21.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  R[Input relation r] --> P[Pair every tuple]
  S[Input relation s] --> P
  P --> F[Keep matching pairs]
  F --> C[Keep requested columns]
```

Supplementary visualisation of the composition on Lecture4a, PDF pp.18–24.

## 5. Natural join matches every common attribute

A natural join combines tuples that agree on **all** common attribute names. The output includes those common attributes once, plus the attributes unique to each input.

If schemas are `(A,B,C,D)` and `(E,B,D)`, agreement is required on both `B` and `D`, not just one. The source defines this as a product, a matching selection, and a projection that removes duplicate common columns. A natural join can accidentally constrain an unrelated same-named attribute; inspect the schemas first. Source: Lecture4a, PDF pp.29–30.

## 6. Division answers an all-of question

Let `r` have attributes `(A,B)` and let `s` list required `B` values. Then $r\div s$ keeps each candidate `A` whose pairing with **every** `B` in `s` occurs in `r`.

In the source p.32 example, `s={1,2}`. Both `a` and `b` have pairings with 1 and 2; `g` and `d` do not. The answer is `{a,b}`. Extra pairings do not disqualify a candidate. Source: Lecture4a, PDF pp.31–33.

The basic-operator construction is easiest to read as “candidates minus failures”:

$$C=\pi_{R-S}(r),\qquad M=(C\times s)-\pi_{R-S,S}(r)$$
$$r\div s=C-\pi_{R-S}(M).$$

`M` contains required pairings that are missing. Project their candidate attributes, then remove those candidates. The attribute-reordering projection aligns the subtraction. Candidates are drawn from `C`; this avoids treating the slide's “largest relation” phrase as an unbounded search over arbitrary values. Source: Lecture4a, PDF pp.34–35.

## 7. Read an expression from the inside out

For customers with Perryridge loans, first connect borrower and loan by `loan_number`, select `branch_name=Perryridge`, and project `customer_name`. The slides also show filtering the loan input before the product. These expressions preserve the intended answer but can lead to different amounts of intermediate work. Source: Lecture4a, PDF p.24.

To find the largest account balance without an aggregate operator, rename a second copy as `d`, find each account whose balance is less than another, project those nonmaximum balances, and subtract them from all balances. This keeps the maximum **balance value**, including the case where multiple accounts share it. Source: Lecture4a, PDF p.25.

Assignment names temporary intermediate relations, making a long expression readable. It is not a persistent table update. Source: Lecture4a, PDF p.35.

## Return to the motivating question

Build customer/branch pairs from `depositor` joined with `account`. Separately select the Brooklyn branches and project their branch names. Divide the pairs by that required branch relation, following p.39. Joining to one Brooklyn branch only proves “at least one”; division checks every branch in the required set.

## Definitions and distinctions

| Need | Operation | Check first |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Qualifying tuples | Selection | Predicate refers to available attributes |
| Selected attributes | Projection | Set duplicate removal |
| Either / both / only in first | Union / intersection / difference | Arity and domain compatibility |
| Every tuple pairing | Product | Names are unambiguous |
| Matching shared values | Natural join | All common attribute names |
| Every required pairing | Division | Divisor attributes belong to the dividend |

Source: Lecture4a, PDF pp.8–35. Physical scan/index choices belong to the next unit; these expressions establish logical results.

## Review

Explain the six basic operators from memory. Trace the source projection and explain why a row disappears. Distinguish “at both named branches” from “at all branches in a relation”. Then attempt the original query translations in Recall & practice with the notes closed.

## Sources and scope

# Relational algebra: recall and practice

Web tutor edition. New practice below is **SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE**, not an official assignment or marking scheme. Sources: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf. Attempt before opening help.

## Atomic Recall

### Card 01 — What does selection change?
> [!success]- Answer
> Selection keeps tuples satisfying a predicate; it preserves the attribute schema.
>
> Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF pp. 10–11.

### Card 02 — What does projection change?
> [!success]- Answer
> Projection keeps named attributes. In set relational algebra identical result tuples collapse to one.
>
> Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF pp. 12–13.

### Card 03 — What is union compatibility?
> [!success]- Answer
> Equal arity and compatible corresponding attribute domains; align names/order before a set operation.
>
> Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF pp. 14–18.

### Card 04 — Is difference commutative?
> [!success]- Answer
> No. r−s keeps tuples in r absent from s; s−r asks the opposite question.
>
> Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF pp. 16–17.

### Card 05 — How large is a Cartesian product?
> [!success]- Answer
> Every left tuple pairs with every right tuple: |r×s|=|r|·|s|. Rename ambiguous attribute names.
>
> Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF pp. 19–22.

### Card 06 — What does natural join match?
> [!success]- Answer
> Equality of all attributes with common names, then one copy of each common attribute remains.
>
> Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF pp. 26–29.

### Card 07 — Why rename a relation?
> [!success]- Answer
> To name an intermediate result or distinguish copies of the same relation and their attributes.
>
> Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF p. 22.

### Card 08 — For relations r(X,Y) and s(Y), what does division r ÷ s return, and where do candidate X values come from?
> [!success]- Answer
> Return X tuples from πX(r) that occur in r paired with every Y tuple in s. Extra Y pairings are allowed; if s is empty, every candidate in πX(r) qualifies.
>
> Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF pp. 30–34.

### Card 09 — For r(X,Y) and s(Y), how does candidates minus failures implement division?
> [!success]- Answer
> Start T=πX(r). Missing pairs are (T×s)−r. Project their X values and subtract those failed candidates from T.
>
> Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF p. 34.

### Card 10 — How can difference find a maximum?
> [!success]- Answer
> Rename a second copy, find values smaller than some other value, and subtract those nonmaximum values from all values. Ties remain.
>
> Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF p. 25.

### Card 11 — How do borrower and depositor answer both versus either?
> [!success]- Answer
> Intersect projected customer names for both; union them for either.
>
> Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF pp. 14–18, 36.

### Card 12 — Does algebra projection equal ordinary SQL SELECT?
> [!success]- Answer
> Not necessarily: this lecture uses sets; SQL without DISTINCT can preserve duplicates and has additional NULL behavior.
>
> Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF pp. 12–13; set-semantics qualification.

## Progressive Practice

### Practice 1 — Selection then projection

**SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE.** Let account(branch_name,balance)={(Downtown,500),(Uptown,500),(Downtown,900)}. Evaluate π_balance(σ_branch_name=Downtown(account)).

> [!tip]- Hint
> Keep Downtown rows first, then remove duplicate projected values.

> [!success]- Solution
> Selection gives {(Downtown,500),(Downtown,900)}. Projection gives {500,900}. Selecting Downtown after projecting only balance is invalid: branch_name was discarded.
>
> Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF pp. 10–13.

### Practice 2 — Both, either, only

**SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE.** borrower names={A,B}; depositor names={B,C}. Find customers with both, either, and loans only.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Choose intersection, union and ordered difference.

> [!success]- Solution
> Both={B}; either={A,B,C}; loans only={A}. Deposits only would be {C}; difference order matters.
>
> Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF pp. 14–18, 36.

### Practice 3 — Join without accidental matches

**SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE.** borrower(customer_name,loan_number)={(A,L1),(B,L2)}; loan(loan_number,branch_name,amount)={(L1,Perryridge,1500),(L2,Downtown,900)}. Find Perryridge borrowers.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Join on loan_number, select branch, project name.

> [!success]- Solution
> π_customer_name(σ_branch_name=Perryridge(borrower ⋈ loan))={A}. The only common attribute is loan_number. With product and selection, qualify the two loan_number attributes and equate them.
>
> Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF pp. 24, 26–29.

### Practice 4 — Division by every required value

**SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE.** r(name,branch)={(A,D),(A,U),(B,D),(C,U)} and s(branch)={D,U}. Compute r÷s using missing pairs.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Build candidate×required pairs and subtract present pairs.

> [!success]- Solution
> Candidates={A,B,C}. Missing pairs={(B,U),(C,D)}. Failed candidates={B,C}. Result={A}. Membership in some required branch is insufficient.
>
> Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF pp. 30–34, 39.

### Practice 5 — Maximum with ties

**SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE.** Four account rows have balances 500, 900, 900 and 200 (a list of values, not a mathematical set). Use a renamed copy to describe a maximum query.

> [!tip]- Hint
> A nonmaximum balance is smaller than at least one other balance.

> [!success]- Solution
> Set projection gives {200,500,900}. Nonmaximum values are {200,500}; difference gives {900}. Returning customer/account tuples with balance 900 can retain multiple accounts; the value relation itself has one 900.
>
> Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF p. 25.

### Practice 6 — Translate the lecture queries

**SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE.** Use `loan(loan_number,branch_name,amount)` and `borrower(customer_name,loan_number)`. Write set relational-algebra expressions for (a) all loan tuples with amount above 1200; (b) customer name, loan number and amount for each borrower’s loan; (c) names of customers with at least one loan at Downtown and at least one at Uptown. Both relations share only `loan_number`.

Source: Lecture4a, PDF pp.23,37–38.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Use selection; join plus projection; then an intersection of two name relations.

> [!success]- Solution
> σ_amount>1200(loan).
> π_customer_name,loan_number,amount(borrower ⋈ loan).
> π_customer_name(σ_branch_name=Downtown(borrower ⋈ loan)) ∩ π_customer_name(σ_branch_name=Uptown(borrower ⋈ loan)).
>
> Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF pp. 23, 37–38.

### Practice 7 — Empty divisor boundary

**SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE.** If s is empty, what is r÷s under the candidate universe πX(r)?

> [!tip]- Hint
> Every required pair is present when there are no requirements.

> [!success]- Solution
> T×s is empty, so missing pairs and failed candidates are empty. The result is T=πX(r). It does not invent X values absent from that candidate universe.
>
> Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF p. 34; boundary derived from displayed formula.

# Query Evaluation Basics

Web tutor edition from `Lecture4b - Query Evaluation Basics.pdf`, PDF pp.1–12.

## In 60 Seconds

A DBMS parses and translates a query, optimises a plan, then evaluates it. An algebra expression describes the logical result; a physical plan adds implementation choices. Equivalent plans can have different estimated costs. The lecture's simple disk model is $b\,t_T+s\,t_S$, where `b` is transfers, `s` is seeks, and the times use the same unit. Source: Lecture4b, PDF pp.4–11.

## Before You Start

Use the preceding unit to identify selection and projection. Use storage and indexing to explain what a scan or index access path does. You do not need database credentials to learn the logical pipeline or calculate the supplied cost model.

## A motivating question

Two plans return account balances below 2500. One scans the account file; the other uses a balance index. Why can equal results require different work, and what evidence is needed before calling either plan faster? This follows the source example on Lecture4b, PDF p.8.

## 1. Follow the query through three stages

**Parsing and translation:** check query syntax and verify the referenced relations, then form an internal representation and an algebra expression. **Optimisation:** consider equivalent expressions and ways of implementing their operations. **Evaluation:** the execution engine follows the selected plan and returns answers. The optimiser consults statistics; the execution engine accesses data. Source: Lecture4b, PDF pp.4–7,9.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Q[Query] --> P[Parse and translate]
  P --> A[Logical algebra]
  A --> O[Choose physical plan]
  S[Catalog statistics] --> O
  O --> E[Evaluate]
  D[Data] --> E
  E --> R[Result]
```

Supplementary rendering of the source pipeline, PDF p.4.

## 2. Separate logical equivalence from physical strategy

The source compares:

$$\sigma_{balance<2500}(\pi_{balance}(account))$$
$$\pi_{balance}(\sigma_{balance<2500}(account)).$$

Both keep the same distinct balance values under the lecture's set model. In the first, the predicate still has its required `balance` attribute after projection. Moving an arbitrary selection past a projection that removes an attribute it needs is invalid. Source: Lecture4b, PDF p.8; Lecture4a, PDF pp.10–13.

The same logical expression may use different algorithms. A physical evaluation plan annotates detailed strategy: for example, use an index or scan linearly and discard failing tuples. The existence of an index does not by itself prove that the chosen plan uses it or that it wins for the actual data. Source: Lecture4b, PDF pp.8–9.

## 3. Estimates depend on the database description

The optimiser estimates using catalog information such as tuple counts, tuple sizes and relation block counts. It chooses among equivalent evaluation plans using estimated cost. An estimate is a model of expected work, not an observed runtime measurement. The lecture lists later algorithm and optimisation questions but does not supply their derivations here; join algorithms and advanced plan enumeration remain outside this unit. Source: Lecture4b, PDF p.9.

## 4. Calculate disk cost without mixing units

The lecture lists disk access, CPU and network resources. It ignores CPU in the simplified model and warns that real systems account for it; parallel systems also need network costs. It treats read and write transfer costs equally for simplicity.

$$\text{estimated disk time}=b\,t_T+s\,t_S.$$

`tT` is transfer time per block and `tS` is time per seek. With the slide's HDD values, `tT=0.1 ms` and `tS=4 ms`. **Supplementary calculation:** 100 transfers and 2 seeks give `100×0.1+2×4=18 ms`; 20 transfers and 10 seeks give `20×0.1+10×4=42 ms`. Fewer transfers can still have higher cost if seeks increase enough. Source model and constants: Lecture4b, PDF pp.10–11.

The slide's SSD values are ranges: seek 20–90 µs and transfer 2–10 µs. They are source examples for 4 KB blocks, not current benchmark guarantees. Convert units before comparing: `1 ms = 1000 µs`. Do not compare a value in microseconds with one in milliseconds as if their numbers had the same unit. Source: Lecture4b, PDF p.11.

## 5. What would turn a claim into evidence?

First establish equal logical results. Then distinguish the model's estimated work from the observed execution plan and elapsed time. The supplied JDBC Task 2 measures only `executeQuery`; its elapsed interval is not identical to this slide's abstract disk model. Consult the separate timing practical for that task boundary. Sources: Lecture4b, PDF pp.8–11; `Lab2-JDBCandIndex-tasks.pdf`, PDF p.3.

## Return to the motivating question

Both candidate plans must return the same qualifying balances. Estimate their work using data statistics and the stated model, then inspect the chosen plan if a DBMS run is available. A scan can be competitive when the index route causes costly access. This lecture gives the decision framework; it does not prove that the source's indexed option always wins.

## Review

Draw the three-stage pipeline from memory. Name two catalog statistics. Explain why logical equivalence does not require identical execution strategy. Calculate a disk estimate with consistent units, then state which resource costs were omitted. Try the calculator in Try & explore before checking the worked problems.

## Sources and scope

All 12 PDF pages of `Lecture4b - Query Evaluation Basics.pdf` were text inspected; the cost model on p.11 was visually checked. The p.12 reading recommendation is textbook 7th edition §§15.1–15.2; the whole chapter is not claimed reviewed. No new assessment-frequency claims or DBMS-version assumptions are made.

# Query evaluation: recall and practice

Web tutor edition. New practice below is **SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE**, not an official assignment or marking scheme. Sources: Lecture4b - Query Evaluation Basics.pdf. Attempt before opening help.

## Atomic Recall

### Card 01 — What are the three query-processing stages, and which stage runs the chosen plan?
> [!success]- Answer
> Parsing/translation, optimization, and evaluation. Evaluation executes the chosen plan.
>
> Source: Lecture4b - Query Evaluation Basics.pdf, PDF pp. 2–3.

### Card 02 — Does equivalent algebra imply equal cost?
> [!success]- Answer
> No. Equivalent results can be computed by different algorithms and access paths with different costs.
>
> Source: Lecture4b - Query Evaluation Basics.pdf, PDF pp. 4–7.

### Card 03 — What does a query plan add?
> [!success]- Answer
> Concrete algorithms and evaluation choices for algebra operations.
>
> Source: Lecture4b - Query Evaluation Basics.pdf, PDF pp. 4–6.

### Card 04 — What information helps cost estimates?
> [!success]- Answer
> Catalog statistics such as relation size, tuple size and distinct values; estimates may differ from measured execution.
>
> Source: Lecture4b - Query Evaluation Basics.pdf, PDF p. 7.

### Card 05 — State the lecture’s estimated disk-time formula and define its counts and time units.
> [!success]- Answer
> b·tT+s·tS, where b counts transferred blocks and s counts seeks; both time parameters must use compatible units.
>
> Source: Lecture4b - Query Evaluation Basics.pdf, PDF p. 11.

### Card 06 — Why can fewer transferred blocks still be slower?
> [!success]- Answer
> A plan may save transfers while adding expensive seeks. Compare both terms.
>
> Source: Lecture4b - Query Evaluation Basics.pdf, PDF pp. 10–11.

### Card 07 — What is omitted from the simplified comparison?
> [!success]- Answer
> The lecture focuses on disk access and typically ignores CPU and network in the model. Real elapsed time has additional factors.
>
> Source: Lecture4b - Query Evaluation Basics.pdf, PDF pp. 8–10.

### Card 08 — What is 1 millisecond in microseconds?
> [!success]- Answer
> 1000 microseconds. Convert units before adding time terms.
>
> Source: Lecture4b - Query Evaluation Basics.pdf, PDF p. 11; unit conversion.

## Progressive Practice

### Practice 1 — Pipeline diagnostic

**SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE.** Is parsing a cost-based choice? Where is the plan executed?

> [!tip]- Hint
> Separate understanding the query from choosing and running a plan.

> [!success]- Solution
> Parsing/translation checks the query and produces an internal representation. Optimization compares candidate evaluation plans using estimated costs. Evaluation executes the selected plan.
>
> Source: Lecture4b - Query Evaluation Basics.pdf, PDF pp. 2–7.

### Practice 2 — HDD plan comparison

**SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE.** Using the lecture example tT=0.1 ms and tS=4 ms, compare A: b=100,s=2 and B: b=20,s=10.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Multiply counts by their respective time costs.

> [!success]- Solution
> A=100×0.1+2×4=18 ms. B=20×0.1+10×4=42 ms. A is cheaper in this model despite more blocks. These plan counts are a supplementary example, not a measured benchmark.
>
> Source: Lecture4b - Query Evaluation Basics.pdf, PDF p. 11.

### Practice 3 — SSD unit conversion

**SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE.** Take tT=5 µs and tS=50 µs (within the displayed ranges), b=100,s=2. Give cost in µs and ms.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Add in microseconds first, then divide by 1000.

> [!success]- Solution
> 100×5+2×50=600 µs=0.6 ms. These selected constants and counts illustrate the model; they do not characterize every SSD or guarantee real query latency.
>
> Source: Lecture4b - Query Evaluation Basics.pdf, PDF p. 11.

### Practice 4 — Safe rewrite

**SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE.** Compare π_balance(σ_balance<2500(account)) and σ_balance<2500(π_balance(account)). Would the same interchange work for a branch_name predicate?

> [!tip]- Hint
> Ask whether the predicate attributes survive projection.

> [!success]- Solution
> The balance predicate remains evaluable in both expressions, so the set results agree. A branch_name predicate cannot be evaluated after projecting only balance. Semantic equivalence must be established before cost comparison.
>
> Source: Lecture4b - Query Evaluation Basics.pdf, PDF p. 8.

### Practice 5 — Estimate versus measurement

**SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE.** A model predicts 18 ms but an execution reports 26 ms. Does this alone prove the optimizer wrong?

> [!tip]- Hint
> Identify model omissions and measurement boundaries.

> [!success]- Solution
> No. Estimated block/seek counts and statistics may differ from actual values; CPU, network, caching and client work may affect elapsed measurement. Compare like boundaries and inspect actual plans/statistics before concluding.
>
> Source: Lecture4b - Query Evaluation Basics.pdf, PDF pp. 7–11.

# Lab 02 — JDBC and index

[[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Tutor Mode/00 Start Here|Tutor Start]] · [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Tutor Mode/Lab 02 - JDBC and Index/02 Recall and Exam Practice|Recall and practice]] · [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Labs/Lab 02 - JDBC and Index/03 Lab|Reference lab]]

> [!info] Local web update
> Task 2 is released. This adaptation preserves the original setup explanations and updates release/runtime boundaries using the newer task sheet and ordinary lab reference. No university connection was performed.

## In 60 Seconds

JDBC is the Java API used here to connect to MySQL, send SQL and read results. The two supplied programs differ by one important database action: `JDBCandIndex.java` attempts to create `numIndex` before running the same logical query. That difference does **not** prove the index was used or that the query became faster. The source environment details contain host, filename, schema-width and setup contradictions that must be confirmed before execution.

This is a course-level practical, not a new theory unit. Task 1.1 and Task 1.2 are released; Task 2 is now released in Lab2-JDBCandIndex-tasks.pdf, p. 3; see the separate Released Query Timing study segment.

## Concept Preview

> [!note] JDBC lifecycle
> **Plain-language meaning:** load/register driver, connect, create a statement, execute SQL, process the result, then close resources.
>
> **Why it matters:** each stage has a different failure mode.
>
> **Source:** `Lab2-JDBCandIndex.pdf`, PDF pp. 12–23.

> [!note] Driver-specific connection
> **Plain-language meaning:** the source uses MySQL Connector/J and driver class `com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver`.
>
> **Why it matters:** this is lab-specific configuration, not a course-wide DBMS conclusion.
>
> **Source:** Lab2, PDF pp. 5, 10, 18.

> [!note] Index experiment boundary
> **Plain-language meaning:** creating an index is not the same as observing the optimiser select it or measuring a speedup.
>
> **Why it matters:** evidence requires a plan/timing method that the supplied programs do not contain.
>
> **Source:** `JDBC.java`; `JDBCandIndex.java`.

## Exam Evidence Snapshot

The supplied four-paper sample contains no JDBC/Lab 02 question: **NOT OBSERVED IN AVAILABLE PAST-PAPER SAMPLE**. This does not make the lab unimportant or excluded.

## Before You Start

You need basic Java classes/methods, SQL `SELECT`/`CREATE INDEX`, and the difference between compilation and runtime connectivity.

> [!question] Prerequisite check
> If Java code compiles without contacting a database, what has compilation not proved?

> [!success]- Check your answer
> It has not proved driver availability at runtime, credentials, network access, schema state, SQL success or query-plan behaviour.
>
> Source boundary: supplied Java files and ordinary Lab 02 validation record.

## A motivating question

Two programs issue the same query for rows where `num=7`; one first creates an index on `num`. What evidence would justify each of these claims?

1. the index statement succeeded;
2. MySQL used the index;
3. the indexed run was faster;
4. the result set stayed logically equivalent.

The supplied programs support source inspection, but not all four conclusions.

## Learn the mechanism

### Architecture and lifecycle

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant J as Java program
    participant D as JDBC driver
    participant M as MySQL server
    J->>D: DriverManager.getConnection(...)
    D->>M: establish protocol connection
    J->>D: executeUpdate / executeQuery
    D->>M: send SQL
    M-->>D: status or rows
    D-->>J: update count or ResultSet
    J->>J: iterate rows and close resources
```

**Figure 1 — JDBC request path**

**Read it:** Java talks through the DBMS-specific JDBC driver; SQL execution happens on the server.

**Key takeaway:** compile success and runtime database success are different evidence.

**Provenance:** teaching construction from Lab2, PDF pp. 10–23.

### What the source actually configures

The lab identifies MySQL, MySQL Connector/J and `com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver`. PDF p. 10 calls Connector/J 9.4.0 current at the time of the slide, but the server/JDK/storage-engine versions are not supplied. The Java source contains placeholders for database name, username and password; do not publish or commit real credentials.

### New setup handout: role and limits

`Database#1 Create privilege.pdf` is a two-page prerequisite handout for the school phpMyAdmin interface. It says:

- use `http://csse-mysql.xjtlu.edu.cn`;
- enter the university username without the dot and preserve case;
- it displays an initial course password and shows manual creation of a database named after the username;
- after creation, use the SQL interface to create tables.

Tutor Mode does not repeat the displayed password. Treat it as sensitive and potentially stale; use current official instructions. No university service was contacted.

> [!warning] Source contradiction — database creation
> `Database#1 Create privilege.pdf`, PDF p. 2 tells the user to create the username-named database manually. `Lab2-JDBCandIndex.pdf`, PDF p. 7 says there is no need to create it explicitly because it is created after login.
>
> **Safest interpretation:** these may describe different interface versions or provisioning states. Confirm current behaviour with the instructor; do not create extra schemas by guesswork.

### Other source discrepancies

| Source A | Source B | Conflict | Safest action |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lab2 p. 6: host `10.7.1.127` | Lab2 p. 11: `10.7.1.36/[DATABASE_NAME]`; Java uses `.127` | current server address unclear | obtain current official connection details |
| Lab2 p. 11: `JDBCIndex.java` | supplied files: `JDBC.java`, `JDBCandIndex.java` | filename mismatch | use supplied filenames; confirm submission expectation |
| SQL declares `mmatch varchar(12)` | supplied data include longer values | import may truncate/error by server mode | inspect actual import warnings before changing schema |
| Lab2 p. 24: `java.Date` | p. 25 table: `java.sql.Date` | type wording differs | use fully qualified JDBC type from mapping table |

### Two programs, four distinct claims

`JDBC.java` connects and queries `Orf_Motif` for the configured key/value. `JDBCandIndex.java` first issues a `CREATE INDEX numIndex ON Orf_Motif(num)` statement, then runs the same logical query.

| Claim | Required evidence | Supplied code alone? |
|---|---|---|
| index statement was attempted | code inspection | yes |
| index creation succeeded | runtime server response/state | no |
| optimiser selected index | execution plan such as `EXPLAIN` | no |
| indexed query was faster | controlled timing/measurement | no |
| returned rows are equivalent | compare actual result sets | no runtime evidence |

The dataset's static parse finds 614 supplied rows with `num=7`, but that is not an observed MySQL query result.

### Statement interfaces

- `Statement`: fixed SQL constructed in code.
- `PreparedStatement`: parameter placeholders for values; improves separation of SQL structure from external data and supports reuse.
- `CallableStatement`: invokes stored procedures.

The source introduces all three. It does not make every SQL identifier parameterisable; table/column/index identifiers need deliberate safe construction.

> [!question] Explain it yourself
> Why does creating `numIndex` not establish a physical B+ tree or a measured speedup?

> [!success]- Check your explanation
> The source does not confirm storage engine/index type, inspect an execution plan or measure comparable runs. Creation, selection and performance are separate claims.
>
> Source: supplied Java files; Lab2, PDF pp. 10–23.

## Worked example — evidence matrix

Suppose a run reports successful index creation, then returns 614 rows. That would establish only the executed server state and result count for that run. To show index selection, capture a plan. To show speed, define warm/cold cache, repeated trials, identical data/server load and timing boundaries. To show logical equivalence, compare result sets with and without the index.

This older explanation distinguishes static reasoning from execution. The updated ordinary Lab reference now reports a historical local run with 607 rows; see Released Query Timing for its exact boundary and limitations. This web app has not run a database experiment.

## Return to the motivating question

1. **Creation succeeded:** needs an actual server response/state.
2. **Index used:** needs a plan.
3. **Faster:** needs controlled measurement.
4. **Equivalent results:** needs compared actual result sets.

Source inspection alone proves only what statements the programs attempt.

## Definitions and distinctions

| Term A | Term B | Decisive distinction | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| compile-time success | runtime success | Java syntax/types versus driver/network/server/schema execution | supplied Java; Lab2 |
| index created | index selected | schema object exists versus optimiser chooses it for a query | supplied Java |
| expected output | observed output | reasoned/source prediction versus recorded execution | Tutor protocol |
| Statement | PreparedStatement | direct SQL string versus parameterised values/reusable prepared operation | Lab2, pp. 20–23 |

## Review

### Full Understanding

Return to [[#Learn the mechanism]] and [[#Worked example — evidence matrix]].

## 5-Minute Review

- JDBC driver mediates Java↔MySQL;
- connect → statement → execute → result → close;
- host/database provisioning details conflict and require current confirmation;
- never expose credentials or contact infrastructure without authorisation;
- index creation, index selection, speed and result equivalence need different evidence;
- Task 2 is released; see the Released Query Timing segment.

## 60-Second Recall

- Connector/J
- driver class
- connection placeholders
- executeUpdate vs executeQuery
- ResultSet cursor
- close resources
- create ≠ select ≠ faster
- setup-source contradiction
- Task 2 released: separate timing segment

# Lab 02 — Recall and practice

[[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Tutor Mode/Lab 02 - JDBC and Index/01 Tutor Notes|Tutor notes]] · [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Labs/Lab 02 - JDBC and Index/03 Lab|Reference lab]]

**Assessment evidence:** NOT OBSERVED IN AVAILABLE PAST-PAPER SAMPLE. These are source-based lab checks, not supported exam-format claims.

> [!info] Local web update
> Task 2 is released. This adaptation preserves the original setup explanations and updates release/runtime boundaries using the newer task sheet and ordinary lab reference. No university connection was performed.

## Atomic recall

### Card 01 — What does JDBC stand for?
> [!success]- Answer
> Java Database Connectivity.
>
> Source: Lab2, PDF p. 13.

### Card 02 — Which driver class does the source use?
> [!success]- Answer
> `com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver`.
>
> Source: Lab2, PDF p. 18.

### Card 03 — Which method executes a query returning rows?
> [!success]- Answer
> `executeQuery`, returning a `ResultSet`.
>
> Source: Lab2, PDF pp. 20–22; supplied Java.

### Card 04 — Which method is suitable for `CREATE INDEX`?
> [!success]- Answer
> `executeUpdate`, because the statement changes schema state rather than returning query rows.
>
> Source: `JDBCandIndex.java`.

### Card 05 — What does `ResultSet.next()` do?
> [!success]- Answer
> Advances the cursor to the next row and reports whether one exists.
>
> Source: Lab2, PDF pp. 21–22.

### Card 06 — What proves index selection?
> [!success]- Answer
> An observed execution plan or equivalent server evidence, not index creation alone.
>
> Source boundary: supplied Java files.

### Card 07 — What proves a speedup?
> [!success]- Answer
> Controlled measurements under comparable data, cache, server and timing conditions.
>
> Source boundary: supplied Java files.

### Card 08 — What exact Java call does released Lab 02 Task 2 ask you to time?
> [!success]- Answer
> The newer task sheet releases timing only rs = stmt.executeQuery(sql); before and after indexing. See the Released Query Timing segment.
>
> Source: Lab2-JDBCandIndex-tasks.pdf, PDF p. 3 (supersedes original Lab2 p. 2 release placeholder).

### Card 09 — What disagreement between the two JDBC setup documents needs confirmation?
> [!success]- Answer
> The privilege handout requires manual database creation, while Lab2 says provisioning is automatic.
>
> Source: privilege PDF p. 2; Lab2 p. 7.

### Card 10 — Does the static count of 614 parsed source records establish the number returned by MySQL for num=7?
> [!success]- Answer
> No. It is a static count from parsing supplied SQL, not an observed SELECT result. The recorded local run returned 607 rows for num=7; that historical count is also environment-specific, not a promised result for a future import.
>
> Source: ordinary course validation record.

## Practice

### Practice 1 — Trace the JDBC lifecycle

**SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE.** Put these in dependency order: iterate results, obtain connection, close resources, create statement, execute query.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Ask what object each later operation requires.

> [!success]- Solution
> Obtain connection → create statement → execute query → iterate results → close result/statement/connection.
>
> Errors may require earlier cleanup, so production code normally uses bounded resource management such as try-with-resources.
>
> Source: Lab2, PDF pp. 16–23.

### Practice 2 — ORIGINAL COURSE TASK 1.1 reasoning

Explain what must be configured before `JDBC.java` can run and what evidence a successful run would provide.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Separate driver/classpath, connection values, database state and query result.

> [!success]- Solution
> Configure Connector/J on the runtime classpath, current official server/database URL, username and password; ensure `Orf_Motif` is imported.
>
> A successful run would show that this environment connected and executed the query, with an observed result set. It would not establish general performance or a course-wide DBMS version.
>
> Source: Lab2, PDF pp. 4–23; `JDBC.java`.

### Practice 3 — ORIGINAL COURSE TASK 1.2 reasoning

Explain the additional state change attempted by `JDBCandIndex.java` and three checks needed before claiming improvement.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Think creation result, plan and measurement.

> [!success]- Solution
> It attempts `CREATE INDEX numIndex ON Orf_Motif(num)` before the query.
>
> Check that creation succeeded (and handle an existing index), inspect the execution plan to see whether MySQL selected it, and compare controlled timings/results with the non-index run. Also verify logical result equivalence.
>
> Source: `JDBCandIndex.java`; Lab2 Task 1.2.

### Practice 4 — Diagnose a second run

**SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE.** The first indexed run succeeds; the second fails before querying. Give a source-grounded hypothesis and a safe response.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Identify persistent schema state created by the first run.

> [!success]- Solution
> `numIndex` may already exist, so repeating the unconditional `CREATE INDEX` can fail. Inspect the actual server error and schema state; do not silently drop or alter objects without the lab's current instructions.
>
> Source: `JDBCandIndex.java`; ordinary Lab 02 notes.

### Practice 5 — Resolve contradictory setup documents

**SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE.** One document says to create the username-named database manually; another says login creates it automatically. What should a student do?

> [!tip]- Hint
> Preserve both sources and avoid guessing about a live service.

> [!success]- Solution
> Treat the provisioning behaviour as unconfirmed, use the current official lab/instructor instructions, inspect the interface without creating duplicate schemas, and never reuse the printed initial password as a general credential.
>
> Source: `Database#1 Create privilege.pdf`, p. 2; Lab2, p. 7.

### Practice 6 — Transfer: design an evidence table

**SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE.** Propose evidence columns for comparing the two programs without claiming unsupported performance.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Include environment, schema, plan, result and timing provenance.

> [!success]- Solution
> Record timestamp, server/version if confirmed, dataset hash/count, index existence and DDL result, exact query, execution plan, result-set checksum/count, cache/run protocol, repeated timings and errors.
>
> This design would support bounded observations; it would not prove universal speed across environments.
>
> Source principles: supplied Lab 02 materials; fields are supplementary engineering guidance.
