- Task 1.1 and Task 1.2 are mapped above and in the ordinary lab.
- Task 2 is released in the newer task sheet, p. 3; the separate timing segment contains its source-grounded walkthrough.
- No university infrastructure, credential or remote database was accessed.

--- title: "Lab 2 · JDBC and Index" course: SOE201 type: laboratory status: reviewed study_status: untested language: en cssclasses: - soe201-study --- [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/SOE201 - Advanced Database Development|Course home]] · [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 01 - Physical Storage/01 Notes|Index foundations]] · [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/01 Notes|B+ tree theory]] · [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Labs/Lab 02 - JDBC and Index/03 Lab|Lab 02]] # Lab 2 — JDBC and Index ## Lab goals By the end of the released work, you should be able to: - explain the role of ==JDBC== between a Java application and MySQL; - trace a query through `DriverManager`, ==MySQL Connector/J==, MySQL, and a ==ResultSet==; - map each stage of the JDBC lifecycle to the supplied Java sources; - explain the exact SQL assembled from `searchKey = "num"` and `searchKeyValue = "7"`; - distinguish the baseline query from the program that first creates `numIndex`; - explain why creating an index does **not** by itself prove that a query became faster or used that index; and - identify source inconsistencies and rerun hazards before changing an official file. ## Official tasks ### Task 1.1 — basic JDBC query Set up the environment, understand the supplied `JDBC.java`, and test its basic JDBC query.[^tasks] ### Task 1.2 — JDBC query with an index Understand and test the supplied `JDBCandIndex.java`, which creates an index and then runs the basic JDBC query.[^tasks] ### Task 2 — query execution timing Implement functionality that prints the time taken by the same query without and with an index. The measured interval must contain only `rs = stmt.executeQuery(sql);`; connection, index changes, result iteration/output, setup, and cleanup remain outside the timer.[^task2] > [!warning] Scope boundary > Task 2 measures the single `executeQuery` call for the Task 1 query. The local solution additionally verifies index state, logical-result equality, and the indexed execution plan; those checks are outside the measured interval. ## Opening practical question — what actually changes? You receive the same imported `Orf_Motif` data and two programs: - `JDBC.java` connects and runs `SELECT * FROM Orf_Motif WHERE num=7`. - `JDBCandIndex.java` first runs `CREATE INDEX numIndex ON Orf_Motif (num)`, then runs the same logical `SELECT`. **Questions:** What path carries the query from Java to MySQL? What is returned to Java? What changes when the index is created, and what remains unproved? **Constraints:** preserve the original sources; use placeholders or environment variables rather than recorded credentials; do not access university infrastructure without current authorised connection details; and do not infer a storage-engine-specific index structure without engine evidence. **Success criteria:** you can trace each source line, predict the SQL text, explain the result-reading loop, distinguish logical equivalence from performance evidence, and identify the checks required before a safe rerun. | Opening question | Concepts needed | |---|---| | How does Java reach MySQL? | JDBC API, `DriverManager`, Connector/J, `Connection` | | How is the query submitted and read? | `Statement`, `executeQuery`, `ResultSet`, `rs.next()` | | What does the second program add? | `CREATE INDEX`, object naming, repeated-run behaviour | | What can the lab prove? | Source behaviour versus execution plan and timing evidence | ## Architecture JDBC is the Java API used to connect Java programs to relational data. The source presents JDBC as classes and interfaces, with database providers supplying drivers.[^jdbc-definition] This lab selects the pure-Java Type 4 MySQL driver, MySQL Connector/J.[^connector] ```mermaid flowchart TB A["Java application"] --> B["JDBC API"] B --> C["DriverManager"] C --> D["MySQL Connector/J
Type 4 JDBC driver"] D --> E["MySQL server"] E --> F["Execute SQL"] F --> G["ResultSet for SELECT"] G --> A ``` **Figure 1 — The Lab 2 JDBC request path** **Read it:** Follow the request downward from the Java program. For a `SELECT`, follow the returned `ResultSet` back to the application. **Key takeaway:** Java calls the standard JDBC interfaces; Connector/J translates that work into the MySQL protocol. The course source also shows other historical/generic driver routes, but this lab uses Connector/J.[^architecture] ## Environment setup ### Course source instructions The official slides provide two environment choices: install MySQL locally, or use the school MySQL service under current institutional access rules. They instruct students to obtain MySQL Connector/J, place the driver on the classpath or import it into the IDE, import `yeast_prosite.sql`, and replace the Java connection placeholders in a working file.[^mysql-setup] | Component | Source-supported requirement | Important boundary | |---|---|---| | Java | Compile and run the supplied class in its declared package | The PDF gives no JDK version | | MySQL | Local installation or the authorized school service | MySQL server version and storage engine are not stated | | Driver | MySQL Connector/J; driver class `com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver` | PDF p. 10 calls Connector/J 9.4.0 current; this is source-stated, not a detected installation | | Dataset | Import `yeast_prosite.sql` | Inspect import messages before assuming all 12,913 inserts succeeded | | Connection | Replace database, username, and password placeholders in a working copy | Never put real credentials in this vault, note, logs, or shared commands | The archived originals are here: - [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Labs/Lab 02 - JDBC and Index/Sources/Lab2-JDBCandIndex.pdf|Official Lab 2 PDF]] - [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Labs/Lab 02 - JDBC and Index/Sources/Lab2-JDBCandIndex-tasks.pdf|Official released task sheet]] - [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Labs/Lab 02 - JDBC and Index/Sources/JDBC.java|JDBC.java]] - [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Labs/Lab 02 - JDBC and Index/Sources/JDBCandIndex.java|JDBCandIndex.java]] - [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Labs/Lab 02 - JDBC and Index/Sources/yeast_prosite.sql|yeast_prosite.sql]] > [!warning] Work on a copy > Both Java files contain literal placeholders. Copy a source into the instructor-approved IDE project before adapting its package or connection parameters. Do not modify the archived original and do not paste a real password into study notes, YAML, screenshots, terminal history, or version control. ### Source discrepancies to check before execution 1. PDF p. 6 gives the school MySQL host as `10.7.1.127`, whereas PDF p. 11 shows `10.7.1.36/[DATABASE_NAME]`. Both supplied Java files contain `jdbc:mysql://10.7.1.127/[DATABASE NAME]`. On 24 September 2026, a direct TCP probe from the current machine reached `10.7.1.127:3306`, while `10.7.1.36:3306` did not respond within three seconds. That observation supports `.127` for the current network but proves neither authentication nor universal availability.[^host-discrepancy] 2. PDF p. 11 names `JDBCIndex.java`, but the supplied originals are `JDBC.java` and `JDBCandIndex.java`. Use the actual supplied filenames for Tasks 1.1 and 1.2.[^preparation-name] 3. The source instructs students to modify a package name if needed. The current files declare `package xjtlu.soe201.JDBC;`, so an IDE project or `javac -d` output must respect that package. 4. The source contains institutional login guidance that may age. Follow current instructor/IT instructions. This pass performed reachability probes only; it did not submit credentials, log in, import data, or execute SQL on university infrastructure. ### Supplementary modern guidance This task's local compile check used JDK 17 and needed no Connector/J JAR because the driver name is loaded reflectively at runtime. That proves only that the Java syntax and standard-library references compile. Running the program requires both Connector/J and a reachable, authorized database. ```sh javac -d out Sources/JDBC.java Sources/JDBCandIndex.java ``` This command contains no credentials and performs no network access. Runtime classpaths differ between operating systems and IDEs; follow the current lab instructions rather than copying an unverified command. ## Dataset — `Orf_Motif` The SQL source drops and recreates one table, deletes earlier rows per `orf`, and supplies 12,913 `INSERT` statements. Static parsing found 418 distinct `orf` values and 216 distinct `acc_num` values. These are source-file observations, not a claim that a remote import completed. | Column | Exact SQL type | Role in this lab | Static source observation | |---|---|---|---| | `orf` | `varchar(12)` | Printed as the second output column | No supplied `NULL`; maximum text length 9 | | `acc_num` | `varchar(12)` | Printed as the first output column | No supplied `NULL`; maximum text length 7 | | `num` | `int(3)` | Search column; the programs filter on `num=7` | No supplied `NULL`; values 1–57; not declared unique | | `pos` | `int(3)` | Motif position | 285 supplied `NULL` values | | `len` | `int(3)` | Motif length | No supplied `NULL`; values 1–565 | | `mmatch` | `varchar(12)` | Matched sequence text | 285 supplied `NULL` values; source-width conflict described below | **Table 1 — Compact schema for the supplied dataset** **Read it:** Start with `num`, the predicate column, then follow the two printed columns `acc_num` and `orf`. The DDL contains no primary key, foreign key, `NOT NULL`, or engine clause. **Key takeaway:** `num` is a repeated occurrence number, not a global identifier. Static inspection finds **614 `INSERT` statements** with `num=7`, spanning 252 distinct `orf` values. The file also contains later per-`orf` deletions, so insert-statement counts are not final table counts. The controlled local import described below ended with **607 rows** matching `num=7`. Each result row prints only `acc_num` and `orf` even though `SELECT *` retrieves all six columns. > [!warning] Dataset import compatibility > The DDL declares `mmatch varchar(12)`, but 771 supplied non-`NULL` values are longer than 12 characters; the maximum is 89. Modern MySQL strict mode treats invalid or overlong assignments as errors, while non-strict handling can adjust values and issue warnings.[^strict-mode] The SQL also begins with unconditional `drop table Orf_Motif;`, which can report an error if the table does not yet exist. Preserve the official SQL unchanged, inspect the import report, and ask the instructor for the intended schema rather than silently widening the archived source. ## JDBC lifecycle The source condenses JDBC work into six phases; the following eight-step trace separates statement creation, result acquisition, and iteration so that every supplied operation is visible.[^lifecycle] ```mermaid flowchart TD A["1 Import java.sql classes"] --> B["2 Load the JDBC driver"] B --> C["3 Establish Connection"] C --> D["4 Create Statement"] D --> E["5 Build and execute SQL"] E --> F["6 Obtain ResultSet"] F --> G["7 Iterate with rs.next and read columns"] G --> H["8 Close ResultSet, Statement, Connection"] ``` **Figure 2 — Lifecycle used by both supplied Java programs** **Read it:** Each box maps to a concrete import, field, call, or cleanup line in the source table below. **Key takeaway:** The second program inserts one DDL operation—index creation—between statement creation and the same logical `SELECT`. | Stage | `JDBC.java` | `JDBCandIndex.java` | |---|---|---| | Import classes | lines 11–15 | lines 11–15 | | Load driver | line 58, `Class.forName(JDBC_DRIVER)` | line 67 | | Establish ==Connection== | line 60 | line 69 | | Create ==Statement== | line 65 | line 74 | | Build SQL | line 38 | lines 39 and 44 | | Execute / obtain ==ResultSet== | line 39 | index: line 40; query: line 47 | | Iterate and read | lines 48–50 | lines 57–59 | | Close resources | lines 72–74 | lines 81–83 | ## `JDBC.java` — without creating the new index ### Configuration fields | Name | Exact supplied meaning | |---|---| | `DB_URL` | JDBC URL placeholder containing host `10.7.1.127` and `[DATABASE NAME]` | | `USER` | `[USERNAME]` placeholder | | `PASS` | `[PASSWORD]` placeholder | | `JDBC_DRIVER` | `com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver` | | `conn` | JDBC `Connection`, initially `null` | | `stmt` | JDBC `Statement`, initially `null` | | `rs` | JDBC `ResultSet`, initially `null` | | `sql` | Current SQL string | | `searchKey` | Column name `num` | | `searchKeyValue` | Text `7`, concatenated without quotes into the numeric predicate | ### Build and submit the query The source constructs: ```java sql = "SELECT * FROM Orf_Motif WHERE " + searchKey + "=" + searchKeyValue; ``` With the supplied constants, the exact SQL is: ```sql SELECT * FROM Orf_Motif WHERE num=7 ``` `stmt.executeQuery(sql)` submits a `SELECT` and returns a `ResultSet`, matching the source tutorial's distinction between `executeQuery` for queries and `executeUpdate` for data-changing statements.[^execute] ### Advance and read `rs.next()` advances the cursor to the next row and returns whether a row is available. Inside that loop: - `rs.getString("acc_num")` converts the current row's `acc_num` value to a Java `String`; - `rs.getString("orf")` does the same for `orf`; and - the program prints the two values separated by a tab.[^resultset] The loop continues until `rs.next()` returns `false`. The text labels “first col” and “second col” are only console headings; the getters select by column name. > [!info] Static expectation, not a runtime observation > The unchanged SQL file contains 614 inserts whose `num` value is 7, and neither printed field is `NULL` in those source rows. A controlled local MySQL 9.4.0 import finished with 607 matching rows because the script's later `DELETE` statements affect the final state. A different database state or failed import can still produce a different result. ## `JDBCandIndex.java` — creating the index After making the connection and `Statement`, the second program constructs and executes: ```sql CREATE INDEX numIndex ON Orf_Motif (num) ``` It then constructs the same logical query: ```sql SELECT * FROM Orf_Motif WHERE num=7 ``` `stmt.execute(sql)` is used for the DDL statement because the program is not expecting a query row set from `CREATE INDEX`. `stmt.executeQuery(sql)` is then used for the `SELECT`. Conceptually, `numIndex` creates an access structure keyed by `num`. That makes an indexed access path *available* to the optimizer. The SQL source does not declare a storage engine, and the Java source does not inspect index metadata, so this note does not assert that the physical index is a B+ tree. Use [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 02 - B+ Tree Indexing/01 Notes|B+ tree theory]] for the course's ordered-tree model and [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Unit 03 - Hash Indexing/01 Notes|hash-index theory]] for the contrasting equality-oriented model; neither identifies this table's actual engine. ### Re-running the program On a first successful run, the named index exists afterward. A later run again requests the same index name. MySQL reports a duplicate-key-name error when an index name already exists, so the program can stop at `stmt.execute(sql)` before reaching the `SELECT`.[^duplicate-index] > [!warning] Troubleshooting decision > First determine whether `numIndex` already exists. Do not repeatedly rerun the program and do not modify the lecturer's archived file merely to hide the failure. **SUPPLEMENTARY GUIDANCE — verified MySQL syntax:** ```sql SHOW INDEX FROM Orf_Motif; ``` This lists table indexes. If the instructor explicitly asks for a reset, MySQL's documented syntax is: ```sql DROP INDEX numIndex ON Orf_Motif; ``` `DROP INDEX` changes schema state; use it only in the intended lab database and only after confirming the index name and reset purpose.[^show-drop-index] ## Without new index versus with new index | Aspect | `JDBC.java` | `JDBCandIndex.java` | |---|---|---| | Schema change before query | None | Requests `CREATE INDEX numIndex ON Orf_Motif (num)` | | Logical predicate | `num=7` | `num=7` | | Selected columns | `*` | `*` | | Printed columns | `acc_num`, `orf` | `acc_num`, `orf` | | Expected logical result if data are unchanged | All rows satisfying `num=7` | The same rows satisfying `num=7` | | Timing code | None | None | | Plan inspection | None | None | | Proof MySQL used `numIndex` | None | None | **Same logical result ≠ proven performance improvement.** The supplied programs demonstrate JDBC connectivity, SQL submission, index creation, and equivalent query structure before and after the schema change. They do not measure latency, page reads, throughput, or optimizer choice. Evidence for a general performance claim would require a controlled setup and additional observations such as repeated timings, stable data/cache conditions, and an identified server version and engine. The released Task 2 run below supplies one local `executeQuery` timing pair plus `EXPLAIN`; it does not establish a universal speedup. ## Statement, PreparedStatement, and CallableStatement | Interface | Course-source role | Relation to this lab | |---|---|---| | `Statement` | General-purpose, simple static SQL with no bind parameters | Used by both supplied programs | | `PreparedStatement` | Precompiled SQL that may accept runtime input parameters; recommended by the source for repeated execution | Not used in the supplied files | | `CallableStatement` | Calls stored procedures/functions and may use input/output parameters | Introduced in the PDF; not used in the supplied files | This comparison comes from PDF p. 26.[^statement-types] The supplied code uses `Statement` because it assembles a complete SQL string before submission. That works for its hard-coded teaching values. If a value came from a user or another external source, a `PreparedStatement` would normally separate SQL structure from parameter values. That is supplementary engineering guidance, not a rewrite of Task 1.1 or 1.2. ## SQL-to-Java data mapping The tutorial explains that SQL values must be mapped to Java types and gives direct, convertible, and special-class cases.[^type-mapping] | SQL type in the PDF | JDBC/Java type shown | Setter shown | |---|---|---| | `VARCHAR`, `CHAR` | `java.lang.String` | `setString()` | | `NUMERIC` | `java.math.BigDecimal` | `setBigDecimal()` | | `INTEGER` | `int` | `setInt()` | | `FLOAT` | `float` | `setFloat()` | | `DOUBLE` | `double` | `setDouble()` | | `DATE` | `java.sql.Date` | `setDate()` | | `TIME` | `java.sql.Time` | `setTime()` | | `TIMESTAMP` | `java.sql.Timestamp` | `setTimestamp()` | > [!note] Internal slide wording discrepancy > PDF p. 24 says SQL `DATE` maps to a Java Date object “defined in `java.Date`,” while the table on p. 25 specifies `java.sql.Date`. The table's fully qualified JDBC type is retained here; the inconsistency is not silently merged. ## Cleanup and failure limits Both programs explicitly close `ResultSet`, `Statement`, and `Connection` in that order, matching PDF p. 23.[^cleanup] This cleanup is reached only if earlier operations complete. Because the source uses `throws` and has no `finally` block or try-with-resources, an exception during connection, index creation, query execution, or row processing can bypass those final close calls. That limitation does not invalidate the teaching sequence, but it matters when interpreting failures. A compile pass is not a runtime pass, and a runtime exception is not evidence about query performance. ## Supplementary engineering notes These notes support safe interpretation; they are not lecturer-required modifications. ### Keep credentials out of source control The official examples use string constants for clarity. In a real project, secrets should come from an approved runtime configuration or secret store rather than committed Java or Markdown. This lab note intentionally contains placeholders only. ### Prefer bounded resource lifetime Modern Java often uses try-with-resources so each JDBC object closes even when an exception occurs. Do not replace the official source during Task 1.1/1.2; first understand the explicit lifecycle the lecturer supplied. ### Use parameters for external values For an externally supplied numeric value, use a parameter marker and `PreparedStatement` rather than concatenating raw input. The current fixed `7` is a teaching constant, not an invitation to concatenate untrusted text. ### Treat import warnings as evidence After importing the SQL in an authorized environment, inspect errors and warnings, confirm the table definition actually created, and verify row counts before attributing a missing or shortened value to JDBC. The `mmatch` width conflict makes this especially important. ## Released-task procedure and checkpoints ### Task 1.1 procedure 1. Preserve the archived `JDBC.java`; place a working copy in the instructor-approved project. 2. Confirm the package path and that Connector/J is on the runtime classpath. 3. Import the SQL only into the intended authorized lab database; inspect the import report. 4. Replace placeholders in the working copy without recording real credentials in this vault or logs. 5. Before execution, predict the exact SQL and explain each lifecycle line. 6. Run only in the authorized environment. Record observed output separately from this source-derived expectation. 7. Close or terminate the client cleanly and remove any insecure working credential copy according to instructor policy. ### Task 1.2 procedure 1. Confirm whether `numIndex` already exists before running. 2. Trace the DDL and the subsequent `SELECT` in `JDBCandIndex.java`. 3. Run in the authorized lab environment only. 4. Check that the logical rows correspond to the Task 1.1 predicate; do not infer a speedup from similar output. 5. Use the released Task 2 procedure below for the timing comparison. ### Task 2 procedure 1. Remove `numIndex` outside the timer, then verify that no index exists on `Orf_Motif(num)`. 2. Start `System.nanoTime()`, call `stmt.executeQuery(sql)`, and stop the timer immediately after the call returns. 3. Iterate the first `ResultSet` only after its timer has stopped. 4. Create `numIndex` outside the timer and verify that it exists. 5. Time only the same `stmt.executeQuery(sql)` call again, then iterate afterward. 6. Compare the two logical result multisets and require them to match. 7. Run `EXPLAIN` after the indexed timer has stopped and require `key=numIndex`. ```java long startNanos = System.nanoTime(); ResultSet resultSet = statement.executeQuery(SELECT_SQL); long elapsedNanos = System.nanoTime() - startNanos; ``` Connection establishment, statement creation, index removal/creation, result iteration/output, comparison, plan inspection, and cleanup are all outside this interval.[^task2] ## Completed reference solution for Tasks 1.1, 1.2, and 2 The runnable solution is [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Labs/Lab 02 - JDBC and Index/Solution/Lab2Solution.java|Lab2Solution.java]], with exact commands in [[10_UNIVERSITY_CS/SOE201/Labs/Lab 02 - JDBC and Index/Solution/README.md|Solution README]]. The five files under `Sources/` remain byte-for-byte unchanged. The solution keeps the source SQL statements, reads connection details from environment variables, closes JDBC resources with try-with-resources, measures only `executeQuery`, compares both result sets without assuming row order, and verifies the indexed query plan. ### Run it safely Compile with JDK 17 and MySQL Connector/J. Set the three environment variables only in the shell used for the lab; do not paste a real password into this note or commit it to source control. ```bash export LAB_DB_URL='jdbc:mysql://HOST:3306/DATABASE' export LAB_DB_USER='USERNAME' read -s LAB_DB_PASSWORD && export LAB_DB_PASSWORD CONNECTOR_JAR='Solution/lib/mysql-connector-j-9.4.0.jar' BUILD_DIR="$(mktemp -d)" javac -Xlint:all -cp "$CONNECTOR_JAR" -d "$BUILD_DIR" \ 'Solution/Lab2Solution.java' java -cp "$BUILD_DIR:$CONNECTOR_JAR" \ xjtlu.soe201.jdbc.Lab2Solution baseline java -cp "$BUILD_DIR:$CONNECTOR_JAR" \ xjtlu.soe201.jdbc.Lab2Solution indexed java -cp "$BUILD_DIR:$CONNECTOR_JAR" \ xjtlu.soe201.jdbc.Lab2Solution timing unset LAB_DB_PASSWORD ``` Use `baseline` before the index exists for Task 1.1. Use `indexed` for Task 1.2; it creates `numIndex` only when metadata shows that it is absent. # Lab 02 — Measure the Released Task 2

This web supplement reflects the released `Lab2-JDBCandIndex-tasks.pdf`, PDF p.3. The older imported Tutor Mode setup notes describe Task 2 as pending; that statement is superseded by this release. The original university files remain unchanged.

## In 60 Seconds

Run the same Task 1 query with and without an index and print the time spent in **only** `rs = stmt.executeQuery(sql);`. Connection setup, creating an index and consuming results belong outside the timed interval. Compare logical results and inspect the index state separately. Source: tasks PDF pp.1–3 and the updated reference lab's Released Task 2 section.

## Before You Start

Complete the preceding JDBC setup practical. Use an isolated, intended lab database with valid configuration. These web activities explain the task and do not connect to the university database or execute Java. Required university server and JDK versions remain unconfirmed by the task sheet.

## 1. Keep the query fixed

Both Task 1 source programs select `SELECT * FROM Orf_Motif WHERE num=7`. The indexed version makes an index on `num` available before submitting that query. Do not compare different predicates, tables, or result interpretations and call that an index experiment. Source: tasks PDF pp.1–2; official `JDBC.java` and `JDBCandIndex.java`.

## 2. Place the timer around exactly one call

The updated reference solution uses:

```java
long startNanos = System.nanoTime();
ResultSet resultSet = statement.executeQuery(SELECT_SQL);
long elapsedNanos = System.nanoTime() - startNanos;
```

Convert nanoseconds to milliseconds by dividing by `1_000_000.0`. Keep the `while (resultSet.next())` loop after the timer. The task defines its interval as the API call; The driver can retrieve and buffer rows during executeQuery; moving the iteration loop afterward does not isolate server execution from transfer time. Supplementary technical reference: [Connector/J implementation notes](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/connector-j/en/connector-j-reference-implementation-notes.html), ResultSet section, checked 2026-10-07. Streaming configurations can change that boundary. Source: tasks PDF p.3; reference `03 Lab.md`, Released Task 2 timing lines.

## 3. Record index state and the chosen plan

An index existing, an optimiser choosing it, and an elapsed time are three different observations. Record the intended before/after index state and inspect a plan separately. The local reference solution records `numIndex`; do not recreate a named index blindly on every rerun. A duplicate-index error can stop the intended experiment before the SELECT. Source: official `JDBCandIndex.java`, index creation; updated reference lab's execution procedure.

## 4. Establish equal results

Consume both result sets outside the timer and compare them without assuming row order. Keep duplicates when comparing multisets rather than changing query semantics. The reference run compared `(acc_num, orf)` multisets with 607 rows in each run. This is recorded local evidence, not a promised row count for every import. Source: updated reference lab's Task 2 logical comparison.

## 5. Explain a measurement honestly

The existing reference records one local pair, 8.723 ms and 2.083 ms. It supports a difference in that controlled run. Cache state, load, statistics, data size and configuration can change the result. These values are not newly measured by this web import and do not establish a universal speedup or university-server behaviour. Source: updated reference lab's observed local execution and limits.

## Review

Point to the exact three timer lines. Identify the operations excluded from the interval. Explain how you would show equal logical results and actual plan selection, then name one condition that could change the timings. Use the local cost activity to separate a theoretical estimate from an actual JDBC interval.

# Selection, Projection and External Sorting

## In 60 Seconds

An index can reduce transferred blocks yet increase expensive seeks. Suppose a file occupies 400 blocks and an unclustered index matches 100 scattered records. With index height 4, transfer time 0.1 ms and seek time 4 ms, a full scan costs 44 ms, while the lecture's pessimistic secondary-index model costs 426.4 ms. The access path matters more than the mere existence of an index. This supplementary calculation uses Lecture5a pp.5,10 and the disk model from Unit 06.

This edition integrates the verified 12 October archive: Lecture5a, 23 pages, dated 10 October 2026. It is a new web lesson, not a claim that the file was first released this week. Week 6 optimisation sources are visible on Learning Mall but remain pending acquisition. Prerequisites: Unit 01 storage, Units 02–04 indexes, Unit 05 algebra and Unit 06 cost units.

## Select an Access Path With Explicit Assumptions

Let b_r be file blocks, h the lecture's number of index-node accesses, b the consecutive matching data blocks and k the matching records. For cold accesses, retain transfers B and seeks S separately, then compute $T=B t_T+S t_S$.

| Access path | Transfers B | Seeks S | Conditions |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Linear scan | $b_r$ | 1 | Contiguous relation; test every record |
| Successful equality scan on a key, average | $b_r/2$ | 1 | Source average model; absence may need full scan |
| Binary search | $\lceil\log_2 b_r\rceil$ plus matching blocks | Same search count, then retrieval | File physically ordered on equality attribute |
| Candidate-key B+ lookup | $h+1$ | $h+1$ | One matching data record |
| Clustered non-key equality | $h+b$ | $h+1$ | Matching records contiguous |
| Unclustered non-key equality, pessimistic | $h+k$ | $h+k$ | Each matching record may be on another block |

The deck calls the clustered non-key case a primary index. Keep its physical locality assumption explicit rather than assuming every primary-key definition implies clustering. Cached index pages, repeated data blocks and storage hardware can change actual costs. These estimates are not measured runtimes. Source: Lecture5a pp.4–10.

## Handle Ranges and Boolean Conditions Completely

For a clustered lower range, seek to the first qualifying key then read the following blocks sequentially. For a prefix range ending at an upper bound, a scan from the start may avoid unnecessary index seeks. An unclustered range can fetch many scattered blocks, so compare against a full scan.

For an AND, one selective indexed condition may generate candidates; test the remaining conditions on every candidate. A suitable composite index is another possibility. For an OR, union the candidate pointers from every disjunct and remove duplicate pointers before retrieval. If any branch lacks a complete access path, its matches still need finding, often by scanning. Lecture5a p.13 loosely says some indexes may be available; using only indexed branches would silently lose valid OR results. Negation requires the complement relative to the relation, not simply returning the positive matches. Source: Lecture5a pp.11–14; the completeness qualification is local reasoning about the stated predicate.

## Project Columns and Remove Duplicates

Relational projection drops unwanted attributes and eliminates duplicate resulting tuples. Sorting the projected tuples makes duplicates adjacent; hashing sends equal tuples to the same group. SQL SELECT without DISTINCT may preserve duplicates, so do not transfer set-algebra semantics automatically to SQL. An index orders references logically; following a secondary index is not equivalent to physically sorting the data and may cause an I/O per tuple. Source: Lecture5a pp.15–16; algebra/SQL distinction retained from Unit 05.

## Create Runs Before Merging

For b blocks and M memory frames, read up to M blocks, sort them in memory and write each sorted run. Initially there are $N=\lceil b/M\rceil$ runs. A merge reserves input buffers for participating runs and an output buffer. With one frame per buffer, merge at most M−1 runs; with b_b frames per buffer, fan-in is $F=\lfloor M/b_b\rfloor-1$. Require F≥2 before using logarithmic multipass formulas. More buffering improves sequential I/O but reduces fan-in and may add a pass. Source: Lecture5a pp.17–21.

For the supplied b=12, M=3 example, runs shrink 4→2→1 in two merge passes. The initial groups of three are sorted separately, then paired and finally merged. The repeated key a has payloads 19 and 14: the figure sorts by key, with equal-key ordering not specified as a stable-sort requirement. Source: Lecture5a p.20; Lab4 Q3 p.5.

## Count Transfers and Seeks With One Output Convention

For b>M and $P=\lceil\log_F\lceil b/M\rceil\rceil$, the source omits the final output write:

$$B=b(2P+1),\qquad S=2\lceil b/M\rceil+\lceil b/b_b\rceil(2P-1).$$

Initial run generation reads and writes 2b blocks; each intermediate merge reads and writes 2b; the final merge reads b. If the final sorted file must be stored, add b writes and $\lceil b/b_b\rceil$ seeks. For b=12, M=3, b_b=1, P=2 gives 60 transfers and 44 seeks when streamed; storing the final file gives 72 and 56. An in-memory input is a separate case; do not apply a negative-pass term mechanically. Source: Lecture5a pp.21–22.

## Return to the Access-Path Decision

For the opening example, scan: $400(0.1)+1(4)=44$ ms. Unclustered index: $104(0.1+4)=426.4$ ms. A clustered lookup retrieving eight consecutive blocks would instead cost $12(0.1)+5(4)=21.2$ ms. The final comparison requires selectivity, locality, available ordering, memory and a consistent output policy. These are supplementary examples with stated parameters, not new measured results.

Lecture5a pp.1–2 introduce scope; pp.3–16 cover selection/projection; pp.17–22 cover sorting and its example; p.23 recommends reading, which is not imported here. No new assessment corpus, exam probabilities or official marks are inferred.

# Recall and Practice

Source-based practice with local worked reasoning, not an official marking scheme. Original source tasks are identified individually. No database execution or student mastery is claimed.

## Atomic recall

### Card 01 — Why can fewer transfers still mean a slower plan?

> [!success]- Answer
> Seek time may dominate: compare B×tT+S×tS using the same time unit.
>
> Source: Lecture5a pp.6–10.

### Card 02 — What enables binary search on a file?

> [!success]- Answer
> Physical ordering on the selection attribute, not merely the existence of some index.
>
> Source: Lecture5a p.6.

### Card 03 — What changes between clustered and unclustered equality retrieval?

> [!success]- Answer
> Clustered matches occupy consecutive blocks; scattered matches can require an I/O and seek for each record.
>
> Source: Lecture5a pp.8–10.

### Card 04 — What must an OR access plan cover?

> [!success]- Answer
> Every disjunct, including unindexed branches, and duplicate candidate pointers must not cause duplicate set results.
>
> Source: Lecture5a p.13, local completeness clarification.

### Card 05 — Why can projection be expensive?

> [!success]- Answer
> Removing duplicate projected tuples requires grouping, often by sorting or hashing.
>
> Source: Lecture5a p.15.

### Card 06 — How many initial runs and which merge fan-in?

> [!success]- Answer
> $N=\lceil b/M\rceil$ and $F=\lfloor M/b_b\rfloor-1$, with F at least two for multipass merging.
>
> Source: Lecture5a pp.17–21.

### Card 07 — What does the external-sort cost formula omit?

> [!success]- Answer
> The final sorted-output write; add it when a persistent sorted file is required.
>
> Source: Lecture5a p.21.

## Worked practice

### Problem 1 — Choose between locality assumptions

SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE. Compare full scan, clustered index and unclustered index for b_r=400, h=4, b=8, k=100, tT=0.1 ms, tS=4 ms. Source: Lecture5a pp.5,8,10.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Keep B and S separate until the final multiplication.

> [!success]- Solution
> Scan: B=400,S=1,T=44 ms. Clustered: B=12,S=5,T=21.2 ms. Unclustered pessimistic: B=S=104,T=426.4 ms. Under these assumptions the clustered path wins; the unclustered path loses despite fewer transfers than scanning.

### Problem 2 — Trace the supplied external sort

SOURCE EXERCISE. b=12, M=3, b_b=1. Give run counts, merge passes and total transfers/seeks with and without final output writing. Source: Lecture5a p.22; Lab4 Q3 p.5.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Initial runs are ceil(12/3)=4 and each merge combines two.

> [!success]- Solution
> Four initial runs merge 4→2→1, so P=2. Streamed transfers:24+24+12=60. Seeks:2×4+12×(2×2−1)=44. Materialised output adds 12 transfers and 12 seeks, giving72/56. Equal-key payload order is not a required stable-sort property.

### Problem 3 — Audit an incomplete OR plan

SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE. For A=1 OR B=2, only A is indexed. Is returning the A index matches complete? Source: Lecture5a p.13.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Consider a tuple satisfying only B=2.

> [!success]- Solution
> No. Such a tuple is a valid result but absent from the A candidate set. Scan for the uncovered branch or scan the whole relation, then combine completely and eliminate duplicate pointers. Existing indexes do not remove predicate-completeness obligations.

# Join, Aggregation and Set Evaluation

## In 60 Seconds

The smaller relation is not always the cheapest outer input, and the fewest transferred blocks do not always yield the shortest time. In Lecture5b's example, indexed nested loops uses 25,100 transfers but also 25,100 seeks; block nested loops uses 40,100 transfers and only 200 seeks. At 0.1 ms per transfer and 4 ms per seek, the estimated times are 102,910 ms and 4,810 ms. This local arithmetic explains the source's comparison without claiming a database benchmark.

Source: Lecture5b, 25 pages, verified against the 12 October acquisition manifest. Keep this physical evaluation unit separate from later query optimisation, whose current Week 6 files have not yet been acquired. Prerequisites: selection costs and external sorting in Unit 07, join semantics in Unit 05.

## Define the Result Before Choosing the Algorithm

A natural join matches all shared attribute names and returns one copy of those shared columns. It is not a Cartesian product without conditions, nor a join on a guessed single attribute when several names are shared. The physical strategy must preserve the same result. Source: Lecture5b pp.3–4.

The lecture uses customer:10,000 records/400 blocks and depositor:5,000 records/100 blocks. Lab4 instead uses much larger relations. Do not carry the lecture's cardinalities into the tutorial. Default lecture estimates are pessimistic unless memory availability says otherwise. Source: Lecture5b pp.5–8; Lab4 p.2.

## Compare Tuple and Block Nested Loops

For outer r, inner s, and little memory, tuple nested loops transfers $B=b_r+n_r b_s$ with $S=b_r+n_r$ seeks. Each outer tuple triggers another inner scan. The two source orientations give depositor outer:2,000,100 transfers/5,100 seeks; customer outer:1,000,400/10,400. Their time ordering depends on the transfer/seek weights.

Block nested loops reuses each outer block for every tuple pair with an inner block. The source's one-outer-block model costs $B=b_r+b_r b_s$, $S=2b_r$. Depositor outer costs40,100/200; customer outer40,400/800. These are the source model, not a formula for an arbitrary multi-block outer buffer. If the smaller relation fits completely as the retained inner input, the source simplifies to $b_r+b_s$ transfers and2 seeks. Source: Lecture5b pp.6–10.

## Probe the Inner Index Without Hiding Retrieval Cost

Indexed nested loops applies to equality/natural joins when the inner join attribute has a suitable index. For each outer tuple, probe the index and fetch all matching inner records. With one matching key record and h index accesses, $B=b_r+n_r(h+1)$ and the deck uses the same count for seeks. In its depositor/customer example, h=4 yields25,100/25,100.

For a non-key clustered lookup, transfer and seek costs differ: per probe, h+b transfers but h+1 seeks, where b is matching data blocks. Estimate b from supplied statistics or state the assumption; “one lookup” does not mean “one block”. Real caching and repeated keys can reduce actual work; do not silently add that benefit to the cold source model. Source: Lecture5b pp.11–13; Lecture5a pp.7–10.

## Merge Sorted Inputs and Account for Sorting

Sort both inputs on the join attributes if necessary, then advance pointers, retaining matching equal-key groups. The stated merge scan costs $b_r+b_s$ transfers and $\lceil b_r/b_b\rceil+\lceil b_s/b_b\rceil$ seeks, assuming each equal-key group fits in memory. Duplicate keys require producing every matching pair. The source's one-pass scan estimate can fail when groups do not fit.

Keep output conventions explicit: materialising sorted files adds their final writes before a later join reads them. If final merges stream directly into the join, do not charge an additional full input scan for the same reads. Buffer feasibility still has to hold for both inputs. Source: Lecture5b pp.14–16; Lecture5a p.21. The accounting clarification prevents incompatible formulas being combined.

## Partition With One Hash and Probe With Another

Partition both relations using the same hash of join attributes so equal keys land in corresponding partitions. Keep the smaller build partition in memory, build a hash table using a different hash function, then scan the corresponding probe partition and emit all actual key matches. A hash collision alone is not equality. Cross-partition comparisons are unnecessary; the probe partition need not fit entirely in memory. The source handles equality/natural joins, not arbitrary inequalities. Source: Lecture5b pp.17–20.

Choose enough partitions for build partitions to fit; allow room for skew, buffers and the in-memory table. A fudge factor is a planning allowance, not a proof that every partition fits. A one-pass partition stage with n_h output buffers of b_b blocks plus an input buffer of b_b blocks requires at least $(n_h+1)b_b$ frames. This direct buffer count is needed when using the tutorial's assumptions.

## Read the Hash-Join Cost as a Conditional Model

The supplied estimate is $B=3(b_r+b_s)+4n_h$ and $S=2(\lceil b_r/b_b\rceil+\lceil b_s/b_b\rceil)+2n_h$. The correction budgets writing and rereading partially filled partition blocks. For b_r=400,b_s=100,n_h=5,b_b=3, B=1,520 and S=346. The simple three-times base counts partition-read, partition-write and join-read; output-result writing is omitted. If the whole build fits and partitioning is unnecessary, the deck gives one scan of both inputs and2 seeks. Source: Lecture5b pp.21–22.

The lecture's example assigns a20-block build partition to20 memory blocks; an implementation also needs buffers and hash-table overhead. Treat its arithmetic as an idealised cost model, not proof that all allocations fit simultaneously. Skew or recursive partitioning changes the cost.

## Aggregate and Implement Set Operations

Sorting or hashing groups equal keys for COUNT,MIN,MAX,SUM and AVG. Partial AVG must retain both sum and count: an unweighted average of group averages is generally wrong. For set union, keep distinct tuples from either side; for intersection, keep tuples present in both; for r−s, remove s tuples from the r set. Corresponding hash partitions must use a compatible first hash and then check actual tuple equality. Preserve the distinction between set semantics and SQL bag variants such as UNION ALL. Source: Lecture5b pp.23–24; SQL distinction retained from Unit 05.

## Return to the Weighted Comparison

The opening indexed join costs $25100(0.1+4)=102910$ ms. Block nested loops costs $40100(0.1)+200(4)=4810$ ms. Hash join costs $1520(0.1)+346(4)=1536$ ms under the source's idealised assumptions. These are conditional estimates; include sorting, partition overflows, output policy and actual statistics before choosing a plan. The required question is “cheapest under which model?”, not “which algorithm is always best?”.

# Query Plans, Materialisation and Pipelining

## In 60 Seconds

**Synthetic opening case.** Two operators form a legal plan. The producer costs 500 block transfers and produces a 40-block intermediate relation. The consumer costs 200 transfers, including reading those 40 blocks. Their formulas exclude output writes. Can you compare a materialised boundary with a permitted pipeline without counting a read twice?

Your goal is to identify the algorithm, the boundary between operators and the cost convention before adding numbers. Prerequisites: Unit 05 relational algebra and Units 06–08 physical evaluation. This lesson covers Lecture6a PDF pp.3–12, with identity/outcomes on pp.1–2. Algebraic rewrite rules on pp.13–29, Lecture6b and Lab5 remain separate pending teaching work. No database timing or official assessment result is claimed.

## Separate a Logical Expression From Its Evaluation Plan

A relational expression specifies the required result. An evaluation plan also chooses an algorithm for each operation and coordinates their execution. The same logical expression can therefore have different physical plans. For example, a selection result may be stored before its parent consumes it, or passed directly along a legal pipeline. Equivalent results do not imply identical disk work. Source: Lecture6a pp.3–4,9,11–12.

For each edge in the expression tree, ask: what does the child produce, what does the parent require, and must the intermediate result be stored? Do not assume that changing an edge permits changing predicates or discarding tuples.

## Store an Intermediate Result or Pass Tuples On

**Materialisation** completes an intermediate operation, writes its result as a temporary relation, then lets a later operation consume it. In the lecture's example, selection feeds a join and the join feeds projection. Materialisation is generally applicable in the supplied evaluation model, but temporary storage adds work. **Pipelining** lets a parent consume tuples while its child is producing them, avoiding a temporary disk relation where permitted. Source: Lecture6a pp.4–7.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Selection] -->|materialised boundary| T[Temporary disk relation]
  T --> B[Parent operator]
  C[Selection] -->|permitted pipeline| D[Parent operator]
```

**Figure 1 — Alternative boundaries, not different query results.** Read it from left to right: the upper path stores an intermediate relation; the lower path passes tuples to its consumer. Key takeaway: removing a temporary file requires a legal execution arrangement. This teaching diagram abstracts the source tree on PDF p.5; it is not an extra official exercise.

## Count Writes Without Counting Reads Twice

The lecture's operator formulas omit output writes. For materialised evaluation, add the intermediate writes to the sum of operator costs; the consuming operator's cost may already include the corresponding reads. Final query-output writes remain excluded unless explicitly requested. Source: Lecture6a p.6, with the streaming contrast on p.7.

Return to the opening case. First identify the ledger:

| Item | Materialised | Pipelined |
|---|---:|---:|
| Producer work | 500 | 500 |
| Consumer work other than the intermediate read | 160 | 160 |
| Read intermediate relation from disk | 40 | 0 |
| Write intermediate relation to disk | 40 | 0 |
| Total block transfers | 740 | 660 |

Materialised cost is $500+200+40=740$. The 200 already contains the 40-block read: adding another 40 for reading would incorrectly give 780. Under the synthetic assumption that all other work is unchanged and streaming is legal, pipelined cost is $500+(200-40)=660$. The saving is 80 transfers, one intermediate write and one intermediate read. These are transfer counts, not milliseconds; seeks and CPU are not modelled. If the two algorithms change, recompute their costs instead of mechanically subtracting 80.

## Explain Push, Pull and Blocking Phases

A **producer-driven (push)** pipeline sends tuples to the parent through a buffer. When that buffer is full, the child waits for space. A **demand-driven (pull)** pipeline starts with a request for the next output tuple; each operator requests tuples from its children as needed and retains state between requests. A pipeline therefore does not mean that no memory or state is needed. Source: Lecture6a p.8.

Pipelining is not possible across every phase. External sorting may need preliminary processing of the whole input; a hash join has a preliminary build phase. This prevents a claim that every operator can immediately stream its final result from its first input tuple. It does not establish that every phase of every such algorithm must always materialise its output. Source: Lecture6a p.7; the phase distinction is a local clarification of that stated limitation.

## Apply the Course Convention Before Comparing Plans

Lecture6a p.10 gives a specific convention: an edge labelled pipeline permits pipelining; an unlabelled edge is assumed not to permit it. For joins, unless explicitly stated otherwise, the source singles out the nested-loop family for its pipelining treatment. Preserve these annotations in course exercises rather than replacing them with assumptions about an arbitrary DBMS. This is a course modelling rule, not a universal statement that all other join implementations can never pipeline.

Use this method: identify the logical result; choose the stated operator algorithms; inspect every boundary; separate intermediate reads and writes; calculate costs in one unit; then check which cost components and final-output policy are excluded. A cost-based optimiser chooses using estimates, so the estimated winner is not guaranteed to be the fastest measured execution. Source: Lecture6a pp.9–12. The opening example establishes a conditional 80-transfer saving, not an unconditional claim that pipelining is always faster.

## Worked practice

### Problem 1 — Audit the transfer ledger

SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE. A producer costs 300 transfers. Its intermediate result occupies 25 blocks. The consumer costs 90 transfers including reading those 25 blocks. Both formulas omit output writes. Compute materialised and legal pipelined costs, assuming all other work is unchanged. Exclude final-output writes. Source model: Lecture6a pp.6–7.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Split the consumer's 90 into its intermediate read and its remaining work.

> [!success]- Solution
> The consumer's other work is 90−25=65 transfers. Materialisation costs 300+65+25+25=415 transfers: producer, other consumer work, intermediate read and intermediate write. The pipeline costs 300+65=365 transfers. It saves 50 transfers. Do not add the intermediate read again to 300+90: that sum already includes it. If pipelining is forbidden or changes the algorithms, the 365 comparison does not apply.

### Problem 2 — Diagnose a full push buffer

SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE. A producer has a tuple ready, but the inter-operator buffer is full. A student proposes discarding an old tuple to keep the producer running. Is this a valid execution of the same query? Contrast push and pull control. Source: Lecture6a p.8.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Separate who initiates production from the obligation to preserve required tuples.

> [!success]- Solution
> No. Dropping a required tuple changes the result. In the described push model, the producer waits until the consumer removes tuples and space becomes available. In the pull model, requests propagate from parent to child as outputs are needed; operators retain their position between requests. Neither approach licenses discarding valid results. Waiting is flow control, not evidence that no pipeline exists.

### Problem 3 — Challenge an unjustified streaming claim

SUPPLEMENTARY PRACTICE. An exercise shows an unlabelled edge from a hash join to its parent. A student says, “Pipelining always saves disk I/O, so I will remove the intermediate write.” What must be checked before accepting that calculation? Source: Lecture6a pp.7,10.

> [!tip]- Hint
> Check both the exercise annotation and the algorithm's phases.

> [!success]- Solution
> Under the lecture's convention, an unlabelled edge does not permit assuming a pipeline. The hash join also has preliminary processing, so streaming capability cannot be inferred from the operation name alone. Retain the materialised boundary unless the exercise explicitly permits another strategy. If permission is supplied, identify which phases stream and whether the parent can consume them, then recompute the ledger. This is not a universal prohibition on all pipelined hash-join implementations.

cards.question: What is the blocking factor for unspanned fixed records?
cards.answer: $\lfloor\text{block size}/\text{record size}\rfloor$: the number of complete records that fit in one block.

cards.question: Why is the final block count rounded upward?
cards.answer: Any remaining record needs a real block even when that block is not full.

cards.question: What makes an index primary in this course?
cards.answer: Its search-key order matches the physical sequential order of the data file.

cards.question: What does a dense index represent, and how are duplicate search-key values handled?
cards.answer: Every search-key value in the data file has an index entry. Duplicate values must lead to all their matching records, for example via a run or pointer list. One entry per record is a particular layout, not the only dense layout.

cards.question: What invariant makes a sparse primary index usable?
cards.answer: Ordered data lets a representative entry select the block/range containing the target.

cards.question: What is an index entry's basic size here?
cards.answer: Search-key bytes plus pointer bytes, unless the source explicitly supplies additional overhead.

cards.question: What are the HDD read-time phases?
cards.answer: Seek time, rotational waiting and transfer time.

cards.question: Why can one page fetch serve several rows?
cards.answer: Several rows may share the fetched page, which remains available while buffered.

cards.question: One 300-byte student and its five 200-byte module records must stay together. What group size must the block-capacity calculation use, and why?
cards.answer: One 300-byte student record together with its five 200-byte module records: a 1300-byte group.

cards.question: Why does a small index not prove a cheap query?
cards.answer: Qualifying records may still occupy many scattered data pages; cache and clustering are unspecified.

cards.question: What does B+ tree order mean in this course?
cards.answer: The maximum number of child pointers in an internal node.

cards.question: How many keys can an order-$n$ leaf hold at most?
cards.answer: $n-1$ search-key entries.

cards.question: In a B+ tree lookup, where is key membership confirmed?
cards.answer: At the reached leaf, not at an internal separator.

cards.question: In this course’s B+ tree convention, which child range is chosen when the search key equals a separator?
cards.answer: Route to the right-hand range beginning at that separator.

cards.question: After splitting a B+ tree leaf, which key is copied into the parent?
cards.answer: The first key of the new right leaf is copied into the parent.

cards.question: After splitting a B+ tree internal node, which separator is promoted?
cards.answer: The middle separator moves to the parent and is removed from the split children.

cards.question: What repair preference does the lecture use after underflow?
cards.answer: Merge first when an eligible sibling combination fits; otherwise redistribute.

cards.question: When does deletion reduce the height of a B+ tree?
cards.answer: When an internal root is left with one child and that child replaces it.

cards.question: Why are leaves linked?
cards.answer: To continue ordered range scans without returning to the root for each next key.

cards.question: What must every root-to-leaf path share?
cards.answer: The same depth; this is the tree's height-balance invariant.

cards.question: What does a hash function return for lookup?
cards.answer: A candidate bucket address; actual keys must still be compared.

cards.question: What handles a full static bucket?
cards.answer: One or more linked overflow pages under the source model.

cards.question: In this course’s extendable hashing, what does global depth measure?
cards.answer: The number of high-order hash bits currently read by the directory.

cards.question: What does a bucket’s local depth measure in extendable hashing?
cards.answer: The number of prefix bits that distinguish one physical bucket.

cards.question: How many directory entries exist at global depth $i$?
cards.answer: $2^i$ pointer entries.

cards.question: At global depth $i$, how many directory entries point to one bucket of local depth $i_j$?
cards.answer: $2^{i-i_j}$ directory pointers.

cards.question: When can a full extendable-hash bucket split without doubling the directory?
cards.answer: When its local depth is less than the global depth.

cards.question: Why preserve leading zeros?
cards.answer: High-order prefix routing depends on the fixed-width bit positions.

cards.question: When can buddy buckets coalesce?
cards.answer: Equal local depth, correct buddy prefixes, and combined entries fitting one bucket.

cards.question: Why is hashing poor for ordered range scans?
cards.answer: Bucket addresses do not preserve adjacent search-key order.

cards.question: What does an LSM tree batch?
cards.answer: Ordered updates, merging memory batches into larger sorted disk levels.

cards.question: What must an LSM lookup reconcile?
cards.answer: Relevant versions and tombstones across every searched level.

cards.question: What does a buffer-tree internal buffer hold?
cards.answer: Pending updates waiting to be partitioned and pushed toward child ranges.

cards.question: What record-position invariant must hold before combining two bitmap indexes?
cards.answer: The same record-position order.

cards.question: If any queried Bloom-filter bit is zero, what can you conclude under the standard insertion-only model?
cards.answer: The queried element is definitely absent under the filter model.

cards.question: If all queried Bloom-filter bits are one, what can you conclude and what must happen next?
cards.answer: Only possible membership; the real structure must verify it.

cards.question: How does a k-d tree divide space?
cards.answer: By recursive coordinate splits, typically alternating dimensions.

cards.question: How does a quadtree divide two-dimensional space?
cards.answer: Recursively into four equal spatial quadrants.

cards.question: What does an R-tree internal entry bound?
cards.answer: A minimum bounding rectangle covering objects or child regions.

cards.question: Why can temporal endpoint assumptions change an answer?
cards.answer: A version at the boundary may be included or excluded depending on interval convention.
cards.source: Source: Lecture3b, PDF pp. 21–22; endpoint rule unconfirmed.

cards.question: What does selection change?
cards.answer: Selection keeps tuples satisfying a predicate; it preserves the attribute schema.
cards.source: Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF pp. 10–11.

cards.question: What does projection change?
cards.answer: Projection keeps named attributes. In set relational algebra identical result tuples collapse to one.
cards.source: Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF pp. 12–13.

cards.question: What is union compatibility?
cards.answer: Equal arity and compatible corresponding attribute domains; align names/order before a set operation.
cards.source: Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF pp. 14–18.

cards.question: Is difference commutative?
cards.answer: No. r−s keeps tuples in r absent from s; s−r asks the opposite question.
cards.source: Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF pp. 16–17.

cards.question: How large is a Cartesian product?
cards.answer: Every left tuple pairs with every right tuple: |r×s|=|r|·|s|. Rename ambiguous attribute names.
cards.source: Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF pp. 19–22.

cards.question: What does natural join match?
cards.answer: Equality of all attributes with common names, then one copy of each common attribute remains.
cards.source: Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF pp. 26–29.

cards.question: Why rename a relation?
cards.answer: To name an intermediate result or distinguish copies of the same relation and their attributes.
cards.source: Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF p. 22.

cards.question: For relations r(X,Y) and s(Y), what does division r ÷ s return, and where do candidate X values come from?
cards.answer: Return X tuples from πX(r) that occur in r paired with every Y tuple in s. Extra Y pairings are allowed; if s is empty, every candidate in πX(r) qualifies.
cards.source: Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF pp. 30–34.

cards.question: For r(X,Y) and s(Y), how does candidates minus failures implement division?
cards.answer: Start T=πX(r). Missing pairs are (T×s)−r. Project their X values and subtract those failed candidates from T.
cards.source: Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF p. 34.

cards.question: How can difference find a maximum?
cards.answer: Rename a second copy, find values smaller than some other value, and subtract those nonmaximum values from all values. Ties remain.
cards.source: Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF p. 25.

cards.question: How do borrower and depositor answer both versus either?
cards.answer: Intersect projected customer names for both; union them for either.
cards.source: Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF pp. 14–18, 36.

cards.question: Does algebra projection equal ordinary SQL SELECT?
cards.answer: Not necessarily: this lecture uses sets; SQL without DISTINCT can preserve duplicates and has additional NULL behavior.
cards.source: Source: Lecture4a - Review of Relational Algebra.pdf, PDF pp. 12–13; set-semantics qualification.

cards.question: What are the three query-processing stages, and which stage runs the chosen plan?
cards.answer: Parsing/translation, optimization, and evaluation. Evaluation executes the chosen plan.
cards.source: Source: Lecture4b - Query Evaluation Basics.pdf, PDF pp. 2–3.

cards.question: Does equivalent algebra imply equal cost?
cards.answer: No. Equivalent results can be computed by different algorithms and access paths with different costs.
cards.source: Source: Lecture4b - Query Evaluation Basics.pdf, PDF pp. 4–7.

cards.question: What does a query plan add?
cards.answer: Concrete algorithms and evaluation choices for algebra operations.
cards.source: Source: Lecture4b - Query Evaluation Basics.pdf, PDF pp. 4–6.

cards.question: What information helps cost estimates?
cards.answer: Catalog statistics such as relation size, tuple size and distinct values; estimates may differ from measured execution.
cards.source: Source: Lecture4b - Query Evaluation Basics.pdf, PDF p. 7.

cards.question: State the lecture’s estimated disk-time formula and define its counts and time units.
cards.answer: b·tT+s·tS, where b counts transferred blocks and s counts seeks; both time parameters must use compatible units.
cards.source: Source: Lecture4b - Query Evaluation Basics.pdf, PDF p. 11.

cards.question: Why can fewer transferred blocks still be slower?
cards.answer: A plan may save transfers while adding expensive seeks. Compare both terms.
cards.source: Source: Lecture4b - Query Evaluation Basics.pdf, PDF pp. 10–11.

cards.question: What is omitted from the simplified comparison?
cards.answer: The lecture focuses on disk access and typically ignores CPU and network in the model. Real elapsed time has additional factors.
cards.source: Source: Lecture4b - Query Evaluation Basics.pdf, PDF pp. 8–10.

cards.question: What is 1 millisecond in microseconds?
cards.answer: 1000 microseconds. Convert units before adding time terms.
cards.source: Source: Lecture4b - Query Evaluation Basics.pdf, PDF p. 11; unit conversion.

cards.question: What does JDBC stand for?
cards.answer: Java Database Connectivity.

cards.question: Which driver class does the source use?
cards.answer: `com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver`.

cards.question: Which method executes a query returning rows?
cards.answer: `executeQuery`, returning a `ResultSet`.
cards.source: Source: Lab2, PDF pp. 20–22; supplied Java.

cards.question: Which method is suitable for `CREATE INDEX`?
cards.answer: `executeUpdate`, because the statement changes schema state rather than returning query rows.

cards.question: What does `ResultSet.next()` do?
cards.answer: Advances the cursor to the next row and reports whether one exists.

cards.question: What proves index selection?
cards.answer: An observed execution plan or equivalent server evidence, not index creation alone.

cards.question: What proves a speedup?
cards.answer: Controlled measurements under comparable data, cache, server and timing conditions.

cards.question: What exact Java call does released Lab 02 Task 2 ask you to time?
cards.answer: The newer task sheet releases timing only rs = stmt.executeQuery(sql); before and after indexing. See the Released Query Timing segment.
cards.source: Source: Lab2-JDBCandIndex-tasks.pdf, PDF p. 3 (supersedes original Lab2 p. 2 release placeholder).

cards.question: What disagreement between the two JDBC setup documents needs confirmation?
cards.answer: The privilege handout requires manual database creation, while Lab2 says provisioning is automatic.
cards.source: Source: privilege PDF p. 2; Lab2 p. 7.

cards.question: Does the static count of 614 parsed source records establish the number returned by MySQL for num=7?
cards.answer: No. It is a static count from parsing supplied SQL, not an observed SELECT result. The recorded local run returned 607 rows for num=7; that historical count is also environment-specific, not a promised result for a future import.

cards.question: Which operation does released Task 2 time?
cards.answer: Only rs = stmt.executeQuery(sql); with timestamps immediately before and after that call.
cards.source: Source: Lab2-JDBCandIndex-tasks.pdf and Labs/Lab 02 - JDBC and Index/03 Lab.md, Task sheet PDF p. 3.

cards.question: Where must the result-iteration loop be placed, and does that exclude all row transfer from executeQuery timing?
cards.answer: Place the application’s ResultSet.next() loop and printing after the ending timestamp. The driver may already retrieve and buffer rows inside executeQuery, so this does not exclude all data transfer from the measured call.
cards.source: Source: Lab2-JDBCandIndex-tasks.pdf and Labs/Lab 02 - JDBC and Index/03 Lab.md, Task sheet PDF p. 3; lab reference Task 2.

cards.question: How are nanoseconds converted to milliseconds?
cards.answer: Subtract nanoTime timestamps and divide by 1_000_000.0.
cards.source: Source: Lab2-JDBCandIndex-tasks.pdf and Labs/Lab 02 - JDBC and Index/03 Lab.md, Task sheet PDF p. 3; lab reference timing code.

cards.question: Which query stays constant?
cards.answer: SELECT * FROM Orf_Motif WHERE num=7, for both index states.
cards.source: Source: Lab2-JDBCandIndex-tasks.pdf and Labs/Lab 02 - JDBC and Index/03 Lab.md, Task sheet PDF p. 3.

cards.question: Why compare multisets rather than row order?
cards.answer: Without ORDER BY row order is not guaranteed; repeated keys/rows still require counts, so plain set equality can hide duplicates.
cards.source: Source: Lab2-JDBCandIndex-tasks.pdf and Labs/Lab 02 - JDBC and Index/03 Lab.md, Lab reference Task 2 validation.

cards.question: Do historical faster timings prove indexing always wins?
cards.answer: No. The recorded local result is a single environment observation with its own plan/data/cache/driver boundary.
cards.source: Source: Lab2-JDBCandIndex-tasks.pdf and Labs/Lab 02 - JDBC and Index/03 Lab.md, Lab reference Task 2 results and limitations.

cards.question: Why can fewer transfers still mean a slower plan?
cards.answer: Seek time may dominate: compare B×tT+S×tS using the same time unit.

cards.question: What enables binary search on a file?
cards.answer: Physical ordering on the selection attribute, not merely the existence of some index.

cards.question: What changes between clustered and unclustered equality retrieval?
cards.answer: Clustered matches occupy consecutive blocks; scattered matches can require an I/O and seek for each record.

cards.question: What must an OR access plan cover?
cards.answer: Every disjunct, including unindexed branches, and duplicate candidate pointers must not cause duplicate set results.
cards.source: Source: Lecture5a p.13, local completeness clarification.

cards.question: Why can projection be expensive?
cards.answer: Removing duplicate projected tuples requires grouping, often by sorting or hashing.

cards.question: How many initial runs and which merge fan-in?
cards.answer: $N=\lceil b/M\rceil$ and $F=\lfloor M/b_b\rfloor-1$, with F at least two for multipass merging.

cards.question: What does the external-sort cost formula omit?
cards.answer: The final sorted-output write; add it when a persistent sorted file is required.

cards.question: What must a natural join compare?
cards.answer: Every shared attribute name, then return one copy of each shared column.

cards.question: What distinguishes tuple from block nested loops?
cards.answer: The former rescans the inner input per outer tuple; the latter reuses an outer block for all its tuple comparisons.

cards.question: Which input needs an index for indexed nested loops?
cards.answer: The inner relation needs an index on the equality join attribute.

cards.question: Why must merge-join costs include an ordering policy?
cards.answer: Unsorted inputs need sorting; final-write and reread costs depend on materialisation versus streaming.

cards.question: Must the whole probe partition fit in memory?
cards.answer: No: retain the build partition and stream the probe partition, subject to buffers and skew.

cards.question: Why is a hash collision insufficient for a join result?
cards.answer: Equal keys hash together, but different keys can collide; check actual equality before emitting.
cards.source: Source: Lecture5b pp.17–19, local correctness explanation.

cards.question: What state supports correct partial AVG?
cards.answer: Sum and count; combine their sums, then divide total sum by total count.

cards.question: What dataset belongs to Lab4 Q1?
cards.answer: Customer1,000,000 records/8,000 blocks; depositor500,000 records/1,000 blocks.

cards.question: What makes Q2 numerically underdetermined?
cards.answer: Physical ordering and per-key matching-block distribution are not fully established by the totals.

cards.question: How many merge passes sort12 blocks with3 frames?
cards.answer: Two:4 initial runs become2 then1 with fan-in2.

cards.question: Why is an in-memory sort not necessarily free in Q6?
cards.answer: The question requires sorted data written to disk, so include reading and writing those3 blocks.

cards.question: What inconsistency must Q5 report?
cards.answer: The inherited M=100 cannot hold51 buffers of20 frames each; the one-pass premise needs clarification.

cards.question: What does an evaluation plan add to a logical expression?
cards.answer: Algorithms for individual operations and a strategy for coordinating their execution.

cards.question: What does materialisation store?
cards.answer: An intermediate result as a temporary relation for later operations to consume.

cards.question: Which cost must be added to the lecture's operator sums?
cards.answer: Intermediate-result writes; check whether their reads are already included in the consuming operators.
cards.source: Source: Lecture6a p.6; local bookkeeping clarification.

cards.question: What happens when a push buffer is full?
cards.answer: The producer waits until the consumer creates space.

cards.question: What must a pull operator retain between requests?
cards.answer: State indicating where to resume when the next tuple is requested.

cards.question: What does an unlabelled plan edge mean in this lecture?
cards.answer: Pipelining is assumed unavailable on that edge under the course convention.

activities.title: Routing at a separator
activities.prompt: Under the course’s B+ tree routing convention, which subtree is searched when the key equals an internal separator?
activities.source: Unit 02 tutor and Lecture2b B+ tree lookup

options.label: Right subtree
options.feedback: Equality routes into the right-hand range. Continue to the leaf to decide membership: a retained separator need not be a current leaf key.

options.label: Left subtree
options.feedback: The left range stops below the separator. Equality routes right; checking an internal key alone does not establish membership.

options.label: Stop at the separator and report a match.
options.feedback: Internal separators route searches. Only the leaf confirms membership; retained boundaries need not still be leaf keys.

activities.title: Hash versus range
activities.prompt: Why is an ordinary hash index a poor fit for a sorted range scan?

options.label: Hashing cannot find exact matches
options.feedback: Hashing supports equality access but does not place neighboring keys in sorted order. A B+ tree supports ordered traversal.

options.label: Hash bucket order does not preserve key order
options.feedback: Hashing supports equality access but does not place neighboring keys in sorted order. A B+ tree supports ordered traversal.

options.label: Hash collisions imply that range results are incorrect.
options.feedback: Collision handling preserves lookup correctness. The problem for ranges is lack of key order, so a range can require visiting many buckets.

activities.title: Bitmap conjunction
activities.source: Lecture3b and Unit 04 bitmap worked example

options.feedback: AND retains a 1 only where both operands have 1. The matching positions are the first and fourth.
AND retains a 1 only where both operands have 1. The matching positions are the first and fourth.
01000 marks where the operands differ. AND keeps only positions where both bits are 1: 10010.

activities.title: Projection and duplicates

options.label: Two output rows: (500), (500)
options.feedback: The set projection removes duplicate result tuples. SQL SELECT without DISTINCT may preserve duplicates.

options.label: One output tuple: (500)
options.feedback: The set projection removes duplicate result tuples. SQL SELECT without DISTINCT may preserve duplicates.

options.label: The projection is invalid because two balances are equal.
options.feedback: Equal projected values are valid. Set projection removes duplicate tuples, leaving one 500.

options.label: A faster single execution, without examining its plan.
options.feedback: A timing difference alone does not identify an access path; caching and other conditions can change time. Inspect the plan.

options.feedback: Take nanoTime immediately before and after executeQuery. Iteration and printing stay outside; driver buffering within the call can still affect the result.
